Interactive browser viewers (Rover, Blast Radius) exist, but the well-known ones are unmaintained (Rover's last release was 2022), so check that a tool is current before relying on it. (See tf-cmd-graph.)

📌 Global provider plugin cache

A shared global provider plugin cache (TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR / plugin_cache_dir) avoids re-downloading providers per project. It historically wasn't safe for concurrent inits; OpenTofu 1.10 added filesystem cache locking (flock/LockFileEx) so parallel CI jobs can share one cache without corruption. (See opentofu-feature-history.)

📌 Provider mirrors for air-gapped setups

For air-gapped or locked-down environments, the CLI config's provider_installation block configures filesystem_mirror (serve providers from a local directory) and network_mirror (serve from an internal HTTPS mirror) instead of the public registry. Populate a mirror with terraform providers mirror DIR. (HCDocs CLI config)

📌 Checkpoint telemetry opt-out

The CLI phones home to HashiCorp's Checkpoint service for version + security-bulletin checks (this drives the "newer version available" line in terraform version). Only anonymous data is sent. Disable it in airgapped/privacy-sensitive setups: CHECKPOINT_DISABLE=1 (env, all HashiCorp tools) or CLI-config disable_checkpoint = true (all calls) / disable_checkpoint_signature = true (keep bulletin checks, drop the anonymous signature). (See tf-cli-commands.)

📌 experiments — not for production

The terraform {} block's experiments = [...] argument opts a module into pre-release language features for feedback (e.g. optional object attrs before 1.3 GA'd them). Advanced and not for production — it warns on every plan/apply and can break in minor/patch releases. (HCDocs terraform block)

📌 OpenTelemetry tracing — OpenTofu documents it, Terraform hides it

Both binaries enable an experimental OTLP trace exporter on OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=otlp, and both delegate every other knob to the standard OTEL_* variables. This path previously said "Terraform has no built-in OTel equivalent" — wrong: the hook exists in telemetry.go, it is simply undocumented (a grep of the Terraform repo's website/ for opentelemetry returns nothing). What differs is what you get back.

OpenTofu 1.10+ traces the graph walk: Validation phase / Plan phase / Apply phase, then one span per graph node (Plan resource instance changes, Apply resource instance changes, Configure provider), tagged with opentofu.resource_instance.address, opentofu.resource.type, and opentofu.provider.source. That is what makes "which resource dominates the apply" answerable.

Terraform 1.15 has ~10 span sites, all in main, checkpoint.go, and internal/command — module and provider installation, backend init. The graph walk is not traced at all, so a trace of terraform apply tells you nothing about which resource was slow. The instrumented plan/apply code lives in the Stacks runtime (internal/stacks/stackruntime, internal/rpcapi), which HCP Terraform drives over RPC rather than the CLI.

Three more differences that decide whether this is usable in CI: OpenTofu reads TRACEPARENT (1.10) so a run nests inside the pipeline's trace, and Terraform does not (hashicorp/terraform#35444, open since 2024-07-10); OpenTofu batches span export while Terraform uses a SimpleSpanProcessor that exports synchronously per span; and Terraform names its root span terraform <full command line>, so a -var="password=…" lands in the tracing backend, where OpenTofu's root span is just tofu. Sampling is fixed at 100% in both. Details and the version gating: ot-otel-tracing, otel-tracing-facts.

📌 High-cardinality perf + rpcapi (Terraform 1.13)

Terraform 1.13 made evaluation of high-cardinality count/for_each (hundreds+ of instances) much faster — relevant when a big config's graph is the bottleneck. For building tooling around Terraform, terraform rpcapi (1.13, GA) exposes core operations over a plugin RPC interface. (See feature-history.)

Read it against TID Ch11 §11.1, which says the CLI is the only way in. Source settles it — commands.go registers rpcapi under a comment saying its "whole point … is to bypass the CLI layer so wrapping automation can get as-direct-as-possible access to Terraform Core functionality", bypassing the command package entirely. Verified out of experimental as of v1.13.0 by git tag --contains. Two limits worth knowing before betting on it: it lives in HiddenCommands, so it is plumbing rather than an advertised interface, and it came out of the Stacks work rather than as a general integration API. For Go specifically there is also hashicorp/terraform-exec, HashiCorp's own CLI wrapper returning terraform-json types, which is what a Go integration should start from instead of hand-rolling one.

⚠️ OpenTofu has neither — no rpcapi package, no registration, zero occurrences in the 1.12.5 tree. So anything that must run on both engines still wraps the CLI, and that, rather than the absence of an API, is the reason the wrapper pattern is worth learning.

Milestone: You can diagnose a failing/slow apply from TF_LOG output and cut plan time on a large config via caching and parallelism tuning.

⬜ E6 — Platform engineering & self-service¶

What it is: Terraform as an internal platform — golden/opinionated modules, self-service via HCP no-code modules or an IDP (e.g. Backstage), run tasks, and org-wide drift detection.

Why you need it: The end state of Terraform maturity is letting product teams provision safely without writing raw HCL; this is the platform-engineering frontier.

How to learn it:

  1. Reference — HCDocs "No-Code modules" + Run Tasks + private registry (~1 hr) — the self-service building blocks.
  2. Video — HashiCorp "Terraform for platform engineers" (Armon Dadgar) (~45 min) — how mature orgs expose Terraform to non-experts via golden modules.
  3. Interactive — HCTut "Create and use no-code modules" (~14 min stated, budget ~1.5 hrs with AWS; HCP Standard edition) — put a golden module in the private registry and let users provision it with no HCL, straight from the HCP UI. Notes: tut-no-code-provisioning. The design rule that defines the model: a no-code workspace's entire change surface is (variable values) × (module version) — "You cannot directly apply configuration changes to existing no-code workspaces" — so anything you did not expose as a variable is fixed until the author ships a release. That makes minimizing inputs (tut-pattern-module-creation) a hard requirement rather than a style preference. It also inverts the no-provider-blocks-in-modules rule and explains why the rule existed: provider blocks are forbidden because they conflict with count/for_each/depends_on, and "Since users will not reference no-code modules in written configuration, there is no risk of this conflict." The cost is that HCP spawns a workspace per provision, so provider credentials must arrive automatically — a project-scoped variable set here, dynamic credentials in practice. Governance sits in Configure Settings → Edit versions and variable options: you pin which module version no-code deploys (pushing a tag publishes a version but does not roll it out), and you can turn a free-text variable into a dropdown of allowed values. ⚠️ Its own 1.0.1 upgrade adds a variable with no default, forcing every consuming workspace to answer a prompt — the breaking way to make an additive change, and a live counterexample to tut-module-object-attributes. Two things not to copy from its module: publicly_accessible = true on the RDS instance, and an ingress CIDR of 192.80.0.0/16 described as an internal VPN when it is public address space. Also cited from I5, which takes the author half — this is the one page documenting where the no-provider-block rule and the standard-structure rule change shape for a module nobody calls from HCL.

📌 OpenTofu — MCP server (1.10)

OpenTofu 1.10 ships an MCP server — exposes OpenTofu operations to AI agents / LLM tooling via the Model Context Protocol, an emerging building block for AI-assisted self-service IaC. OpenTofu-only. (See opentofu-feature-history.)

📌 Multi-tenant note — no-code provisioning is the one thing here a tenant can run for itself

Most platform capabilities need an organization-level grant, which is why A9 keeps pushing them back to the platform team. No-code provisioning is the exception, and it fits the project boundary cleanly. Provisioning requires Manage all projects, Manage all workspaces, or project Admin, and with custom project permissions a team needs only the ability to create workspaces, write variables and apply runs. So a tenant with admin over its own project self-serves without any org-wide permission.

Two mechanics make it work inside a tenant boundary. The provisioning flow asks which project the new workspace goes in, and "teams with access to the specified project can view the workspace automatically", so the tenant's existing team access carries over. And "if the specified project contains any project-scoped variable sets, HCP Terraform automatically applies those sets to the workspace", which is exactly how a per-tenant dynamic-credential set reaches a workspace nobody configured by hand.

Two cautions. Auto apply is the default for a no-code workspace, so self-service provisioning applies without review unless you change it. And no-code readiness is a property of a module in the organization's private registry, which has no per-team read scope, so every tenant can provision every no-code module you publish. Restricting who may provision what is a policy question (A5), not a registry one.

Milestone: You can publish a governed golden module to a private registry and let another team provision it self-service with policy enforcement.

⬜ Expert Checkpoint¶

You have mastered Terraform when you can: - Build and ship a custom provider with the Plugin Framework. - Architect large-scale, multi-team state with Stacks/Terragrunt and fast, small plans. - Choose and migrate between Terraform and OpenTofu on real technical merits, and stand up a self-service platform with governance.

Suggested study sequence¶

Beginner (B1–B9)        → ~30 hrs
    ↓
Intermediate (I1–I8)    → ~45 hrs  →  [Terraform Associate 004]
    ↓
Advanced (A1–A10)       → ~76 hrs  →  [Authoring & Operations Professional]
    ↓
Expert (E1–E6)          → ~70 hrs

2026-08-28 (eleventh) — Not a corpus audit but a single-claim sweep, prompted by an A1 readiness check, and it falsified the ninth audit's closing sentence. That entry ends “Written chapters make no version-currency claims — grepped, not assumed.” They do, and three of them did. The pattern this pass establishes: an audit that fixes a claim in the corpus it is auditing does not fix the copies living in the other corpora, and every audit so far has been scoped to one corpus. The starting defect was the one the eighth audit thought it had already fixed. action_trigger's “only four events exist … there is no destroy event” was corrected in the topic pages on 2026-08-28 and three copies survived elsewhere: the A1 callout in this file, which contradicted itself four lines after its own 1.16 bullet announced the destroy events; tf-block-resource, whose body carried a correct 🔄 Superseded box under an ungated heading, so skimming the headings returned the wrong half; and tf-meta-lifecycle, which stated it as a flat fact about the world rather than a record of its 2026-08-03 capture. Settled in source rather than from the changelog: at tag v1.16.0, internal/configs/action.go defines six trigger events and resourceLifecycleBlockSchema accepts action_trigger beside precondition and postcondition. Sweeping rc1 then found the same shape across the book, which is where it costs most. Ch 9 dated its state-encryption absence to “1.15 (nor in 1.16.0-rc1)”; Ch 11 said “as of this writing 1.16 is at rc1, so the measurement stands for every stable release”; Ch 16 said “until 1.16 is stable, the removed block is Terraform's only route”; and TID Ch 2 carried the identical “once 1.16 is stable (rc1 as of 2026-08-13)” sentence the eighth audit had corrected in the topic page. This page's own header was the worst of them, because it is line 4: it named 1.15.8 and OpenTofu 1.12.5 as current and told the reader “no v1.16.0 tag exists”. The ninth audit had established both facts and updated version-facts.md without touching the header that every reader hits first — and since both named versions carry published advisories, the header was pointing readers at vulnerable releases a day after the corpus knew better. It now carries the advisories explicitly. Every stale label was checked before being rewritten, and all four underlying claims held at GA: state_store is still experiment-gated (parser_config.go:143), language = TF2021 is still inert, parser_config.go still declares no encryption block, and destroy = false is now one of five lifecycle attributes. So this was label rot, not content rot, exactly as the ninth audit found on the reference pages — which is the argument for sweeping every copy rather than re-deriving each one. One genuine content defect, and it was also a survivor: Ch 11 called count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0 “the only way to make a single resource optional in Terraform”, the same only the eighth audit demoted to usual in the topic page. Corrected the same way, with the TUR Ch5 sentence that presupposes the alternative now quoted. A defect I introduced and the tooling caught: I first quoted that sentence with emphasis TUR does not have. check_quotes.py went from 313 passages to 314, still 0 unverified, once it was quoted faithfully — the checker only counts a passage it can match, so the gain is the verification. An absence claim I narrowed rather than defended: I first wrote that OpenTofu has “no announced plan” for actions, having checked the repository and not the issue tracker; it now claims only what was measured, that no RFC proposes one. New divergence recorded, and it is the largest open one on that page: OpenTofu has no actions feature at all. At its newest tag v1.13.0-beta1 (2026-08-27), action_trigger appears nowhere in the Go source, resourceLifecycleBlockSchema accepts only precondition and postcondition as nested blocks, parser_config.go's top-level list has no action entry, and rfc/ holds no proposal. So every provider-native escape-hatch replacement in A1 is Terraform-only, and on OpenTofu the four holes in when = destroy stay open. Recorded in Provisioners and escape hatches and Meta-arguments and lifecycle. No topic flips. Ch 11's only was a precision defect on a page whose subject is enabled, handled as the eighth audit handled its twin; everything else was a label. The rule this pass earns: fix a claim, then grep the whole corpus for it before closing. Three of the four defects here were copies of a claim someone had already corrected once. A1 stays ⬜, and its notes are complete — 21 of 21 sources captured.

2026-08-28 (tenth) — Audited the thirty research-cache notes, the corpus whose entire purpose is provenance, and the audit reduced almost entirely to one question: which dated facts have expired? These files are not arguments, they are measurements — verified on X against Y at tag Z. That makes them the most honest corpus in the notes and the most perishable. Every one of the thirty carries at least one explicit date; none had to be dug out. Mechanical layers clean: 33 admonitions, 75 tables over 658 rows, 68 fenced blocks, 62 wikilinks. The ragged-row check fired once, on feature-coverage-matrix.md, and was a third false positive of the same kind — `&&` / `||` inside a code span, which the renderer keeps whole. Three files, three false positives, one cause; the check is only ever evidence to go read the built HTML. The find worth the whole pass: a Terraform-versus-OpenTofu boundary moved in the direction nobody was watching. tf115-ot112-features said “Terraform-only — OpenTofu has no convert()”. OpenTofu shipped convert in v1.13.0-beta1 (opentofu#4449), measured directly: the function is registered in internal/lang/functions.go at that tag and absent at v1.12.6, so the flip is dated, not inferred. Every copy was swept — the fact appeared in six places across four files, including two written chapters. Ch 7's first box was already correctly scoped (“as of 1.12.4”) and its title was not; Ch 12 and the TID Ch 4 note carried bare “Terraform-only”. All now read “Terraform-only through OpenTofu 1.12”, with a dated box in Ch 7. No chapter flips to 🔄, and the reasoning is the same distinction Ch 9 and Ch 11 established last time: 1.13 is a beta, so the claim remains true of every released OpenTofu. A claim that has been outgrown gets an !!! info; only one that actively misleads gets 🔄. The same boundary had moved the other way and was already half-recorded, which is how the second defect surfaced. feature-coverage-matrix still listed destroy = false as OpenTofu-only in two places, though Terraform 1.16 shipped it — a fact the eighth and ninth audits had already fixed in the topic pages and reference maps without anyone thinking to check the coverage matrix. The same file's scope note excluded “unreleased features (TF 1.16, OT 1.13)”; both have since shipped, so that exclusion now needs re-running rather than re-reading, and it says so. Four pinned-tool notes had drifted, all within the last fortnight. terragrunt-facts stopped at v1.1.3 and v1.1.4 was tagged 2026-08-27; terrakube-facts called 2.33.0-beta.9 the current beta when 2.33.0-rc.1 landed 2026-08-27, with three betas in between; opentofu-migration-mechanics pinned tags to v1.12.5, now v1.12.6 plus the 1.13 beta; and otel-tracing-facts still described the 1.13 TRACEPARENT propagation as “unreleased as of 2026-08-15”. Each was annotated rather than rewritten — the capture date is the value, so a pin is corrected by adding a re-check, never by silently advancing the number. floci-facts's “no tag after 1.6.0” was tested the same way and holds. And a fifth near-accusation avoided, which now makes this a reliable pattern rather than a run of luck. conditional-branch-evaluation claims “OpenTofu has no typed outputs”. A grep for "type" in OpenTofu's named_values.go at v1.13.0-beta1 returns hits, which reads as a contradiction — until you check which schema: the hits are variableBlockSchema, and outputBlockSchema has no type attribute at all. The claim holds. Every one of these five has had the same shape: the search finds the word, and only reading what it belongs to settles the question. Also re-verified as still true: -exclude has no Terraform counterpart in 1.16.0's argument parsing.

2026-08-28 (ninth) — Audited the six reference pages plus version-facts.md, following the exposure the topic-page audit flagged, and it turned out to be worse and better than predicted: the stale labels were hiding a security finding, and the stale content was almost entirely fine. These pages are fact tables rather than prose, so the failure modes differ — misattributed releases, the two maps disagreeing with each other, and currency claims going quietly out of date. The last one is the dangerous one, because version-facts.md is the version ground truth every other page reads. The headline: three of the releases these pages pointed readers past carry published security advisories. The tables named Terraform 1.15.8 and OpenTofu 1.12.5 as current. Freshly fetched tags say otherwise. Terraform 1.15.9 (2026-08-19) mitigates CVE-2026-14978, a Unicode-normalisation flaw in go-slug that could stop files being excluded by .terraformignore when uploading to HCP Terraform or Terraform Enterprise (terraform#39036). OpenTofu 1.12.5 fixes an Encrypted Client Hello flaw leaking pre-shared key identities during the handshake, de-anonymising the server hostname to a passive observer. OpenTofu 1.12.6 (2026-08-19) fixes two more: credentials for one origin resent to the target of an HTTP redirect when installing from OCI registries, and CPU/memory exhaustion in tofu init resolving crafted relative URLs from an attacker-controlled registry or state backend. Current stable is now recorded as Terraform 1.16.0 and OpenTofu 1.12.6, with the advisories spelled out in a !!! danger box rather than left as a version number the reader is expected to compare. The rc1 rot itself was label-deep, and measuring that mattered more than fixing it. Rather than assume the rc1-derived content had drifted, I diffed v1.16.0-rc1 against v1.16.0 in the local checkout: the CHANGELOG delta is one added line — “test: Optional ephemeral values do not have to be set at plan time” (terraform#38974). Nothing removed, nothing reworded. So the seven 1.16-rc1 table rows, the “treat everything here as provisional” note and the “will change before GA” footnote were all wrong about their status and right about their substance. Relabelled, with the diff recorded on the page so the next reader does not have to re-derive it, and the one missing fix added. The pass also turned up a v1.16.0-rc2 these notes never recorded at all. The OpenTofu pages were internally inconsistent in a way only a cross-file sweep finds. Yesterday's OpenTofu-docs audit updated opentofu-feature-history.md to record v1.13.0-beta1 (2026-08-27) — and left the footnote 100 lines below it still saying the 1.13 entry “is from the main branch changelog and will change before GA.” One file, two answers. Meanwhile opentofu-release-feature-map.md had not been touched at all and still called 1.13 main-only across four rows. And the corpus disagreed with itself on OpenTofu's current patch: version-facts.md said 1.12.5, opentofu-feature-history.md said 1.12.4, and the truth was 1.12.6. That three-way split is the argument for auditing a corpus rather than a file. The consistency checks that passed are worth recording too, because they were the ones most likely to fail. The glossary's 27 version claims were extracted and sampled against the maps; -target / -exclude was the sharpest test, since the glossary calls -exclude OpenTofu-only (1.9+) — an absence claim about the other tool, the exact class that has broken three times this week. It holds: there is no -exclude in Terraform 1.16.0's argument parsing, and the Terraform map correspondingly never mentions it. The state_store gating claim agrees across both pages. Mechanical layers clean: 35 admonitions, 39 tables over 843 rows, 192 wikilinks, zero problems. A new ragged-row check — comparing cell counts against each table's header — fired twice on glossary.md, and both were false positives: unescaped | inside backtick code spans (echo 'expr' | terraform console, destroy = true|false), which the renderer handles correctly, confirmed by reading the built HTML rather than trusting the source heuristic. Same lesson as the fence-tag near-miss in the seventh audit: count the pairs the renderer sees, not the characters in the line. No learning-path topic flips. Written chapters make no version-currency claims — grepped, not assumed — and dated measurements stamped 1.15.8 or 1.12.4 stay exactly as written. A measurement is evidence about the version it ran on; only the tables that say current can go stale, and those are now the ones carrying re-check dates.

2026-08-28 (eighth) — Audited the thirteen topic pages, and the defect class here is one no earlier corpus produced: a page contradicting itself. A source note records what one page said on one day, so it can only be wrong about that page. A topic page is a synthesis — it holds several sources in one argument — so it has an interior, and the interior can disagree. Three of the four content defects found are exactly that: a flat declarative sentence contradicting evidence already present in the same file, sometimes a dozen lines away, sometimes two hundred. In every case the wrong half was the confident summarising line and the right half was the qualified passage beneath it, which is the same drift the book audit named and the first time it has been caught inside a single document. Mechanical layers clean: 45 admonitions, 20 tables over 122 rows, 19 fenced blocks, 352 wikilinks, zero problems — the highest wikilink density in the notes at one link every 4.5 lines, which is what a hub page is for. topics/index.md lists all twelve pages with no orphans. The one harness hit was a false positive: a nested admonition inside another admonition's body, which my indent check cannot distinguish from a callout wrongly indented into a list. The cause of three defects is datable: these pages were written while Terraform 1.16 was rc1, and 1.16.0 shipped on 2026-08-26. Meta-arguments and lifecycle carried an !!! info box headed “Terraform 1.16 widens action_trigger (rc1, not yet stable)” that correctly listed before_destroy and after_destroy among the new events — and then, fourteen lines below it, the running prose still said “Only four events exist … There is no destroy event” as bare present tense. A reader skimming gets the wrong half. Now version-gated in both directions: four events through 1.15 with the v1.15.6 measurement kept, six from 1.16 (terraform#38668). The same page's OpenTofu box still said destroy = false was “converging … once 1.16 is stable (rc1 as of 2026-08-13)”; it shipped (terraform#38784), so the divergence is now marked closed with the removed-block detour labelled as the 1.15-and-earlier answer. Dependency graph had the third stale rc1 title. The fourth defect is a uniqueness claim the page itself disproves 255 lines later. It read “count = x ? 1 : 0 … is the only way to make a single resource optional in Terraform”, while the TUR section further down quotes Brikman recommending count because it “tends to be simpler than setting for_each to an empty or nonempty collection” — an argument that presupposes the alternative exists. Only is now usual, with the for_each route named and cross-linked to the passage that settles it. A fifth, swept into its source. The page claimed every argument for provisioner and connection lives in the resource block reference only — and tf-provisioners, the note it was drawn from, records the provisioners page listing the seven bastion_* attributes as a flat set, printing script_path values, and stating when and on_failure. Both now say the accurate thing: the usage page names arguments in passing but never types, defaults or completes them, and the normative reference is elsewhere. That is the third time this session a bastion-adjacent absence claim has needed correcting, which is now less a coincidence than a signal about how confidently I write sentences containing the word only. Two absence claims survived a real attempt to break them, and one repeated a pattern worth naming a third time. “The failure contract is in the provider docs and in neither book” looked false — grep found the contract in 10-advanced-topics — until the hit turned out to be my own annotation there, an admonition literally titled “The failure contract is in the docs, not the chapter.” Same shape as the v1.7-docs quote and the state mv -help output in the previous entry: the checker finds the words, the attribution says who wrote them, and only the second one settles it. The claim that neither book pairs a connection block with a removed block also held under targeted search. No topic page flips a learning-path topic — every corrected claim was about tool behaviour at a version, not about a topic being unlearned. Out of scope but found while sweeping, and worth stating plainly: the same rc1 rot sits in the reference pages, which is where it does the most damage. release-feature-map.md labels roughly eight rows 1.16-rc1 and says “1.15.8 is the newest stable release”; feature-history.md has a section headed “1.16 (release candidate, not yet stable)” telling the reader to treat it as provisional; and version-facts.md, whose entire job is to be the version ground truth for everything else, still names 1.15.8 as current. Those three feed every other page. Next audit.

2026-08-28 (seventh) — Audited the eighteen written book chapters, the last corpus the seven audit dimensions had never been run over, and the one where a stale claim costs the most. Everything before this was a source note — a record of what a page said on a day. A chapter is the thing that gets read as true, so the standard is different: a source note goes stale honestly, a chapter goes stale silently. Every mechanical layer was clean across all eighteen: 431 admonitions, 114 tables over 514 rows, 1113 fenced blocks, 83 wikilinks — zero malformed, zero broken. That now holds for every corpus in the notes, which retires the mechanical dimensions; the remaining risk is entirely in prose and quotation. The quote layer was the work, and it began with correcting myself twice. check_quotes.py reported 32 unverified passages, and I twice told you they were “all in ch17”. They are not — they span eight chapters (ch01×3, ch05×2, ch07×4, ch10×5, ch12×2, ch13×2, ch14×2, ch17×12). I had generalised from the visible tail of a truncated output, which is the same defect class this whole audit series exists to catch, committed while running it. All 32 were then checked against the source each chapter's own prose names, and none is fabricated. They resolve to Terraform and OpenTofu source comments (transform_provider.go, transform_reference.go, node_resource_validate.go, module_call.go:132, init2_test.go, OpenTofu's config_test.go), CLI diagnostics, the OpenTofu 1.10 and 1.11.4 release notes, the AWS provider's enhanced-region-support and version-6-upgrade guides, Terragrunt's documentation, and the S3 API reference. Two near-accusations were avoided by reading the attribution before reaching for a verdict: a passage absent from the v1.11–v1.16 docs is quoted from v1.7.x, and two others are terraform state mv -help output — both stated as such in the sentences that carry them. That is now a rule with three instances behind it: the note's own attribution tells the auditor where to look, and a checker that only knows about cached web pages cannot see any of those places. scripts/check_quotes.py is green for the first time — 313 passages against 462 cached sources, 0 unverified — with every one of the ~30 new ALLOWED_NON_WEB entries carrying its provenance in the value rather than being waved through. One subtlety worth recording for the next person adding to that list: the checker's norm() deletes apostrophes, underscores and backticks rather than replacing them with spaces, so a key must be written its for “it's” and foreach for for_each or it silently never matches. Two claims in written chapters have been overtaken by Terraform 1.16, and both are now marked rather than quietly edited. Ch 9 says terraform state show output is “explicitly not a machine interface”; v1.16 gave it -json (terraform#23940, open since 2020), so the chapter carries a dated 🔄 box and B9 flips from ✅ to 🔄 under the standing rule — the human/machine distinction it draws still holds, but the sentence overstates it. And Ch 11 presents destroy = false as a removed-block-only rule, which was true through 1.15 and is not now (terraform#38784); it gains an !!! info box rather than a revisit marker, because nothing it says about the removed form became wrong — the rule merely acquired a second home, closing an OpenTofu divergence in passing. Ch 11 does not flip. The distinction is deliberate: 🔄 is for a chapter that now misleads, not for one that has been outgrown. One defect was introduced during this audit and caught by its own tooling — the new Ch 9 box quoted my paraphrase of the chapter back at itself in quotation marks, and check_quotes.py failed it. Fixed by dropping the quote marks, which is what it should have been: it is my summary, not anyone's sentence.

2026-08-28 (sixth) — The seven remaining source courses audited in one pass, which completes every course in the collection. Denominator: 15 files across bitbucket-docs, github-docs, gitlab-docs, infisical-blog, terraform-best-practices, terrakube-docs and tools. 25 attributed quotes, 62 wikilinks, 21 admonitions, 12 tables with 25 rows, 56 fenced blocks. Mechanically clean, and zero quote defects. Two notes had no cache — the only audit-trail gaps left in the collection. code-styling's page is now fetched. pyinfra never had one because its sources are a repository and a docs site, not a page, so one was assembled from the repository description and src/pyinfra/connectors/terraform.py and saved as cache/web/pyinfra.txt. Both of its quotes were then verified at source: the “turns Python code into shell commands” tagline is the repo description verbatim, and “Generate one or more SSH hosts from a Terraform output variable” is the connector's docstring. The best result is that a flag this collection raised months ago turned out to be right, and is now measured. code-styling recorded that the page's rev: v1.99.4 pre-commit pin “is the one line here that goes stale” and said to check the repo before copying. Checked: antonbabenko/pre-commit-terraform is at v1.109.0 (2026-08-21) — ten minor versions ahead. So copying that block installs a hook release roughly a year old. The note now says so with the number rather than the warning. Smaller drift: pyinfra moved v3.9.2 → v3.10.0 (2026-07-27), and the @terraform connector the note exists for is unchanged in it. Terrakube is at 2.32.2; its note already dates itself from the page footer rather than a release. Six audit passes now cover every source course — 12 courses, and the shape of the result is consistent enough to state as a rule. The mechanical layers were clean in all of them. Quote and code defects appeared only in notes written in the same session as the audit, never in older ones. And in mature courses the finding was always the world moving, not the writing drifting: a provider major, an abandoned repository estate, a release that resolved a prediction, a docs page that got worse in a newer version, a pinned tag ten releases behind. The habit worth keeping from all of it: when a note flags something as likely to go stale, that flag is a scheduled measurement, not a disclaimer. Three of the six passes closed one. No status changes.

2026-08-28 (fifth) — Audited the OpenTofu Docs course, and its course-specific risk paid out: two recorded predictions about OpenTofu 1.13 resolved while the audit was running. Denominator: 8 files (7 notes + index). 15 attributed quotes, 33 wikilinks, 17 admonitions, 4 tables with 19 rows, 18 fenced blocks. Mechanically clean; every note has a cache and a complete header; index rows and nav entries agree. v1.13.0-beta1 was published 2026-08-27, one day before this pass. Latest stable is v1.12.6 (2026-08-19), so the notes' “1.12.x is latest” still holds — but 1.13 has moved from on main to in a tagged prerelease, and that changes what two claims are worth. The winrm prediction resolves. 10-advanced-topics recorded that OpenTofu 1.12 deprecated the winrm connection type and that removal was “expected” in 1.13, checked against repos/opentofu on 2026-08-16 as unreleased. The beta changelog now states it outright — “The winrm connection type for provisioners is no longer supported” (opentofu#4012) — with the same migration advice the note independently gave: “Modern Windows versions now support OpenSSH, and so we suggest that anyone currently relying on WinRM plan to migrate to using SSH instead.” So scheduled became shipped in a prerelease, and since Terraform has still made no equivalent move, that divergence is now real rather than pending. The OpenTelemetry predictions resolve too. ot-otel-tracing's “already merged for 1.13” items are all three in the beta changelog: local-exec setting TRACEPARENT (opentofu#4014), OTel library logs copied into TF_LOG (opentofu#4285), and the TRACESTATE-printing-TRACEPARENT fix (opentofu#4168). Recorded precisely rather than loosely: the beta's own changelog header still reads “1.13.0 (Unreleased)”, so these are prerelease facts, not GA facts. opentofu-feature-history's 1.13 entry is retitled from unreleased, in development to in beta since 2026-08-27, not yet GA, with two items spot-confirmed against the tag. Zero quote defects out of 15 — and all three flags were checked rather than waved through, which is the habit the previous audit's near-miss bought. “BEWARE! This is not a committed external interface” is a Go source comment, and the note says so; found at internal/tracing/init.go:36 in the local checkout. The TOFU_CPU_PROFILE line is from OpenTofu's environment-variable docs, a different page from the note's own source, and the note says that too; found at website/docs/cli/config/environment-variables.mdx:206. The third was my own phrase in scare quotes. Five courses audited in two days. The pattern across them: mechanical layers are reliably clean, quote defects cluster in newly written notes rather than old ones, and the findings in mature courses are almost always the world moving — a provider major, an abandoned repo estate, a release that invalidates a claim. No status changes.

2026-08-28 (fourth) — Audited the HashiCorp Terraform Docs course, the largest at 98 files, and it had a decisive mechanical check the other courses did not: diff every page's .mdx blob SHA between v1.15.x and v1.16.x. Two tree calls settle which captured notes the release invalidated, instead of guessing. Result: 18 of 387 pages changed. Four were already handled yesterday (tf-block-action, tf-invoke-actions, tf-block-resource, tf-terraform-data). Three needed work and got it. tf-cmd-state-show is the sharpest. v1.16 added -json, the largest single change of the eighteen — “JSON output via the -json option requires Terraform v1.16 or later”, returning format_version / resource / diagnostics, with the caveat that state must be upgraded first if provider schemas have moved. That undercuts the note's own framing, which quoted the page's “intended for human consumption, not programmatic consumption” and built an argument on it. The box is now scoped to v1.15-and-earlier. The changelog issue is terraform#23940 — outstanding since 2020. tf-meta-lifecycle changed three ways, and one of them is a regression. on_failure joined the action_trigger table, matching the other two pages that document that block. The destroy = false restriction was deleted — v1.15 said “You can only use this rule in removed block” and v1.16 drops the sentence, completing what tf-block-removed recorded. And under the postcondition heading, v1.15 correctly said “arguments in the postcondition block” where v1.16 now says precondition. The newer page is wrong where the older was right. tf-block-module is a documentation regression across a version boundary, and the direction is the surprise. The v1.15.x page was improved on 2026-08-19 (web-unified-docs#2322, “Document full AWS credential chain for S3 module sources”), and the v1.16 branch cut on 2026-08-26 did not carry it forward. So on this page the older version's documentation is better than the newer one's, and “read the latest” is wrong advice. What v1.16 lacks: AWS_PROFILE, the shared config file including SSO and assume-role, container credentials alongside EC2 IMDS — and, entirely absent, credentials passed as query parameters on the source URL (aws_profile, aws_access_key_id, aws_access_key_secret, aws_access_token), which makes a module source string a secret-bearing field. Nothing in v1.16 tells you that. The note now carries the fuller chain. Three of the eighteen changed only their created_at frontmatter with no content change — tf-block-import, tf-data-sources, tf-style-guide — a fourth data point for the rule that this site's date metadata tracks branch mechanics, not content. The rest of the course: 214 admonitions, 91 tables with 555 rows, 339 fenced blocks, 226 quotes, 1223 wikilinks — one mechanical defect (an untitled !!! tip in tf-expr-strings, now titled) and two missing caches (provider-requirements and tf-import, the only notes in the collection with no audit trail; both re-fetched, and tf-import's turned out to exist under a wrong slug, now removed as an orphan). Zero quote defects out of 226 — and the way that was nearly got wrong is the lesson. Twenty-four flagged; all resolved to corpus scope. Two came within a step of being declared fabricated: tf-block-removed's “should not be destroyed” lead-in appears in no version from v1.11 to v1.16 — it is in v1.7.x, which the note says in its own prose. And tf-cmd-state-mv's two backup sentences appear on no web page in any version — they are terraform state mv -help, which the note also says, and which a native binary confirmed verbatim. An audit that only knows page caches will accuse correctly-attributed quotes of fabrication. The note's own attribution is the instruction for where to look, and reading it is part of the check. No status changes.

2026-08-28 (third) — Audited the Terraform Tutorials course, the largest yet, and the finding is systemic rather than textual. Denominator: 35 files (34 notes + index). 52 attributed quotes, 519 wikilinks, 110 admonitions, 24 tables with 98 rows, 242 fenced blocks. Mechanically clean throughout — no invalid admonition type, untitled or unindented box, mismatched table row, or broken wikilink anywhere. All 34 notes have a cache and a complete metadata header; index rows, nav entries and file count agree. Zero real quote defects: all four flags were harness artifacts, and one is worth recording because it will recur — the editorial-bracket stripping that makes [required]-style completions matchable also destroys code containing brackets, so module.vpc[each.key].vpc_id failed against a quote that is verbatim in the cache. The finding is that the tutorial repository estate is largely abandoned. Every tutorial says git clone; measured pushed_at on all 23 distinct repositories these notes reference: 11 last pushed in 2023, 8 in 2024, 2 in 2025, 2 in 2026. So 19 of 23 have had no commit since 2024 or earlier, and none is archived, so neither the page nor GitHub's UI signals it. Yesterday's single-repo finding on learn-terraform-provisioning was not an outlier; it was the median. The worked consequence, and it is pointed: the oldest is learn-terraform-move (2023-02-20) — the Move resources tutorial, whose entire subject is refactoring configurations safely. It pins terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws at 3.14.4, against v6.7.1 published 2026-08-27. Three majors behind. A reader learns refactoring on a configuration that never has to be refactored, and meets none of the upgrade problems vp-upgrade-modules documents, because the pin never moves. Recorded as a table in the course index rather than repeated across 32 notes; tut-cloud-init and tut-packer keep theirs because that is where it was found. The tutorials still teach what they set out to teach — the code is a period piece, and a cloned repo should be read as a fixed exhibit rather than a current example. No defects to correct, which is itself the result worth stating: three courses audited in two days, and this is the first where the notes were clean and only the world had moved. No status changes.

2026-08-28 (second) — Audited the Terraform Registry course, and this is the one whose sources move under it, so the finding is a version rather than a defect. Denominator: 6 files (5 notes + index). 20 attributed quotes, 44 wikilinks, 16 admonitions, 6 tables with 35 rows. Mechanically clean throughout; index rows, nav entries and files all agree. Three quotes flagged only because the corpus was the page caches — all three are quotations of book chapter notes (08-production-grade, 10-advanced-topics) and were confirmed there. The find: hashicorp/google went v7.39.0 → **v8.0.0 on 2026-08-26, two days before this audit.** Measured, not inferred, by asking the release API for all five providers. It is a genuine breaking release — the changelog has four separate breaking sections. google_iap_brand, google_iap_client, google_ml_engine_model and the whole google_notebooks_* family are removed; google_compute_backend_service and google_compute_global_forwarding_rule changed the default load_balancing_scheme from EXTERNAL to EXTERNAL_MANAGED, so a configuration that never named the field behaves differently; several fields moved from list to set, changing how they diff. google-provider's example pins ~> 7.0, which now excludes the current major — the example is preserved as the page-as-captured, with a 🔄 revisit box saying so. Its sibling-providers callout also claimed Google was “a major ahead of AWS's 6.x”; it is now two. AWS moved too but harmlessly: v6.54.0 → v6.62.0, eight minors inside the same line, so aws-provider's ~> 6.0 pin is unaffected. cloudinit, external and local are all still at the versions their notes state. Both provider notes now distinguish as captured from re-measured, which they did not before. No chapter flips to 🔄 — checked: google-provider is cited from the path, the glossary, three HCDocs notes and providers, and none of them repeats a version number. Two smaller defects, both the consistency class. cloudinit-config had two documentation-gap findings in the same file at different severities, one warning and one danger; normalised. And local-provider claimed neither TID nor its chapter note “mentions permissions at all” — the note does mention permissions, once, about a file provisioner's destination directory. The claim is true when scoped to file permissions on local_file, and now says that. Version drift is the standing risk for this course specifically, and re-measuring all five providers took one API call each. No status changes.

2026-08-28 — Audited the Validated Patterns course as a whole, which is not the same as having audited each note as it was written — and it found one more of the day's recurring defect. Denominator: 13 files (12 notes + the course index). 125 attributed quotes, 124 wikilinks, 30 admonitions, 14 tables with 79 rows, 15 code blocks. Quotes were matched against all twelve caches at once rather than each note against its own, so cross-note quotations resolve; 0 unverified, 0 broken wikilinks. Tables and admonitions mechanically clean. All twelve notes carry a complete metadata header, and the index's slug table cross-checks against each note's own Source URL — 12 slugs, 12 notes, 12 nav entries, no drift. The real find was an absence claim, for the third time today. vp-azure-landing-zone said its separate-federations control “has no counterpart in vp-aws-landing-zone”. The AWS guide has one: “Plan/Apply separation - Separate the plan and apply phases in production environments with a manual approval gate. This supports change control and audit.” I had not recorded that line when capturing the AWS note, then asserted its absence from the Azure one. The distinction that survives is better than the claim I made: AWS separates the phases with a human between them — a workflow control, and a gate someone can be given permission to skip; Azure separates the identities used for each phase — an authorisation control, which cannot be skipped by permission. Complementary, and worth having both. Corrected in the Azure note, and the missed line is now recorded in the AWS one, where it belongs to A5. Two code blocks were silent abridgements, the class the code audit named yesterday: vp-integrate-vault's MongoDB example had dropped the trailing mongodbatlas_project resource, and vp-aap-integration had merged two separate page snippets into one fenced block. The first is restored, the second says so. Two admonition severities were inconsistent with precedent I set yesterday. A correction notice and an enterprise-scope caveat were both danger; yesterday's audit demoted exactly those two shapes in tf-invoke-actions and the topic page. Both now warning — and the three edition-scope boxes across the course now agree: restrictions warn, wider applicability informs. The lesson the whole day converges on: auditing notes individually as they are written does not catch claims between notes. Every defect this pass found was cross-note — an absence asserted about a sibling, a block merged from two places, a severity inconsistent with another file's. A per-note check cannot see any of them. No status changes.

2026-08-27 (twenty-first) — The five patterns believed 404 are captured, and fetching them was the final disproof: every one returned real content on the first attempt. The Validated Patterns collection is now complete at twelve of twelve. vp-azure-landing-zone is the one the 2026-08-17 audit named as the absence that cost this path something, and it delivers. It is the twin of vp-aws-landing-zone, so A7 now has both clouds: subscriptions and management groups where AWS has accounts and OUs, Entra ID where AWS has IAM, Azure Policy where AWS has SCPs, Sentinel in both. Terminology drift worth knowing — AWS says workload landing zone, Azure says application landing zone, for the same thing. Its sharpest control has no AWS counterpart: separate federations for the plan and apply stages, so proposing and executing are different privileges. Terraform's plan/apply split is usually taught as a safety mechanism; here it is an authorisation boundary. That belongs in A6 as much as A5. Both landing-zone guides also align themselves to the cloud vendor's framework — Well-Architected and Microsoft CAF — which is the honest description of what a validated pattern is. vp-orgs-to-projects supplies history the notes lacked: organizations were the original segregation unit, projects arrived through 2023 to give RBAC delegation inside one line of business, and the recommendation is now to minimise organizations. Its operational half is a list of what does not migrate — run history cannot be migrated at all, and sensitive variable values cannot be retrieved via the UI or API by design, so they are unmigratable by construction. That is the strongest argument in the collection for sourcing secrets from Vault: a Vault-sourced value migrates because there is nothing to migrate. Ordering matters too — policy sets before workspaces, or runs execute in an unguarded window. vp-vulnerability-patch-management answers what tut-packer leaves open: what keeps a golden image current. A 30-day repave cycle, with scheduled image revocation in the HCP Packer registry, channels rather than image IDs in the configuration, and drift detection turning a channel update into a work queue. Revoke → channel → drift → remediate, with no one maintaining a list. It also splits two cadences deliberately: merge freely, build only on git tags and releases. vp-cortex-cloud is the collection's only third-party run task, and it is the counterweight to vp-aap-integration ruling the same mechanism out. Together they give the rule: run tasks suit verdicts, not work — the 10-minute response ceiling is fatal for an Ansible run and irrelevant for a policy scan. It completes the enforcement-point set alongside Sentinel and SCPs, adds the practice worth generalising (ship the local runner with the gate — Checkov CLI and an IDE plugin, so the gate is a backstop and not the discovery mechanism), and is unusually honest that enabling it retroactively blocks runs that previously worked. vp-servicenow-catalog is the self-service story, and its load-bearing setting is stated in half a sentence: auto-apply is true, so nobody sees the plan. Approval moves entirely to the ServiceNow request workflow, and the only remaining bounds are the no-code module and the variable set. The guide does not flag that trade; the note does. Its underrated half is that the run log lands in the RITM ticket, making the ITSM record the audit trail. The pre-commit audit found four defects across the five, two of them the fabricated-tail class again. “…to trust it” where the page says “…to trust the TLS connection”; a Cortex quote where I had silently corrected the page's grammar (“Platform operators owns” → own) and joined two separate bullets into one sentence; “propagates down” quoted where the page says “propagate downward through the management hierarchy”; and a phrase from my own changelog quoted in a way that read as the page's. All corrected. 52 quotes now verify clean across the five; 46 wikilinks resolve. Shortening a trailing clause inside quotation marks is now the single most repeated defect of the day, and it is invisible without matching against the source. Nav gains five; the course index records twelve of twelve captured. No status changes.

2026-08-27 (twentieth) — The six cached Validated Patterns captured, closing the borrowing the course was opened to stop. All seven guides read on 2026-08-17 now have notes; their prose summaries in that entry point at them rather than standing in for them. Wired into A5, A6, A7, A8, A10 and I7. vp-aws-landing-zone is still the only landing-zone material anywhere in these notes, and its artifact is a vocabulary rather than a procedure: platform landing zone versus workload landing zone, “autonomous in terms of deployment but compliant with the policies and controls defined in the PLZ”; the rule that one AWS account = one HCP workspace = one state, so the IAM boundary and the state boundary cannot drift apart; and the Sentinel-versus-SCP table that A5 needed — Sentinel evaluates plans, resource-level, pre-deployment, and is bypassed by anything not going through Terraform, while an SCP evaluates every AWS API call at account level and cannot be bypassed. A control that must hold against a console user was never a Sentinel control. vp-integrate-vault separates four Terraform–Vault surfaces the path had been treating as one, and one runs backwards: the Terraform secrets engine has Vault issue HCP Terraform API tokens. Its sharpest operational fact is that the HCP Terraform API allows one active org or team token at a time, so Vault caches and re-serves those rather than minting per read — a “dynamic secret” that is deliberately not new each time, and a rotation schedule built on the opposite assumption would revoke every other consumer. Marked beta, and it shows: one garbled sentence and a typo in a code explanation. vp-vault-dynamic-credentials implements that guide's AWS surface end to end and ships modules. Two facts worth carrying: the STS credentials are scoped to the intersection of the Vault secrets-engine role and the AWS IAM role, so least privilege has two places to get wrong; and align the STS TTL with the JWT lifetime or a long apply dies partway, which compounds with the one-hour role-chaining ceiling A6 already records. vp-upgrade-modules and vp-provider-upgrades are one author's pair, both Community-Edition-applicable unlike the rest of the collection, and both hold the bar no errors, warnings, or actions — stricter than an empty diff, because the provider guide's worked example produces a plan that reports no changes and four deprecation warnings. The module guide adds the acceptance criterion A8 needed: “Imports are the only acceptable change to see in a speculative plan when upgrading to a newer module version.” The provider guide adds an artifact the notes lacked — ignore_changes used as a documented, temporary workaround with the upstream issue URL in the comment, which is the difference between suppressing a diff and dating a known defect. Both document their own dead ends, which is rare. Also new: a module producer can deprecate a version to push a warning at consumers who are not watching, complementing Renovate's pull. vp-cloudformation-migration separates three jobs usually run together — translate the template, wrap it with aws_cloudformation_stack, or import the resources — and its rollback strategy is to keep both tools live in parallel until Terraform is proven, which is honest about what an import cannot undo. Nav gains six entries; the course index now records seven captured and five never read, the Azure landing zone among them. The pre-commit audit caught the worst defect of the day, and it is a new class. In vp-upgrade-modules I had written a quoted sentence whose second half was invented — “…allows a reviewer to follow the work”, where the page says “…allows you to easily document changes in the CHANGELOG as well.” Not a shortened quote, not a word altered for flow: fabricated content inside quotation marks, which is exactly what the harness exists to catch and what no amount of re-reading my own prose would have found. Corrected, and the point it makes is better than the one I invented — the commit split exists so the CHANGELOG can be written afterwards. Two illustrative phrasings of mine in vp-aws-landing-zone were also sitting in quotation marks and are now marked as mine. 55 quotes across the six now verify clean; 62 wikilinks resolve. No status changes.

2026-08-27 (nineteenth) — vp-aap-integration captured, opening a Validated Patterns course and closing the last uncaptured reference A1 names. It is now A1 item 6, and it earns the slot for one reason: it is the only captured source in which Terraform pushes to the configuration tool rather than the configuration tool pulling from Terraform. pyinfra pulls via terraform output -json; Ansible's terraform_provider inventory plugin pulls via the state file; the AAP provider writes the inventory (aap_inventory) and launches the job (aap_job) from inside the apply, reading nothing. That reintroduces in-apply work — wait_for_completion = true blocks exactly as a remote-exec does — but a provider models the operation, so a failure is a failed resource rather than a taint on a healthy VM. Same distinction tf-invoke-actions draws for the actions block, reached from the vendor-integration side. The topic page gains the third direction. Scope stated rather than assumed: this one is enterprise-only and says so — “relying on Terraform Community Edition or Ansible OSS is not recommended”. Every other A1 source works on CE. Its architecture assumes agents, workspaces, variable sets, projects, run tasks and workspace notifications, none of which CE has. Two facts worth carrying beyond Ansible. Terraform Run Tasks have a hard 10-minute limit on responses from the external system, which is why the pattern rules the run-task route Not Recommended rather than merely inelegant (→ A5). And aap_job runs once by default, with a triggers map deciding re-runs — the same shape as terraform_data's triggers_replace, and the opposite default to a creation-time provisioner. Also recorded: the “Prompt on Launch” requirement on the AAP side, stated twice on the page, without which the provider cannot override inventory or extra_vars and the job fails — a cross-platform coupling the platform team owns and the application team hits; reserved workspace variables must be declared with empty values to be referenceable; and the provider is published by Ansible, not HashiCorp (ansible/terraform-provider-aap, v1.5.0, 2026-04-28). One near-miss caught before commit, and it is the reason the link is right: the page's Related resources entry for the signed-SSH pattern was about to ship as a URL I had constructed rather than read. The real one is under /validated-patterns/**vault**/integrate-vault-ssh-with-ansible-automation-platform — a Vault-collection page, so it is not among the nine Terraform-collection pages cached here. Read off the live page instead of inferred. The pre-commit pass also caught a paraphrase sitting inside quotation marks, the same class as this morning's audit; 15 quotes now verify clean. Course opened with its caveats attached. docs/sources/validated-patterns/ records that the collection is not linked from the tutorial library, and carries the 2026-08-17 finding that five of twelve advertised Terraform patterns returned 404 while the sitemaps disagreed — explicitly dated, and marked as not re-checked, since only the AAP page was re-tested today. Eight cached-but-uncaptured guides remain, cited from A5, A6, A7, A8, A10 and I7. A1 stays ⬜.

2026-08-27 (eighteenth) — Checked whether A1 still has uncaptured references, mechanically rather than by memory, and closed the three that mattered. Of the 11 external links A1 names, six documentation and tutorial pages are captured and four are GitHub issue citations. One is not captured — the Integrate Terraform with Ansible Automation Platform Validated Pattern. But the sharper finding was one level down: A1's material already quotes facts from five sources with no note behind them, and those sources are where several of its corrections came from. Three are now captured as Registry notes 3–5: cloudinit-config, external-data-source, local-provider. Each closes a borrowing. 10-advanced-topics corrects TID on the empty-query case, on content_base64sha256 being the hash-then-base64 order, and on direxists erroring for a file path and not expanding ~ — all four corrections were sourced from provider pages that had never been captured. They now sit at the source. And each turned up something no captured source held. The external data source passes every environment variable visible to the Terraform process through to the child program, which makes it a credential-exposure surface as wide as the runner — an access-boundary fact belonging beside the outputs-versus-state argument, and stated in neither book. It also re-runs on every refresh, because Terraform assumes a data source has no observable side effects, so it is not a once-per-apply hook. local_file's file_permission and directory_permission default to 0777, before umask, on the resource whose purpose is writing files — and TID's §10.5.3 example writes a tls_private_key with it. local_file's content replaces invalid UTF-8 with the replacement character instead of erroring, so binary data through the wrong attribute is silent corruption. And cloudinit_config's output attribute is rendered — which tf-post-apply-operations never names, so across both captured HashiCorp cloud-init pages the consuming half of the example is missing. Smaller items recorded: external's id is always the literal -; Terraform does not run program through a shell, so no metacharacter escaping is needed; cloudinit_config's part block is Required and the maintainers had to hand-edit the generated schema to say so; and provider functions such as direxists need a required_providers entry plus Terraform 1.8, against OpenTofu's 1.7. Still open, and now recorded rather than rediscovered: the AAP Validated Pattern A1 cites, and the nine cache/web/vp-*.txt pages captured as cache on 2026-08-17 with no notes behind any of them — cited across A1, A5, A6, A7, A8, A10 and I7. That is a course-sized gap, not a note-sized one. A1 stays ⬜.

2026-08-27 (seventeenth) — Re-checked the Cloud-Init tutorial against this morning's capture. The page has not changed — and the check turned up a number neither tutorial note had. The fetched text is byte-identical to the morning's cache, so nothing to re-capture. What was worth doing was the check the notes had inferred rather than measured: both said the tutorial repository is “pinned hard” and “behind”, reasoning backwards from aws ~> 5.47.0 and a committed lock file. Measured instead: the cloudinit branch tip is 2024-05-03, the packer branch tip is 2024-04-03, and the repository's pushed_at matches the later of the two — so no branch of hashicorp-education/learn-terraform-provisioning has had a commit in over two years, and it is not archived, so unmaintained rather than retired. That is the fact behind the pins rather than a deduction from them, and neither tutorial page mentions the age of the repository it tells you to clone. Added to tut-cloud-init and tut-packer. 2026-08-27 (sixteenth) — Seventh audit, over prose claims — the first of the seven whose scope had to be argued for rather than read off the syntax. A quote, a fence, a [[link]], a !!! opener and a | row are all extractable; “prose claims” is everything else, which is most of eight files. So the subset was chosen from what the six previous audits had already shown: every defect so far had been a quantity, count or identity claim about evidence sitting next to it. Extracting exactly those gave a real denominator — 170 claims: 47 count, 51 uniqueness, 61 version, 11 identity. The 47 count claims were checked one by one; the version claims were each verified when written (tags, changelog entries, blob SHAs) and were not re-derived; uniqueness and identity were spot-checked. That is a partial audit and is recorded as one. Two defects, and both are a shape worth naming separately: a count that was correct when written and that my own later work in the same session invalidated. tf-invoke-actions opens “First of the three pages in Extend CRUD operations” — true when written, and then tf-block-action was captured into the same group an hour later, making it four. And tf-post-apply-operations headed a section “four rows that should not be copied” where the four bad resources sit in three rows, two of them sharing the Microsoft Azure row; its own admonition underneath already said “four resources”, so the heading disagreed with the box below it. Both fixed, and the admonition now names the three rows. And one near-miss worth more than the defects. The audit flagged “the new example's code fence carries no language tag, where every other block on the page is tagged hcl”, because a naive count of `` lines in the.mdxfound six fences with only two tagged. Checking the **pairs** rather than the lines shows three blocks: twohcl, one untagged, and the untagged one is the new example. **The claim was right and the audit was wrong**, and correcting it would have introduced a defect into a clean line. Recorded because six audits of finding my own errors builds a momentum that is itself a hazard. **Seven audits: 31 absence claims, 177 quotes, 32 code blocks, 186 wikilinks, 35 admonitions, 16 tables, 170 prose claims. Sixteen defects, all mine, none from a source, and every one of them in a line summarising adjacent evidence.** Two sub-patterns are now distinct: **counts never taken** (I estimated where I could have counted), and **counts invalidated by my own later work in the same session** — three of the sixteen, which no single-pass review would catch because they were true when written. Harness kept asscripts/audit_prose_claims_session.py`. No status changes. A1 stays ⬜.

2026-08-27 (fifteenth) — Sixth audit, over tables, and it produced the highest defect rate of the six — which is what the previous entry predicted. Denominator: 16 tables, 66 data rows across today's eight files. Mechanically clean: no header/separator width mismatch, no row wider or narrower than its header, no table run into the paragraph above it. Three defects, and all three are the pattern this run keeps finding — a claim about the table that the table does not support. A miscount. tf-post-apply-operations said “Four of the fourteen resources named here”. Counted from the column: thirteen. Fixed in the note and in this log's third entry, which had copied it. A second miscount, of my own additions. The topic page's alternatives table said the notes “add two rows above it and one below” to TID §10.3.6's table. TID's has five rows, mine has seven, so it is one above and one below. The arithmetic was visible in the table the sentence introduces. And a table that had gone stale within the same day. tf-block-action's date-metadata table was written as the settling third data point, with three rows. tf-terraform-data added a fourth an hour later — same last_modified across v1.15.x and v1.16.x, contents differing by the entire store block — and pointed back at this table as the canonical list without the list being extended. 2026-08-27 (fourteenth) — Fifth audit, over admonitions, and for once the interesting failures were about judgement rather than fact. Denominator: 35 admonitions across today's eight files — 11 warning, 9 note, 8 danger, 5 info, 2 tip. Mechanically clean, and three of the checks were already covered. check_markdown.py enforces escaped quotes in titles, parser-refused openers, and admonitions that terminate an ordered list; it has run green all day. The new harness adds what it does not check: an invalid type keyword, a missing title or empty body, a body line under-indented so it silently falls outside the box, and a straight quote in a title. All four came back zero. Four defects in the semantic layer, which is the layer no checker covers. Three were type against severity, and the test that exposed them was consistency rather than taste — comparing each box to the others in the same set. danger was carrying a correction notice (“This page changes what these notes said about destroy hooks”) and a capability gain (“Terraform 1.16 moved the line under all four holes”), neither of which is a hazard; they are now warning and info. Meanwhile the tutorial's world-open SSH port sat in a warning while “SSH host key validation is off by default” — the same class of inherited security defect, arguably milder — sat in a danger two notes away. Promoted to danger. The fourth was a title overstating its own body. tf-block-action read “…does not parse — and neither does any other block reference's”, where the body says six of seven do it and check is exempt because it supports neither count nor for_each. Retitled to “nor does any other one that has for_each”. Same shape as the annotation defects in the last audit: the summary line drifted past what the evidence under it supports. Five audits: 31 absence claims, 177 quotes, 32 code blocks, 186 wikilinks, 35 admonitions. Eleven defects, all mine, none from a source. 2026-08-27 (thirteenth) — Fourth audit, over wikilinks, and the mechanical half was clean — which is why it was not the half worth auditing. One defect: an internal contradiction inside a single note. tf-provisioners opens with a table of six old URLs and then, in its own Related: line, said the redirect “generalises to all five old pages.” Five is defensible if you exclude syntax, which was the page itself rather than a sub-page, but a note should not print six and then say five. And the cloud-config file was labelled “in full” when its section comments had been stripped. All three now reproduce faithfully or mark what was cut; the YAML was diffed line by line against the repository and is otherwise identical. The fourth is the one worth remembering. The pyinfra command in A1's handoff callout and on the topic page — pyinfra @terraform/…/server_group_node_ips apt.packages iftop _sudo=true — appears in no source. It is a splice of pyinfra's two documented halves: the @terraform inventory address, which its docs show with a trailing ..., and an apt.packages operation its docs show against @docker/ubuntu.
