2026-08-27 (eleventh) — Same audit run over the quotes, and it was the harness that needed fixing more than the notes. Denominator: 177 attributed quotes across today's eight files — blockquote lines and quoted spans, with !!! admonition titles excluded since those are my own prose, not attribution. Each was matched against a corpus of 453 files: every page cache, the .mdx sources at v1.14/1.15/1.16, the Terraform source files read this session, the AWS, Azure and cloudinit provider docs, the two tutorial repositories, and the book chapter notes. Five quotes that come from places that are not files — two git commit messages and three measured CLI diagnostics — are allowlisted by name with their provenance rather than silently skipped. One real defect. tf-post-apply-operations rendered “This makes the data immediately available on system boot” as “which makes …”, the leading word changed to fit my sentence while still inside quotation marks. Restored verbatim as its own quoted sentence. Small, and exactly the class worth catching: an attributed string that had been edited for flow. Two harness artifacts, not defects. The azurerm deprecation quotes failed only because the provider docs put inline markdown links inside the quoted span; checked directly with links stripped, both fragments are present and in order. And one flag was a table cell the extractor sliced mid-code-span. Three flags that are correct as written: a self-quotation of this session's own retracted wording inside the correction that retracts it, and two sets of scare quotes around phrases of mine rather than anyone's. Two limits of this audit, stated rather than papered over. Quotes attributed to TID and TUR verify only against my own chapter notes, not against the books, so they confirm faithful copying and not faithful quotation. And the first run returned a false all-clear — zero misses — because the corpus glob had swept in the eight audited files themselves, so every quote matched itself. That is the failure a denominator alone does not catch, and it is why the count of corpus files is recorded here alongside the count of quotes. No status changes. A1 stays ⬜.

2026-08-27 (tenth) — Audited every absence claim written today for the error the previous entry caught, and found one more. The class is: asserting the docs do not say something, on the strength of having found it in the source, without checking whether the docs already say it. Denominator: 31 absence claims across the eight files touched today (tf-provisioners, tf-post-apply-operations, tf-invoke-actions, tf-block-action, tf-terraform-data, tut-cloud-init, tut-packer and the topic page), extracted mechanically rather than by memory and each checked against the cached page or the mdx source. One was wrong, and in the same direction as the last. The WinRM script path was recorded as “an omission rather than an error … no captured page says so”. The resource block reference does document a WinRM script_path — its row lists ssh and winrm in the applies-to column — and documents it wrongly, giving C:/windows/temp/terraform_%RAND%.cmd via target_platform. At tag v1.15.8 the WinRM communicator sets C:/Temp/terraform_%RAND%.cmd and has no target_platform handling at all (zero occurrences), which the table's own next row concedes by listing target_platform as ssh-only. So a gap I had excused is really a docs error plus an internal contradiction. Corrected in the note, the topic page, and recorded with the other connection defects in tf-block-resource. The other 30 held, including the ones most exposed to this failure: the provisioners page really does not mention the removed-block connection position (its one “removed” is the verb); neither provisioner page mentions the 16 KB User Data cap; tf-post-apply-operations really never names the hashicorp/cloudinit provider in prose and never links Invoke actions; tf-invoke-actions really contains no before_destroy and no condition; the Packer page really omits required_plugins; and the terraform_data docs really never state the store block's cardinality. One claim re-verified rather than assumed while auditing: count's Supported constructs list at v1.16.x is data, ephemeral, module, resource, list, and for_each's is those plus the three Stacks blocks — neither names action, and for_each's omits import too, so the finding in tf-block-action stands as written. Recorded in passing: for_each misspells its own heading as “Supported constucts” where count's is correct. No status changes; no new note. A1 stays ⬜.

2026-08-27 (ninth) — The connection section read properly for the first time, because A1 item 2 now links to it — and doing that caught an error this path and two notes had been repeating since this morning. The correction first. tf-provisioners recorded the bastion-argument defaults as “what neither page says” and as covering every bastion attribute. Both halves were wrong. The resource block reference states each fallback in its Default column (“value of the user field”, and so on), so only the provisioners page omits them; and it is five of seven, not all — bastion_host is the trigger itself and bastion_host_key has no fallback, which the source confirms by leaving it out of the if connInfo.BastionHost != "" block that fills the other five. Fixed in the note, the topic page and A1 item 2. The lesson is the one the verify-my-own-edits rule keeps making: the finding came from reading the source and was written up without checking whether the docs table already said it. The count was wrong too: “roughly 25” arguments. Counted from the table, it is 29. Three further defects in that section, none previously recorded. Its own configuration-model summary lists script_path twice and omits proxy_host, so it shows 29 entries for 28 distinct arguments and still misses one the table documents. agent is typed string with default false; it is a boolean, and the real default is environment-dependent — internal/communicator/ssh/provisioner.go at tag v1.15.8 sets it true when the argument is unset and SSH_AUTH_SOCK is present, so a laptop with an agent running and a CI runner without one behave differently on identical configuration and the table says neither. And target_platform prints the Windows default with backslashes where the script_path row two rows up prints it with forward slashes, against the provisioners page's own warning that backslash is the string escape character. Plus “arugment” in the certificate row. Nothing else in the page changed between v1.15.x and v1.16.x beyond what the previous two entries already folded in: on_failure and the two destroy events on action_trigger, the caller sentence, and a caller.id example in the Ansible action. The connection section itself is untouched across the two releases. No status changes. A1 stays ⬜.

2026-08-27 (eighth) — tf-terraform-data re-fetched and extended rather than re-captured: Terraform 1.16 gave it a third job. The flag raised two entries ago is now followed up. The new store block “can hold ephemeral and sensitive values across plan and apply” (terraform#38298), which stated plainly means it exists to write an ephemeral value into state on purpose — an exit from the property that defines ephemeral values (tf-manage-sensitive-data), for the case where regenerating a secret would rotate the live credential. That makes it an A6 item as much as an A1 one. Four arguments: input (write-only, hence able to take ephemeral values), sensitive (routes to sensitive_output rather than output, and the two are mutually exclusive), version (the stored value is pinned until this changes), and replace (an output change replaces rather than updates). version is the one that makes the feature work: without it a freshly generated ephemeral value differs every run and the stored output would churn, so it is rotate-on-demand rather than rotate-on-every-plan. Three facts source-verified at tag v1.16.0 and stated nowhere in the docs: store is NestingSingle, so at most one block — which is why the example addresses it unindexed as terraform_data.test.store.sensitive_output; input carries WriteOnly: true in the schema rather than only in prose; and a code comment spells out the comparison the docs describe only by its outcome — “If there is no version value, then input will be compared directly against output.” Diffed against v1.15.8 in the local checkout: the whole block type is new and nothing else in the schema changed. So the resource now has two independent replacement triggers, triggers_replace and store.replace, and the store path is the only one with a deliberate gate in front of it. The note's comparison section is rewritten as a three-way. Four docs bugs, all inside the v1.16 additions: “argumnet”, “These attribute are mutually exclusive”, a code fence with no language tag where every other block on the page is tagged hcl, and sub-arguments indented one space so they render as siblings rather than children. And a fourth data point on the date rule: this file's last_modified: 2025-11-19 is identical in v1.15.x and v1.16.x while the two differ by the entire store block. That is now four files — one correct, one backfilled, two carrying the same stamp across different content — so the field is settled as unusable and blob-SHA diffing is the check. No new note, no nav change: the page was already captured on 2026-07-10 and was extended in place. A1 stays ⬜.

2026-08-27 (seventh) — tf-block-action captured, completing Extend CRUD operations, and the smallest page in the group produced the widest finding. It settles what tf-invoke-actions would only call “some” meta-arguments: exactly three — count, for_each, provider. No depends_on, no lifecycle, anywhere on the page. So ordering is not something you declare on an action: one fired from an action_trigger inherits its position from the triggering resource, -invoke makes the action the entire plan, and everything else comes from references inside config as ordinary implicit dependencies — which the 1.16 changelog shows was not always honoured (“Actions are now invoked with respect to all resource dependencies”, terraform#38668). It also contradicts the meta-argument pages and is the one that is right: tf-meta-count's Supported-constructs list omits action while its body describes it, and tf-meta-for-each's omits action and import. One feature now demonstrably needs three pages, and none of them says so: usage and -invoke on tf-invoke-actions, the block's arguments here, and action_trigger's events / condition / on_failure on tf-block-resource, filed under a different nav group. condition is mentioned on neither of the first two. The finding that generalises beyond actions: every block reference's “Complete configuration” snippet is invalid HCL. Introduced as containing “all supported built-in arguments”, they print for_each twice — map form then set form — and count once beside it, against their own # mutually exclusive comment. Checked across the v1.16.x sources: resource, data, action, import, module and ephemeral all do it; only check, which supports neither, is exempt. So it is a house convention, not a slip. As a menu of what exists it is useful; as something to copy it never works. Folded back into tf-block-resource, which had not caught it on first capture. And the date-metadata rule is now settled with a third data point. block/action.mdx carries the identical last_modified: 2026-01-12 in both v1.15.x and v1.16.x while their contents differ by the caller sentence. Two files, one timestamp, different bytes. With tf-post-apply-operations (correct) and tf-provisioners (backfilled), the conclusion is that on developer.hashicorp.com the field is not a change signal in either direction — diff blob SHAs across version branches instead, one API call per branch, which caught every content change in this group. Smaller items: the page is explicit that an action's label “does not affect the operation”; its caller sentence says resource instance where tf-invoke-actions says resource, which is the more precise of the two; and its first example uses an account-qualified Lambda ARN where every other example on both pages uses a bare name. Nav at rung 1, last in the group, which is now complete. A1 stays ⬜.

2026-08-27 (sixth) — tf-invoke-actions captured, completing the Extend CRUD operations group, and it does not merely add to A1 — it moves the line the whole topic rests on. Terraform 1.16.0 shipped 2026-08-26, one day before this capture, and three of its changes land here. action_trigger now accepts before_destroy and after_destroy (terraform#38668). Through 1.15 it accepted only the create/update pair — not inferred but measured, in tf-block-resource, where both destroy events were rejected with “No events specified”. So the strongest remaining argument for a destroy-time provisioner, that nothing else could hook teardown, is now provider-dependent rather than absolute: where a provider ships the action, none of the four holes in when = destroy applies. Second, on_failure on an action_trigger inverts the provisioner's default (terraform#38722). The values do not even overlap — halt / continue / taint against continue / fail — and the default halt explicitly “is not tainted” where the provisioner's default fail taints. This topic's fourth objection, the one these notes contributed because no book states it, is precisely what the replacement mechanism designs out. Tainting survives as an opt-in. Third, caller — self for actions, letting one action block serve many resource instances without a reference per instance — and the same release let -invoke combine with -target to say which caller (terraform#38845), which the page documents nowhere even though it documents caller. Two stale claims corrected rather than left standing. tf-block-resource's measured conclusion and the glossary's action_trigger entry both said there is no destroy event; both are now version-gated with the 1.15 measurement kept and the 1.16 changelog cited. No chapter flips to 🔄 — Ch11 names action_trigger and defers it to Ch18 without making a destroy claim, so nothing written has gone stale. One unrelated pending marker closed while reading the same changelog: tf-block-removed carried “⏳ Terraform 1.16 adds the resource-level form too (rc1 as of 2026-08-13)” for destroy = false; it shipped (terraform#38784), so that OpenTofu divergence is closed. Docs bugs recorded: a sentence saying Terraform “also updates the resource” where it means invokes the action, present since v1.15 and left untouched by the v1.16 edit that reflowed the paragraph around it; “meta-argments”; event in prose against events in every sample; and the conditions-versus-condition bug from first capture survives into v1.16. The page also states no version floor anywhere, and never lists its own event set. Two things the 1.16 changelog flags for later, not chased here: terraform_data gained a store block for ephemeral and sensitive values across plan and apply (terraform#38298), which tf-terraform-data does not have; and terraform graph gained -format=mermaid (terraform#38719), which tf-cmd-graph does not have. Nav at rung 1, first in Extend CRUD operations, which is now complete apart from the action block reference. Topic page extended in three places. A1 stays ⬜.

2026-08-27 (fifth) — tut-packer captured, the last uncaptured link out of tf-post-apply-operations, and now A1 item 4. It is the deliberate mirror of tut-cloud-init — same repository, same network, same terraform user, same Go demo, same closing sentence — with the configuration work moved from boot to image build. The framing worth keeping: the alternative to a Terraform provisioner is a Packer provisioner. The image is built by provisioner "file" and provisioner "shell" blocks inside a Packer build. Same two types, same two jobs; what changes is that they run once, against a throwaway instance, producing an artifact, so nothing runs inside an apply and none of this topic's objections attach. And Packer's own transcript shows it “Authorizing access to port 22 from [0.0.0.0/0] in the temporary security groups” — so the docs' “avoid direct network access” argument is not that SSH never happens, it is that SSH happens once at build time into a machine that is then destroyed. Worth stating, because the docs phrasing invites the stronger and wrong reading. The payoff neither tutorial names: this one has no “may take a few minutes to complete” warning, because the machine boots configured. That is item 3's wait, removed. The seam between the two tools is a copy-paste, and the same repository already shows the better answer. The shipped configuration is ami = "ami-YOUR-AMI-ID", edited by hand from the packer build output, while the cloudinit branch of the same repo resolves its AMI with an aws_ami data source. A Packer image named learn-terraform-packer-${local.timestamp} with owners = ["self"] is exactly as filterable, and the timestamp makes most_recent = true pick the newest build. The hand-copy does make the artifact boundary visible, which may be the point, but the page never says so. One factual error, verified against AWS. The destroy section says “Your Packer image will not incur costs in your AWS account” and then, in the next sentence, tells you to check the cost of maintaining your images. An amazon-ebs build produces an EBS-backed AMI, and AWS's EBS user guide states “Charges for your snapshots are based on the amount of data stored.” The section's stated purpose is avoiding unnecessary charges, and it ends leaving an AMI and its snapshot behind with no instruction to deregister or delete either. Two more staleness findings. The pasted build transcript reads “Prevalidating AMI Name: learn-terraform-packer” with no timestamp suffix, so it was captured before the locals block the same page prints — a tutorial transcript can be years out of date while the prose around it reads as current. And the setup.sh heredoc is unquoted (<< EOF), so $PATH, $GOROOT and $GOPATH expand in the outer shell before the text reaches the inner one, and the export PATH line appends /bin:/bin to root's path rather than Go's; << 'EOF' is the fix. It costs nothing here, which is the instructive part. Version drift is now measured across both branches: cloudinit pins aws ~> 5.47.0 and Ubuntu noble 24.04; packer pins aws ~> 4.42.0 with required_version = ">= 0.14.5" and Ubuntu jammy 22.04. Two different provider majors in one repository, on two branches a reader is told to visit in sequence, both behind the v6 line Ch17 covers. Nav: Provision now shows two of six. A1 stays ⬜.

2026-08-27 (fourth) — tut-cloud-init captured, the hands-on half of the previous two entries, and it is now A1 item 3. Five minutes of tutorial, and its real subject is narrower than its title: getting an SSH login onto a fresh instance with no AWS key material at all — no aws_key_pair, no tls_private_key, and therefore no private key in state, which is precisely the cost TUR Ch8 admits its remote-exec walkthrough pays (08-production-grade). Its timing note is the honest statement of what cloud-init costs, and belongs next to the topic page's failure-semantics argument: “Cloud-Init runs after the instance is provisioned, and may take a few minutes to complete.” Apply completes when the instance exists, not when the machine is ready. A remote-exec closes that window by blocking inside the apply and pays with taint-on-failure and the ASG problem; neither option removes the wait, they differ in who does the waiting. Read the repository, not the page. hashicorp-education/learn-terraform-provisioning branch cloudinit, checked file by file. The page's YAML excerpt omits the top-level groups: block that creates the group its own primary_group: hashicorp names, so on the page that line refers to nothing; it also drops shell: /bin/bash, invents an empty ssh_import_id:, and shows an empty ssh_authorized_keys entry where the file actually holds a placeholder ssh-rsa AAAAHHHHHH — so the instruction to paste your key is really an instruction to replace one. And the security group the page never prints opens 22, 80 and 8080 to 0.0.0.0/0, under a comment reading “SSH access from the VPC”. The port is open for the reader's own verification rather than for Terraform, which keeps tf-post-apply-operations's no-network-access argument intact, but a learner copying the configuration inherits it unremarked. The two HashiCorp cloud-init sources split and neither says so: this tutorial shows the file() path and never uses cloudinit_config, while tf-post-apply-operations shows cloudinit_config and has no end-to-end example — and the tutorial's Next Steps links the hashicorp/cloudinit provider it did not use. Neither shows templatefile() feeding user_data, which is the combination B7 builds toward without landing. One thing it does not demonstrate despite being the ASG argument's exhibit: runcmd installs the demo app, and the reader starts it by hand over SSH, so no service is shown coming up unattended. Also recorded: sudo su terraform on the first runcmd line cannot put the following lines under that user, since cloud-init writes all string entries into one script run later by scripts_user; the export GOPATH / export HOME pair two lines down is what actually carries the intent. Not measured — the tutorial needs a real AWS account. Freshness: the page is undated like every tutorial, and the repo is pinned hard at aws ~> 5.47.0 with a committed lock at exactly 5.47.0, a major line behind the v6.x provider Ch17 covers. Nav gains a Provision collection group at rung 3, one of its six tutorials captured; Packer is the remaining link from tf-post-apply-operations. A1 stays ⬜.

2026-08-27 (third) — tf-post-apply-operations captured, closing the gap the previous entry opened, and it is the better half of the pair. This is the 114 lines that left provisioners.mdx on 2025-12-04, and it holds the strongest sentence in either page: passing data at creation time “is required when you use your cloud provider to automatically launch and destroy servers in a group because individual servers will launch unattended when Terraform is not available to provision them.” That is TUR Ch8's ASG argument in HashiCorp's own words, and the split put it on the page a reader looking up provisioner syntax never opens. Folded into A1 item 1 and into the topic page. What it still does not give is the handoff. “Use configuration management tools” is one bullet in its Overview and is never mentioned again — no seam, no inventory, no example — so pyinfra remains the only source in this collection that shows where Terraform hands over. The gap A1's handoff callout was written to fill is confirmed open at the source. Four of the thirteen resources in its per-cloud argument table should not be copied, each checked against that provider's own repository documentation. aws_launch_configuration carries “WARNING: The use of launch configurations is discouraged in favor of launch templates” and sits in the same row as its replacement. azurerm_virtual_machine is “superseded … feature-frozen”, and the page's own example two paragraphs earlier uses azurerm_linux_virtual_machine, the replacement the table omits. azurerm_virtual_machine_scale_set is outright “deprecated … will be removed in the future”. And google_compute_instance_group is wrong rather than stale — it has no metadata argument at all (name, zone, description, instances, named_port, project, network, deletion_policy is the whole set), because it is an unmanaged group of instances that already exist; the resource that pairs with google_compute_instance for cloud-init data is google_compute_instance_template, which has metadata and metadata_startup_script. Two smaller findings. Its cloudinit_config example sets gzip and base64_encode to false without comment; both default to true and base64_encode “cannot be disabled if gzip is true”, which is the same default that makes TID Ch10's aws_instance.user_data listing miswired. And the data source is called three different things on one page (cloudinit-config, cloud-config, cloudinit_config), with the hashicorp/cloudinit provider never named in prose. A capture-hygiene refinement on the previous entry. This file's last_modified is 2025-12-04 and is correct — it matches its only content commit. The rule is mechanical: the field is trustworthy on a file created after the date-metadata mechanism existed, and untrustworthy where it was backfilled, as on tf-provisioners. Its frontmatter is wrong about something else, though: page_title and description are byte-identical to the provisioners page's, so the alternatives page advertises itself as being about provisioners, and the description carries “config-init” for cloud-init. One blob SHA across v1.14.x, v1.15.x and v1.16.x. One rung missing from its own ladder. Its Run CLI commands and Execute remote scripts sections say only to open a feature request with the provider, and neither mentions the actions block (Terraform 1.14, the same release as this page), which is a sibling in the same nav group. Both hands-on tutorials it links are now captured: tut-cloud-init and tut-packer. Nav at rung 1, above Provisioners in the Extend CRUD operations group, matching the sidebar. Topic page Provisioners and escape hatches extended in place. A1 stays ⬜.

2026-08-27 (later) — Topic page Provisioners and escape hatches written, promoting the backlog entry that had been sitting on three sources and now has four. The synthesis the page exists for is that each source objects for a reason none of the others state: HashiCorp on modelling (“Terraform cannot predictably model provisioner behaviors”) plus the network-and-credentials cost, TID on portability (a remote provisioner codes a network-topology decision into the module), TUR on operational visibility (User Data is in the console with a log at /var/log/cloud-init*.log, and “Provisioners take effect only while Terraform is running and don't work with ASGs at all”), and these notes on failure semantics (on_failure defaults to fail, which taints). Only the fourth changes behaviour rather than taste. Writing it turned up a hard constraint stated in none of the four sources, and A1 now carries it as the fourth hole in when = destroy. A destroy-time provisioner and its connection block may reference only self, count.index, each.key, path.* and terraform.* — no variables, no locals, no other resources. Reproduced on Terraform v1.15.8: var.msg and local.m each fail at init, not at plan, with “Invalid reference from destroy provisioner”, while self.id, path.module and terraform.workspace pass. The rule is onlySelfRefs in internal/configs/provisioner.go at tag v1.15.8, and its allowed roots are wider than its own error message admits — path and terraform are permitted but unmentioned, and locals are rejected without being named. The bite is on connection: a destroy-time remote-exec cannot take its user, key or bastion address from a variable, which is a strong argument for keeping destroy-time work to local-exec. A TUR error corrected by measurement. 08-production-grade records on_failure as taking “continue” or “abort”; abort is not a value. On v1.15.8 it fails with “Invalid on_failure keyword … requires one of the following keywords: continue or fail”, matching internal/configs/provisioner.go. In the same pass, TID's “bare keyword, not a string” held as guidance but is softer than stated: when = "destroy" is valid with a deprecation warning, not an error. The page also collects what was already scattered — the three connection positions including the removed one, the bastion_host contradiction and the undocumented bastion defaulting, the SSH-versus-WinRM script-path split, the environment/interpreter/working_dir/quiet gap in both books' argument lists, the null_resource → terraform_data moved path, and the handoff seam with its outputs-versus-state blast-radius choice. Alternatives are ranked with the actions block (Terraform 1.14) at the top as the provider-native successor. Nav gains it under Topics; tf-provisioners, tf-terraform-data and pyinfra link back. A1 stays ⬜ — a topic page is not a chapter.

2026-08-27 — tf-provisioners captured, which is the page **A1 item 1 has been pointing at without a note behind it — and the URL it pointed at is no longer the page.** HashiCorp consolidated the provisioner documentation during the v1.14 cycle: syntax, connection, file, local-exec, remote-exec and null_resource all now redirect to a single /language/provisioners, verified by navigation on 2026-08-27, with null_resource landing on the Run provisioners without a resource anchor that recommends terraform_data. That generalises the one redirect tf-block-resource recorded on 2026-08-02, and the path's item-1 link is updated. The restructure also moved the argument this topic most needs out of the page. A commit titled “split post-apply ops topic” on 2025-12-04 cut 187 lines from provisioners.mdx and created a 114-line post-apply-operations.mdx beside it, so the surviving page carries only the cost side — Terraform cannot model provisioner behaviour, and provisioners need direct network access plus credentials. Post-apply operations is not captured, and A1 now names it as the next capture. One contradiction inside the docs set, settled in the source. The provisioners page says “bastion_host: Set to true to enable the bastion host connection”; the resource block reference types it string and calls it the bastion's address. internal/communicator/ssh/provisioner.go at tag v1.15.8 does connInfo.BastionHost = v.AsString() and takes the bastion path when the value is non-empty, so the reference is right and the usage page is wrong. Following it literally is not even an error, because HCL coerces the bool: you get a connection to a host named true. The same function shows what neither page says — every bastion attribute defaults to its non-bastion counterpart (bastion_user←user, bastion_password←password, bastion_private_key←private_key, bastion_certificate←certificate, bastion_port←port), so a jump host sharing credentials needs bastion_host and nothing else. Both folded into A1 item 2. Two smaller source-settled items. %RAND% is a full int31 rendered decimal (ssh/communicator.go), so its digit count varies; and the Windows script-path default the page prints, C:/windows/temp/terraform_%RAND%.cmd, is the SSH communicator's — the WinRM communicator uses C:/Temp/terraform_%RAND%.cmd (winrm/provisioner.go), which no captured page states. And its requirements list is wrong about its own floor: “Terraform v0.9 is required to use provisioners” is really the floor for destroy-time provisioners, which the v0.9.0 changelog lists as a headline feature (terraform#11329) while carrying provisioner fixes from 0.7.x and 0.8.x in the same file. Two gaps worth knowing before teaching from it: the page offers only the four-step count = 0 dance for removing a resource that has a destroy-time provisioner and never mentions the removed-block route that tf-destroy-resource and tf-block-removed document; and it cites terraform taint without the deprecation tf-cli-state-taint records. Two typos noted (“set the when argument a Terraform stage control”, “configure add provisioner and connection blocks”). A capture-hygiene finding that applies beyond this page: the file's auto-generated last_modified frontmatter reads 2025-11-19, the day the v1.14 branch was cut, and was backfilled by a later commit — so it predates the 2025-12-04 edit to the same file. On developer.hashicorp.com, treat that field as a lower bound. The v1.15.x and v1.16.x copies share one blob SHA, so the page is unchanged between those releases even though the version selector offers both; the terraform-docs course index now records that v1.16.x is latest. Nav at rung 1, under a new Extend CRUD operations group, which is where the site's own sidebar puts it. Topic backlog entry provisioners-and-escape-hatches gains this as its fourth and canonical source. A1 stays ⬜.

2026-08-26 (Ch17 §6, emulator IAM enforcement) — A written chapter claimed the lab could not show something the emulator has been able to show since 1.5.30, and the correction ships with the lab that proves it. §6's cross-account danger box said "the lab cannot show you this" about the double opt-in. Read in Floci's source at 1.6.0, the tag labs/docker-compose.yml pins, StsQueryHandler.handleAssumeRole mints the session and then calls enforceTrustPolicy, which permits the call in exactly three cases: enforcement disabled (FLOCI_SERVICES_IAM_ENFORCEMENT_ENABLED, default false), the role unknown to Floci (permissive on purpose, commented as backward-compatible), or the trust policy allowing the caller. The caller's half is separate and equally real: IamActionRegistry maps a query-protocol Action=AssumeRole to sts:AssumeRole, so IamEnforcementFilter evaluates the caller's identity policies for it, bypassing only the key test, an access key IAM has never seen, and an unresolvable action. So the green lab run had three independent reasons to be green, and the box named none of them. Trust enforcement shipped in 1.5.30 (floci-io/floci#1552), which is why the original sentence was defensible when written and is not now. Measured twice from the committed lab directory, each time on a freshly restarted emulator, Terraform 1.15.8 / AWS provider 6.61.0 / Floci 1.6.0, with identical results: a role that does not exist gets a session and then fails on the session's first call (AccessDenied … sts:GetCallerIdentity); a role trusting another account fails at provider configuration with the principal and the resource both named; a caller lacking sts:AssumeRole fails at the same position with neither named; granting the action brings the run back. The third grant the section never had to mention is the role's own policies, since a session inherits them. New 🧪 Lab 5 walks all four states, labs/chapter17/section6/trust-policy/ holds the four policy documents, and labs/chapter17/section6/README.md gives the per-directory cleanup, which is recreating the container rather than a destroy, because the emulator holds this state in memory. Two supporting changes: labs/tf-docker.sh and labs/tf-docker.ps1 now take the override's credentials from AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID / AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY when set, falling back to test, without which no lab can run as a principal enforcement can see; and the chapter's Emulation is not AWS warning no longer says trust policies go unenforced. Also recorded in floci-facts: AssumeRolePolicyEvaluator handles AWS principals only (*, bare account ID, root ARN, glob principal ARN, assumed-role canonicalised back to its role), never Service principals or NotPrincipal; and 1.6.0 seeds 58 managed policies, not the 50 noted from :latest in July. I8 stays ✅ — the contradiction and its fix landed in the same pass.

2026-08-25 (later) — Ch17's duration row fixed, and I8 is back to ✅. The row gave the maximum as "from 15 minutes up to the role's maximum", a paraphrase of the AWS provider's own description, four lines above the paragraph that teaches chaining by repeating the block. It now carries the exception on the row itself, and a new !!! warning after the chaining paragraph gives the rule with both quotes, the refusal rather than a silent clamp, and the reason a web-identity exchange escapes it. The sweep found only the one copy: up to the role's maximum and maximum session duration setting appear nowhere else in docs/book/, docs/sources/ or docs/reference/, and the assume_role reading notes make no duration claim at all. check_quotes.py verifies the four new quotes against the AWS caches, and the six it still reports unverified in this chapter are unchanged from before the edit. Build clean.

2026-08-25 — A6 gains the one-hour role-chaining ceiling, an AWS limit the Terraform provider documentation walks you straight past. The question that surfaced it was whether the backend and the apply should hold separate credentials, which A7 already answers with HashiCorp's own multi-account recipe: the backend authenticates as the administrative account's principal and the provider assumes the environment role. Under OIDC that split has two shapes, and they are not equivalent. Chaining from one bootstrap role costs the whole run its session length. AWS defines role chaining as one role assuming a second, and "Role chaining limits your AWS Management Console, AWS CLI or AWS API role session to a maximum of one hour. It applies regardless of the maximum session duration configured for individual roles." Over-asking is refused rather than clamped. The provider never warns. hashicorp/aws raises role chaining three times, including "IAM Role Chaining is supported by specifying the roles to assume in order", and gives duration one identical description on assume_role and assume_role_with_web_identity alike, "a value from 15 minutes up to the maximum session duration setting for the role", which holds only when the block is not chaining. The escape is that a web-identity exchange is not chaining at all, since its base is a token and not a role session, so its DurationSeconds reaches the role's full maximum of up to 12 hours and the word chaining appears on that page only in the session-tag paragraph. So the two-role split wants two independent exchanges of one identity token, not a bootstrap role with two hops. ⚠️ This makes a written chapter stale. Book Ch 17 teaches chaining by repeating the block and carries the unqualified duration wording in its argument table, so I8 flips to 🔄 with the missing qualification named. Cached as aws-iam-role-chaining.txt, aws-sts-assumerole.txt and aws-sts-assumerolewithwebidentity.txt.

2026-08-25 (Ch17 §2, OSS deferral research) — A reader question exposed a claim that was true and useless. §2 ended its early-evaluation subsection with "OpenTofu 1.12.5 has no equivalent flag at all", which reads as though open source had not got round to provider deferral. It considered it and withdrew it. OpenTofu 1.11.4: "Providers are not configured anymore with DeferralAllowed capability of OpenTofu since having that created unwanted behaviour from some providers." 1.11.2 reverted the automatic -exclude= suggestion while keeping the technique, and in the same release made planning with unknown provider configuration work again for helm and kubernetes "as long as the configuration is carefully written to avoid the plan phase actually depending on those values." ⚠️ A tool divergence §2 had never recorded. Measured: -exclude=resource is documented in tofu plan -help on OpenTofu 1.12.5 and does not exist on Terraform 1.15.8, neither in plan -help nor in internal/command/arguments/. Now an OpenTofu box in §2. The orchestrators do not close the gap. Terragrunt (docs read from the local clone at v1.1.3) automates the split rather than removing it: run --all apply "will not attempt to deploy the config until all the units referenced in dependency blocks have been applied", so a downstream unit reads applied outputs, and planning before that needs mock_outputs, which its own docs caution give a plan that "doesn't give you any indication of what is actually going to be created". Terrakube (2.32.2) sequences steps inside a single workspace and has no cross-workspace ordering, so it replaces HCP Terraform's platform half, not Stacks. ⚠️ Caught in my own draft: a fabricated citation. I wrote "Terragrunt is Chapter 30's subject"; no such mapping exists, the book's numbering only evidences 21, 25, 27 and 31. Replaced with a reference by name, because an ordinal citation rots the moment an entry is inserted above it. Also this session: the -replace half of the intermittency is now measured and documented as a fourth lab step, const = true is disambiguated from §2's "evaluated early", and the process-per-configuration claim was re-measured end to end. I8 stays ✅.

2026-08-24 — Chapter 17 written — I8 (Provider configuration in depth) ✅ (docs/book/ch17-provider-configuration.md), which completes the Intermediate level. The provider guide's rules were verified at tag v6.61.0 and cached in aws-enhanced-region-support: changing region forces replacement (measured, # forces replacement on the plan line), removing it does not, import takes an @<region> suffix, and the value is validated against the partition. The migration is a zero-diff refactor, and its apply is not zero-impact. apply -refresh-only, then swap provider = aws.replica for region = "us-west-2", and the plan reads No changes. Corrected in version-facts, Ch2 and tf-aws-create. Seven behaviours measured that no note recorded, all on Terraform 1.15.8 / OpenTofu 1.12.5 / AWS provider 6.61.0: the implied empty default reports its source position as on <empty> line 0 with (source code not available), which is as clear a statement of "this configuration is in no file" as Terraform gives; a partial providers map does not cancel inheritance, proven by a child bucket landing in the root default's region while the map named only aws.replica, settling terraform#35781 in favour of the per-provider reading; deleting a provider block whose resources are still in state gives Error: Provider configuration not present, and the recovery is provider-block-back → destroy → block-out; each.value in a providers map is parsed as a provider reference, so Terraform reports a provider named hashicorp/each rather than a type error, which is what "static association" means concretely; constraint intersection prints itself (Finding hashicorp/aws versions matching "~> 6.0, >= 7.0.0") and points at terraform providers; OpenTofu emits a proactive warning, Provider configuration for_each matches resource, on the first apply of the same-collection antipattern, before any removal has been attempted; and Terraform rejects provider for_each with The provider argument name "for_each" is reserved for use by Terraform in a future version, which is a roadmap statement rather than a refusal. ⚠️ One docs defect found: Providers Within Modules still quotes the v0.13-era Error: Module does not support count; 1.15.8 prints Error: Module is incompatible with count, for_each, and depends_on. 2026-08-24 — Six frozen-scope verification passes over Ch16 sections 2, 4, 5, 7, 8 and 9, none of which had reached this log. Its closing callout said five state-writing paths lose the forced backup. Four do. The fifth item in §10's structure is a hole rather than a path: the backup filename is whole seconds, so a second operation inside the same second overwrites the first. The count was right for holes and wrong for paths. §4 mis-attributed two quotes. Terraform answers Removed resource still exists, cites the resource block, and gives no instruction; OpenTofu 1.12.5 answers Removed resource block still exists, cites the removed block because its Subject is rs.DeclRange, and ends "Please remove the resource block." Each engine supplies the half the other is missing. Its OpenTofu counter box also quoted a transcript from labs/chapter16/opentofu, which is a resource-level lifecycle { destroy = false } and not a removed block at all; re-measured in section5/opentofu-bare, the three claims stand. §7 corrected a mechanism that had spread. The PowerShell flag trap breaks at the first . in the value, not at the =, and the = stays attached to the left half, so -target=aws_s3_bucket.a becomes -target=aws_s3_bucket and .a. A value with no dot survives, which is what makes the trap look intermittent. The consequence is not a misplaced file either: the stray fragment is an extra positional argument, so the command refuses to run. "A destroy plan suppresses the drift note" is false; an ordinary terraform plan prints no drift note either. precomputeDiffs in internal/command/jsonformat/diff.go installs an AlwaysMatcher over drifted attributes only when the mode is plans.RefreshOnlyMode, so the note is a property of -refresh-only rather than of destroy mode. The section's point survives once attributed correctly: detection happens on every run, reporting is what the flag is for. §9 stopped borrowing its numbers. The -target subsection had taken its measurement, its worked example and its voice from HashiCorp's Target resources tutorial, and none of it was reproducible here. Three new lab directories under labs/chapter16/section9/ replace it: target-graph gives a 6/⅙/4 closure table from this repository's own configuration and an apply that fails on BucketNotEmpty, turning "downstream is left stale" into an exit code; target-desync is the smallest configuration whose successful targeted apply leaves two outputs describing different moments; target-exclude measures OpenTofu 1.12.5's -exclude instead of quoting its changelog. 2026-08-23 (later) — Three further verification passes over Ch16 §10, and the pattern worth recording is that each pass found defects the previous pass introduced. ⚠️ A sourced claim that contradicted this repository's own cache. §10 listed a Terraform → OpenTofu move as a real use of state replace-provider. It is not, and opentofu-migration-mechanics already said so: internal/tofumigrate at v1.12.5 updates the in-memory view of state to registry.opentofu.org addresses on init, on every local plan and apply, and on state show, editing a copy rather than the stored file. An explicit source = "registry.terraform.io/…" pin defeats it by design. The reverse direction is the genuine case — opentofu.org appears nowhere under internal/ at v1.15.8 — so an OpenTofu-written state means nothing to Terraform. tf-cmd-state-replace-provider carried the same error and is corrected. ⚠️ A table that contradicted the same chapter's §3. §10's Preview column read a flat "no" for state mv and state rm; both have -dry-run at v1.15.8, and §3 already used it. Measured: prints Would move … / Would remove …, leaves state untouched, and writes no backup either. state push and replace-provider have no such flag, so the wholesale overwrite is the one operation that cannot be rehearsed. ⚠️ A causal claim that was a guess. The chapter told readers not to use -refresh-only on an encoding-corrupted state, reasoning about which attributes a provider returns. Measured instead, three times: it reports "found no differences", repairs nothing, and rewrites the raw E9 byte as EF BF BD — U+FFFD encoded correctly — so the lossy substitution becomes a valid, wrong character. And the follow-up falsified the correction's own generalisation: "any state write does this" is false. state push, state mv and plan all leave the raw E9 intact; only the paths that decode state through the provider and type system normalise it. The state family treats state as a file, everything else as data — the same boundary the backup rule draws, seen from the other side. One recovery detail measured and worth keeping: immediately after a bad push the local backend's single-slot terraform.tfstate.backup still holds good UTF-8, while the forced timestamped backup holds the already-corrupt bytes; the -refresh-only run then overwrites the good one, so the window is a single state-writing apply wide. Two OpenTofu divergences added, both measured: tofu state identities does not exist, and tofu registers the aliases state ls, state move and state remove that terraform does not — so a script written against tofu does not necessarily run under terraform. OpenTofu's state hub also lists no subcommands at all, where HashiCorp's prints six of eight, and it carries the identical false remote-state sentence, inherited at the fork. ⚠️ The sweep that was incomplete the first time: the inverted remote-backup claim had also reached docs/reference/glossary.md and the chapter's own Summary bullet, neither of which the first pass touched — a reminder that the standing "sweep every copy" rule includes the chapter's own back matter. labs/chapter16/section10/ now has a fourth directory, ansi-push/, and the section's -dry-run, -backup and encoding transcripts all name the directory they were run in. I7 stays ✅.

2026-08-23 — Chapter 16 §10 re-verified end to end against v1.15.8, and the family's headline rule turned out to be recorded backwards. tf-cmd-state's second rule — the subcommands "work with remote state just as if it was local state" and "backups are still written to disk" — is false in its last clause. Measured against an S3 backend in the new labs/chapter16/section10/remote/: state mv and state rm write no backup anywhere, taint/untaint likewise, and -backup is refused outright with "legacy options that operate on a local state file only." The cause is in internal/command/state_meta.go at tag v1.15.8, which builds the timestamped path unconditionally and then applies it only behind if lb, ok := realState.(*statemgr.Filesystem); ok, under a comment asserting the backend "should always be" local. So the forced-backup guarantee belongs to the local backend, not to the terraform state family — the opposite of what both the docs and this log previously recorded, and the direction that costs the recovery path rather than the confidentiality one. The tf-cmd-state note now carries the correction and the access-control pairing it drew with tf-state-backends and gitlab-tf-state is withdrawn. A fourth hole found while measuring: the backup filename is time.Now().UTC().Unix(), whole seconds, so two state operations in the same second share one filename and the second overwrites the first. Eight runs of labs/chapter16/section10/same-second/ from scratch gave 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 backup files — seven collisions out of eight, and on a collision the surviving file holds the state after the first move, so the original snapshot is gone. It is a race, not a rule, and a migration script issuing several state mv calls is exactly the shape that hits it. Also: the family has eight subcommands on v1.15.8, and the hub documents six. state push's omission was already recorded; terraform state identities has no reference page at all — /terraform/cli/commands/state/identities returns 404 and it is absent from the site's own search — while being registered in commands.go since v1.12.0 and working: terraform state identities -json prints each resource's identity object, and without the flag it refuses. Two smaller corrections into Ch16 §10: refresh was described as having -auto-approve permanently on, when it has no such flag and no approval step to skip; and "three commands in this chapter write state" undercounted a chapter that also covers taint, untaint, state rm and state push. Three lab directories added under labs/chapter16/section10/ (backups/, remote/, same-second/) with a README giving each one's starting file, expected output and cleanup — §10 previously asserted a backup filename "from the lab" with no lab behind it, and the timestamp it quoted was unreproducible. I7 stays ✅: everything here sharpens Ch16 rather than contradicting a claim the chapter shipped, and the falsified sentence was the documentation's, not the chapter's own measurement.

2026-08-21 — tf-cmd-state-push captured, and it is the capture where reading the source changed the conclusion. Both documented safety checks reproduce on v1.15.8 against a non-empty state: an unrelated lineage fails with “cannot import state with lineage … over unrelated state with lineage …”, a lower serial with “cannot import state with serial 2 over newer state with serial 5”, both exit 1, and -force pushes the downgrade through silently — serial 5 became serial 2 with no output at all, since a successful push prints nothing. The first test showed neither check firing, which looked like a local-backend exemption. It is not. statemgr.CheckValidImport (source at tag v1.15.8, matching the tested binary) returns early in three undocumented cases: an empty destination state is “always okay to overwrite… regardless of its lineage/serial”, a legacy state with no lineage allows anything, and same lineage + same serial + identical content is permitted. The practical form: pushing into a workspace whose state was emptied — by a destroy, or by an earlier bad push — is unguarded, no -force required. ⚠️ And this command breaks the forced-backup rule the family hub states. An accepted push leaves no terraform.tfstate.*.backup, and internal/command/state_push.go contains no backup handling at all where state_mv.go threads one through. “All terraform state subcommands that modify the state write backup files” is overstated by exactly its most destructive member. The I7 callout and the tf-cmd-state note now carry the exception. Two more divergences: the web page omits -lock and -lock-timeout, which the binary documents, and its UTF-8/BOM example is tf-cmd-state-pull's pasted — terraform state push | Set-Content terraform.tfstate pipes an empty stream into the state file, since push takes a PATH and prints nothing. With this, the Manually Update State section is 15 of 16 pages — only taint and state rm remain. I7 stays ⬜.

2026-08-21 — tf-cmd-state-pull captured, and it breaks an assumption this path has been making since tf-state-refactor landed: that terraform state pull > backup is a copy of the state. It is not. The command “upgrades the local copy to the latest state file version compatible with locally-installed Terraform”, so “you cannot use this command to inspect the Terraform version of the remote state.” Measured on v1.15.8: a file reading "terraform_version": "1.9.0" came back as "1.15.8", with "check_results": null materialised on the way out. serial and lineage are preserved, which is what keeps the pull-edit-push loop legal at all. Two callouts added to I7: use it as a rollback source, not as evidence of what wrote the original, and take the automatic terraform.tfstate.<unix>.backup when a byte copy is what you need. The command is read-only — no -lock flags, no backup, only -var/-var-file — which independently confirms the forced-backup boundary recorded with tf-cmd-state. ⚠️ And its PowerShell instruction is the third in this collection that does not survive testing. State files must be “UTF-8 without a byte order mark”, and the page says to pipe into Set-Content. On PowerShell 7.6.5 that is redundant, since plain > is already BOM-free UTF-8. On Windows PowerShell 5.1 > produces UTF-16LE with an FF FE BOM, and Set-Content avoids the BOM but writes ANSI — é lands as E9 rather than C3 A9, so the file is not the UTF-8 the same paragraph demands. -Encoding UTF8 on 5.1 writes UTF-8 with a BOM, so the reliable form is [System.IO.File]::WriteAllText(path, text, (New-Object System.Text.UTF8Encoding $false)), verified. After tf-cmd-state-show and tf-cmd-state-mv, all three Windows instructions captured in this section have failed on the shell in front of me — recorded in I7 as a standing caution rather than three separate incidents. I7 stays ⬜; taint, state rm and state push remain.

2026-08-21 — tf-cli-state-recover captured — three sentences, and it closes the loop the forced-backup rule opens. The section exists for “an accident when performing other state manipulation actions”, which is what all those terraform.tfstate.<unix>.backup files are for: tf-cmd-state forces them, tf-cmd-state-mv measured them, this page is where they get used. The documented repair loop is pull → fix by hand → push, with the fix step undescribed. tut-cloud-state-api supplies what is missing on the HCP side — a hand-edited state needs its serial bumped or the backend rejects it — and that is the piece to carry across, since nothing in the CLI section mentions it. Step one is force-unlock, with a sequencing rule stated plainly: “We do not recommend unlocking until you determine what caused the lock to get stuck.” Diagnose, then unlock — consistent with tf-cmd-force-unlock and tf-state-locking, and structurally enforced by the required LOCK_ID nonce. ⚠️ And it confirms the omission flagged when the family hub was captured: state push is documented here and nowhere in the terraform state command index, so a reader navigating by that index never learns the command exists. With this, the Manually Update State section is 12 of 16 pages captured — taint, state rm, state pull and state push remain. I7 stays ⬜.

2026-08-21 — tf-cmd-state-replace-provider captured, and it turns out to be the **only state-writing command in this topic that asks before acting.** Verified on v1.15.8: without -auto-approve it prints a preview naming every affected address, then asks “Do you want to make these changes? Only 'yes' will be accepted to continue.”, and with no terminal attached it aborts — Error asking for approval: EOF. That is worth a callout because the approval defaults across this topic run backwards from the risk: replace-provider rewrites a source string and asks; tf-cmd-state-mv rebinds objects to new addresses and does not; tf-cmd-refresh can empty state on bad credentials and cannot be made to ask. Added as a table in I7. It also already has the property the docs use to argue for language blocks over CLI surgery — a preview of the outcome before committing to it, which is exactly the case tf-state-remove makes for removed over state rm and tf-block-moved for moved over state mv. Mechanics worth keeping: the unit of operation is a provider, not an address — “update all resources using the 'from' provider”, with no address argument, so it is the one command in the family that cannot be scoped to one resource. Both arguments accept the shorthand (hashicorp/null matched the fully-qualified registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/null in state and expanded the same way on the destination side), despite the argument names saying FQN. And the forced-backup sentence “Due to the destructive nature of this command, backups are required” appears in this page's own text — where tf-cmd-state-mv's web page omits it and only the binary's help carries it, on the more destructive of the two. The run wrote the timestamped terraform.tfstate.<unix>.backup form measured earlier. One cosmetic bug recorded: “Changing 1 resources”. I7 stays ⬜ — state rm, state pull and state push are what remain in the family.

2026-08-21 — tf-cmd-state-mv captured, and it hands **I7 the sharpest argument yet for preferring moved blocks — plus two divergences between the web page and the binary.** ⚠️ The race window. The page's own warning: in a collaborative environment you “must ensure that nobody makes any other changes between your configuration change and your terraform state mv command, because otherwise they might inadvertently create a plan that will destroy the old object and create a new object at the new address.” A CLI refactor is two operations with a gap, and during that gap the repository describes a rename that state does not know about. That is the atomicity argument, and it now sits beside the mechanism argument (tf-block-moved) and the module-author argument (tf-cli-state-move) as a third, independent reason. It is also the same defect that got taint deprecated — intent parked in state ahead of the action. The address rules are stricter than the grammar: both sides must be the same kind of object, and a resource move must keep the same resource type, so state mv relocates and renames but never converts. Non-indexed ↔ indexed is legal in both directions ('packet_device.main' → 'packet_device.all[0]'), which is worth knowing since it is usually credited to moved. ⚠️ The page omits the one thing this command can do that moved cannot. terraform state mv -help leads with it — “can also move to a destination address in a completely different state file… refactoring one configuration into multiple separately managed Terraform configurations” — while the web reference mentions cross-state moves only as the legacy -state-out flag. That is the operation tf-state-refactor and tut-state-cli are built on. Two things verified rather than read. The page's PowerShell quoting row fails on PowerShell 7 exactly as tf-cmd-state-show's does — '…[\"key\"]' errors with “Invalid character… This character is not used within the language” plus “Index value required”, while plain single quotes report Successfully moved 1 object(s). And the forced backup is named terraform.tfstate.<unix-timestamp>.backup, which corrects the collision guess recorded with tf-cmd-state: automatic backups accumulate, they do not overwrite each other or the local backend's own file. The callout above now says so. One more page flaw: -dry-run is documented as reporting matches “without actually 'forgetting' any of them” — state rm's text pasted in. The binary's help has it right. I7 stays ⬜.

2026-08-21 — tf-cli-state-move captured — the one section index in this collection that argues a position instead of listing links, and it supplies a second, better argument for moved blocks. The path had the mechanism justification (tf-block-moved: the state rename happens before the plan is computed). This page gives the audience one: refactoring features “document in your module exactly how the resource names have changed over time”, and “users of your module do not need to take any unusual extra steps.” A state mv fixes your state; a moved block fixes everyone's — the CLI path cannot be shipped to consumers. Added as a callout in I7 beside the mechanism one. It also confirms an inference the tf-cli-state capture had to leave as a guess. Terraform loses track of an object when you rename it, move it to another module, “or change its provider” — so a provider change is an address change, and replace-provider sits under Moving Resources for a real reason rather than as a filing quirk. And it states the default outcome as normal rather than as a hazard: on a changed address Terraform destroys and recreates, and “usually that's fine”. Everything in the section exists for the minority case where the object must survive, which is a cleaner framing than the path's own destroy-avoidance one. ⚠️ One gap recorded: the page recommends language features over CLI surgery “for most cases”, then lists state rm without mentioning the removed block, the language feature for exactly that operation — the one tf-state-remove says HashiCorp prefers because it “lets you preview the results of the operation.” An omission rather than a contradiction, but it points readers at the command the docs elsewhere point them away from. Also kept: state rm plus import is stated here as the documented cross-configuration handoff, matching tf-state-refactor's removed + import recommendation and the same leaving-is-not-reversible asymmetry. Nav at rung 1 under Moving Resources. I7 stays ⬜ — none of the three commands it indexes is captured yet.

2026-08-21 — tf-cmd-untaint captured, and it settles why one half of a deprecated pair is not deprecated. taint was a way to schedule a replacement, and -replace does that directly. untaint answers a different question — Terraform thinks this object is damaged and I disagree — which no flag expresses, so the command stays. The page also states the marker itself better than anything else captured: tainted means an object “might be damaged and so a future Terraform plan ought to replace it”, hedged in both halves because it records a suspicion rather than a finding. Its auto-tainting trigger is narrower than the overview's two: “an error… during a multi-step 'create' action”, which arguably subsumes the failed-provisioner case, since a provisioner is a step of the create. Read together the rule is the marker is set when a create was interrupted partway. A practical consequence worth knowing before you untaint anything: changing your mind back needs no re-taint — “you can create and apply a plan to replace it without first re-tainting the object”, apply -replace="aws_instance.example[0]". ⚠️ And a correction to the scope of the forced-backup rule folded in above. untaint modifies state and takes the state lock, but it is not a terraform state subcommand, and its -backup is grouped with -state/-state-out as legacy, local-backend-only — the flags tf-backend-local records the docs as having disowned. So untaint against a remote backend writes state with no automatic backup. The forced backup is a property of the state command family, not of state modification, which is now stated that way in the callout. Two glossary rows corrected while wiring this in: the old single taint/untaint row called both commands deprecated. They are now three rows — the deprecated command, the marker Terraform sets itself, and the command that is not deprecated. Also recorded: the address argument is the strict parser (one instance, like state show), -allow-missing makes the command idempotent by forgiving only a missing resource and nothing else, and -ignore-remote-version dates to 0.14.1 with the remote-workspace compatibility checks it opts out of (feature-history). Nav at rung 1 under Forcing Re-creation (Tainting). I7 stays ⬜.

2026-08-21 — tf-cli-state-taint captured, and it **corrects a claim this path made two entries ago.** The Re-create resources link and the sidebar group Forcing Re-creation (Tainting) both point at a tainting-named URL with -replace in neither label — from which the tf-cli-state entry inferred that a reader following the sidebar meets the deprecated pair first. The destination says otherwise. It opens on -replace as the manual workflow and names taint only in its last paragraph, to deprecate it. So the staleness there is naming, not guidance, and the genuine index-lags-reference case in this collection is tf-cli-state-inspect on refresh. Both notes and the I7 callout now draw that line. What the page adds is a reason for the deprecation that no other captured source states as mechanism: -replace is preferred because it “avoids the need to create an interim state snapshot with a tainted object.” The path, TID Ch5 and tut-state-cli all say taint mutated state out-of-band with no plan to review; this is HashiCorp saying the same thing structurally — taint had to write state to record the intent, -replace carries the intent through the plan, so state is written once at apply like any other change. And tainting is a state field, not only a command. Terraform sets it itself when it can infer damage, in two named cases: an object “partially created in the remote system”, and a failed provisioner step — which is the other half of the on_failure = fail sentence already in A1. The status is what makes untaint still useful after the command that wrote it by hand was deprecated: it is the override for Terraform's own inference, and after it the object is “ready for use by any downstream resource declarations”, which is the reminder that a tainted object poisons its dependents too. One sentence worth keeping for the resource model itself: Terraform cannot detect a crashed process inside a running VM “because Terraform only directly manages the machine as a whole” — the cleanest statement in the captured docs of where the resource abstraction stops, and the same boundary tut-state-import hits from the adoption side and pyinfra from the configuration-management side. Three typos recorded (“does not have no way”, “when you meed to replace”, “in a tainted states”). Nav at rung 1 under Forcing Re-creation (Tainting). I7 stays ⬜.

2026-08-21 — tf-cli-state-inspect captured — four sentences, and the interesting part is what it omits. All three commands it names were already captured (tf-cmd-state-list, tf-cmd-state-show, tf-cmd-refresh), so this is not a gap-filling capture. ⚠️ It describes terraform refresh in neutral present tense with no deprecation notice and no mention of -refresh-only, one click above the reference that opens with “This command is deprecated” and explains that the command is apply -refresh-only -auto-approve with -auto-approve unremovable. That turns an observation into a pattern: the path already flagged tut-state-cli's final exercise for teaching bare refresh, and tf-cli-state for routing Re-create resources to taint/untaint without naming -replace. Three index pages, all lagging the references they point at, so the I7 callout now says to read the reference before trusting the index that led you there. The page's one genuine contribution is the only justification anything captured gives for a standalone refresh: refreshing happens automatically during plans and applies, “but not when interacting with state directly” — nothing in the state family refreshes, so state read through those subcommands is as stale as the last plan left it. Two smaller things kept. The group is defined as “reading and updating state without taking any other actions”, so its cut is no infrastructure side effects, not read-only — which is why state list and state show are filed here and under Inspecting Infrastructure (tf-cli-inspect), where the criterion genuinely is read-only. And state list's filter is described as taking a “partial resource address”, the only place this section names the incomplete-address idea that tf-resource-addressing documents. Nav at rung 1, first in Inspecting State above the refresh note already there. I7 stays ⬜.

2026-08-21 — tf-cmd-state captured — the terraform state hub, whose value is two rules that apply to the whole family and appear on none of the individual command pages. The first is forced backups. “All terraform state subcommands that modify the state write backup files”, the path is set with -backup, read-only subcommands write none, and “backups for state modification can not be disabled… You'll have to remove these files manually.” Folded into I7 as a callout, with the boundary spelled out: the guarantee covers terraform state <subcommand> and not the removed/moved path, which goes through apply — so the config-driven route this topic recommends is exactly the route with no automatic backup. It also sharpens a flaw already recorded on tf-state-refactor: that page's manual terraform state pull > terraform.tfstate.backup not only reuses the local backend's own backup filename, it now also collides with the backup the following state mv writes by itself. The second is that remote state changes nothing except latency and locality — the subcommands “work with remote state just as if it was local state”, each read and write costing “a full network roundtrip”, and “backups are still written to disk”. So a state mv against a remote backend leaves a complete copy of the state file on the machine that ran it, which is a hole in the access-control argument gitlab-tf-state and tf-state-backends make. ⚠️ And the hub is incomplete: it lists six subcommands — list, mv, pull, replace-provider, rm, show — and omits state push, verified to exist with its own reference page (“uploads a local state file to remote state or a local state”) and a sidebar slot beside state pull. The one subcommand that overwrites a state file wholesale is missing from the index of state subcommands; use the sidebar for the full set. Also recorded: the family's output is designed for grep/awk piping, which is the reason tf-cmd-state-list's sort order is specified at all. Nav at rung 1, third in Manually Update State. I7 stays ⬜ — four of the family's six pages are still uncaptured.

2026-08-21 — tf-resource-addressing captured, and it supplies the missing reason behind an asymmetry this path had already recorded as a fact. The page is the grammar — [module path][resource spec], [N] for count, ["KEY"] for for_each — but the load-bearing sentence is a caveat: an incomplete address is legal, and “the meaning depends on the context, so you'll need to refer to the documentation for the specific feature you are using which parses resource addresses.” One grammar, several parsers. That is why import's to takes an instance key, moved takes them on both sides, and removed's from refuses them — nothing in the notation forbids it, each feature decides what completeness it demands. The I7 instance-key table now says so instead of leaving the asymmetry unexplained. The rule worth memorising is about omission, not syntax: “Omitting an index when addressing a resource where count > 1 means that the address references all instances.” Same one level up — module.foo is every resource in every instance of that module call. Added as a callout with the four parsers side by side, because they disagree: state list filters to all instances, state show errors unless the address resolves to exactly one (tf-cmd-state-list, tf-cmd-state-show), -target takes the set and walks dependencies per resource regardless, and state rm takes the set — which is the one that costs something. Two legacy rules recorded for reading old configurations and old advice: module indexes require v0.13+, and a bare resource spec has meant root module only since v0.12, where earlier versions matched the same type and name in any descendant module — so a pre-0.12 terraform taint aws_instance.web reached into child modules and today's identical command does not. One imprecision flagged rather than repeated: the page calls for_each keys “alphanumerical”, but they are arbitrary strings, and HashiCorp's own for_each page keys a set on subnet-012345 (tf-meta-for-each). The quoting in the grammar is what does the work, which is why tf-cmd-state-show needs a whole section on shell escaping. Nav at rung 1, second in Manually Update State as the sidebar has it. I7 stays ⬜.

2026-08-21 — tf-cli-state captured — the Manually Update State section index, and the piece **I7 had been quoting an inventory from without a source behind it.** The page is four paragraphs, and it is the write-side counterpart to tf-cli-inspect: same shape, no mechanics, framing plus links. Three things it supplies. The risk is stated in consequences rather than in cautions — modifying state outside plan/apply “can cause Terraform to lose track of managed resources, leading to increased costs, reduced productivity, or compromised security” — and the backup instruction is unconditional, with no “if remote” or “if a team” qualifier. tf-state-refactor is where that becomes a concrete state pull step, and where the page's own example names the backup file after the one the local backend already writes. plan is named as a writer of state, next to apply, on the section index itself — the same fact tut-state-cli closes on, now stated where a reader meets the group rather than at the end of a tutorial. And the sidebar is the toolkit inventory: Resource Addressing, the state command reference, then Inspecting State, Forcing Re-creation (Tainting), Moving Resources (state mv, state rm, state replace-provider) and Disaster Recovery (state pull, state push, force-unlock). That is the list I7 step 2 enumerates in prose, and only four of its sixteen pages are captured. Worth keeping from it: replace-provider is filed under Moving Resources, not under anything provider-shaped — rewriting a provider source address is classed as a state move, which is the right model for it, since the resources do not change and the provider half of their addresses does. The index names re-creation after tainting — its Re-create resources link goes to cli/state/taint, under a sidebar group called Forcing Re-creation (Tainting), with -replace nowhere in either label. (Corrected 2026-08-21, on capturing the destination: that page leads with -replace and deprecates taint outright, so the staleness is in the naming, not the guidance — see the entry above.) Also recorded: three grammatical errors in four paragraphs (“real-world object that correspond”, “manually adjustment state data”, “state interations”), and the page's one hands-on link is tut-state-cli, already captured. Nav mirrored at rung 1 as Terraform CLI › Manually Update State › Overview, above the two sub-groups already there. Topics → State gains the write-side entry. I7 stays ⬜.

2026-08-20 — tf-block-moved captured. Thin page — two arguments and one paragraph — but that paragraph states a mechanism every other source only states as an outcome. tf-modules-refactoring already carried the deep treatment (instance-key moves, count ↔ for_each migrations, what moved cannot do) and tut-move-config the hands-on, so almost nothing here is new. The exception: "Before creating a new plan […] Terraform checks the state for an existing object at the address specified in the from field. Terraform renames existing objects […] and then creates a plan. As a result, Terraform does not destroy the resource during the Terraform run." The state rename happens before the plan is computed. That is why moved turns a destroy-and-recreate into a no-op: by diff time the new address already has an object bound to it, where without the block the plan sees an empty new address and an unclaimed old one — one creation and one deletion, because an address is an identity. It also explains why the block is safe to leave in place, since a from matching nothing simply finds nothing to rename. Folded into I7 as a callout. The capture's real payoff is a completed comparison. With all three refactoring block references now in hand, the instance-key question resolves three ways and is not symmetric: import's to takes instance keys, moved takes them on either side (mixing an index with a key is precisely how a count → for_each migration is written), and removed's from cannot take them at all. So a multi-instance resource can be adopted per instance and rearranged per instance, but only forgotten wholesale — the sharper form of the two-way asymmetry recorded when tf-import-single landed, and now with the third data point that identifies removed as the outlier rather than import as the exception. One defect, and it makes three in a row: the configuration model types from/to as reference while the Specification table below types both as string; the unquoted example settles it in the model's favour. That follows identity (map versus String) in tf-block-import and include_resource (Default: None versus false) in tf-block-list — three consecutive block references contradicting themselves between their own sections, always with the prose and the configuration model correct and the summary tables wrong. I7 stays ⬜.

2026-08-20 — tf-block-list captured, and its most useful sentence is about a word everyone thinks they already understand. limit on a list block is not a filter over a complete result set: "When the number of results reaches the specified limit, Terraform breaks the connection to the provider and stops reporting results." So a query returns the first N in whatever order the provider produced them, not the N most relevant — and for an adoption sweep that is the difference between "there are 100 of these" and "there are at least 100 of these". Raising limit is how you find out which. Three more additions to I7's bulk-import callout. list blocks are legal only in .tfquery.hcl files, stated as a restriction rather than a convention. count is supported, mutually exclusive with for_each, with the standard split — count = length(var.subnet_ids) for near-identical queries, for_each = toset([…]) for map- or set-driven ones — where tf-import-bulk had mentioned meta-arguments only in passing. And lists can reference other lists: with include_resource = true on the first, a second reads list.<type>.<label>.data[<index>].state.<attribute>, which both reveals the result shape (a data list of state objects) and means queries chain — discover one set, then size or filter a second from what it found. A referencing-syntax contradiction resolved by majority: the Specification says to use list.<label>.<attribute>, but the page's own example and tf-import-bulk both use list.<type>.<label>.…, so the prose sentence is the outlier. And a pattern now worth stating as a rule for this project.
