This page has seven defects — provider = concept, count written inside a config block, an azurerm_resource_group declared with provider = aws, a "Complete configuration" block with for_each [ missing its =, an include_resource Summary reading "Default: None" against its own prose, and an "attriubtes" typo — on top of tf-block-import's six the capture before. Two consecutive block-reference pages whose prose is authoritative and whose samples do not survive inspection. The I7 callout now says so explicitly: read these for the argument tables and the behavioural sentences, take working syntax from the workflow pages or from a real plan. I7 stays ⬜.

2026-08-20 — tf-block-import captured, closing the import tree and answering the question three previous captures had to leave open. Each of tf-import, tf-import-single and tf-import-generate defers to this page, and each of my notes carried a ⚠️ saying that what id accepts as an expression was unverified and must not be inferred from tutorials that only ever use literals. The reference answers it in one sentence: "You must specify a string or an expression that evaluates to a string", and "the ID must be known during the plan operation." So each.value, a var or a local are all legal, and another managed resource's attribute is not, because it is (known after apply). That is the plan-time-known rule met in a third place — the path already tracks it as the constraint on count/for_each arguments (TID §4.8.4, from the plan side in 05-terraform-plan §5.7) and hit it again via OpenTofu's issensitive() change. It is not a rule about loops; it is a rule about anything Terraform must resolve before it can build a plan, and importing qualifies because it has to ask the provider about the object while planning. The ⚠️ in I7 is replaced with the answer. identity is an object of key-value pairs, not a string, and is stated mutually exclusive with id on both arguments. for_each gets promoted from a one-line feature note to a worked callout. The reference's first example adopts three buckets from a locals map with to = aws_s3_bucket.this[each.key] and id = each.value, the destination resource's own for_each driven by the same local so the addresses line up. Its second example is the one worth remembering: for_each over a list of objects importing into module instances — to = module.group[each.value.group].aws_s3_bucket.this[each.value.key], a module instance key and a resource instance key in one address, both computed from the loop. That is what adopting a real estate looks like and nothing in the tutorials approaches it. Also captured: a placement recommendation no other page gives — an imports.tf holding every block, or each block beside its destination resource — which maps neatly onto the two dispositions tf-import-single describes, delete-after-adoption versus keep-as-provenance. Six defects on the page recorded rather than reproduced: the single-resource example has an extra closing brace and does not parse; identity's Summary box says "Data type: String" against both the configuration model (map) and its own prose (object); the "Complete configuration" block declares for_each twice, as map and as list, which is invalid HCL as printed; that block is introduced as "The following module block"; provider is shown quoted in the Specification and unquoted in the example, and only the latter is a reference; and the alias example sets region = "us-westl-1". The prose is authoritative, the samples are unproofread. The import reference tree is now complete — hub, two workflows, generation, and the block reference. I7 stays ⬜.

2026-08-20 — tf-import-generate captured, and it corrects something three other captures had quietly assumed: -generate-config-out is still flagged experimental. The page carries an Experimental banner — "Configuration generation is available in Terraform v1.5 as an experimental feature. Later minor versions may contain changes to the formatting of generated configuration and behavior of the terraform plan command" — and every run prints Warning: Config generation is experimental beside the plan. The page is banner-versioned v1.15.x (latest), so this is current rather than stale 1.5-era text: three years and ten minor releases after it shipped. Nothing that uses the flag mentions it. tut-state-import demonstrates it without a word on its status, tf-import-single recommends it for complex resources unqualified, and the TUR Ch5 reading note called generation one of three advantages of the declarative form — that note now carries the caveat. The distinction that matters: the import block itself is not experimental, only the generation, so config-driven import stays the recommended path. Three operational rules folded into I7. An existing output path is an error — the same rule tf-import-bulk records for terraform query, so it belongs to the flag rather than to either command. A provider block is mandatory when the configuration has no other resources for that provider, "otherwise Terraform displays an error if it can not determine which provider to use", and adding one costs a re-init — which bites exactly in the empty-repository adoption case that generation exists to serve. And generation is self-limiting: "Terraform knows it doesn't need to generate configuration for resources that already exist in your state." The limitation section documents invalid output, not merely verbose output: for "resources with complex schemas" Terraform may emit mutually-exclusive arguments — the worked case is ipv6_address_count conflicting with ipv6_addresses on aws_instance. ⚠️ And two of the page's own rules collide without either section noticing: the failing run "still generates configuration and writes it to generated.tf", while an existing path "throws an error" — so a generation that errors leaves behind the very file that makes re-running the identical command fail for a different reason. Recorded as a callout, since the loop is edit-in-place or delete-then-regenerate. One tension left open rather than resolved: tut-state-import says the generated draft contains "all possible arguments… including those set to default values and those without values", while this page's own example generated.tf is a single line and its prose is softer — "Terraform's best guess at the appropriate value for each resource argument." Schema size plausibly explains it, but the two claims are not the same and nothing captured reconciles them; the note says to plan for the tutorial's version, since the verbose draft is the case that needs work. Also recorded: the clean generate-plan renders the resource with no action symbol at all and 1 to import, 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy — a pure import proposes no infrastructure action. I7 stays ⬜; no written chapter used the flag, so nothing flips to 🔄.

2026-08-20 — tf-import-single captured, and its sharpest finding is an asymmetry no single page states: you can adopt one instance of a count/for_each resource, but you cannot forget one. import's to takes an instance key — aws_instance.example[0], aws_instance.example["env"] — with worked examples for both meta-arguments. The removed block's from explicitly cannot: "You cannot include instance keys… if the resource is configured to provision multiple instances" (tf-state-remove, captured 2026-07-30). Neither page mentions the other, so the consequence only appears when both are in view — a multi-instance resource is populated per instance and forgotten wholesale, which means a staged migration into Terraform is possible and a staged migration out is not. Folded into I7 as a ⚠️ callout. Two more things the block accepts, both absent from the path: a module. prefix on to, so the destination resource block lives in a child module while the import block stays in the root, and a provider argument taking an alias (provider = aws.europe) — which is the correct fix for tut-refresh's scenario, where a wrong-region provider configuration made a live instance refresh as has been deleted. A decision rule the path lacked: "manually writing the resource block when you know how to configure all or most of the resource's arguments", and generated configuration "when importing multiple resources or a single complex resource that you do not already have the configuration for." So -generate-config-out is the fallback for resources you do not understand, not the default — which reframes tut-state-import, which generates because it is teaching the flag. And the two pages state the same target from opposite ends, which is worth having as one sentence: hand-writing starts from an empty block and adds "arguments that have non-default values", generating starts from an all-arguments draft and prunes to "required arguments and arguments whose values differ from defaults" — so the configuration should name exactly the arguments differing from provider defaults, no more and no fewer. Too few is tut-state-import's env = null, which turned an adoption into a destroy. Idempotency now has a mechanism behind the advice: "applying an import action and running another plan does not generate another import action as long as that resource remains in your state", and importing to the same address twice "has no impact" — which is why both import pages recommend keeping the block as "a record of the resource's origin for future module maintainers", and it is the only thing in a configuration distinguishing an adopted resource from a created one. The standing ⚠️ is narrowed rather than cleared: the shape of to is settled (type and label, optional instance key, optional module. prefix), but what id accepts as an expression still is not — this page only ever shows a literal and defers to the import block reference, the last uncaptured child. One broken sample recorded: the count example opens its block as resource "aws_instance" "example {, missing the label's closing quote. I7 stays ⬜.

2026-08-20 — tf-import-bulk captured, and it turns list resources from a curiosity this path had noted into the front half of an adoption pipeline. The previous capture flagged bulk import as a documented workflow with no hands-on; this is the page, and the mechanics were entirely absent from the path. The list block takes two labels like a resource block, and four arguments worth memorising: provider is required (defaults to the terraform block's configuration, but an in-query-file provider block can point at another region or account without touching main.tf), config is provider-specific including filter, include_resource defaults to false so only identities come back and must be flipped to reference any attribute — at a stated performance cost — and limit defaults to 100 per block. Query files also take variable and locals, and list accepts meta-arguments including count, so a .tfquery.hcl is a small reusable program rather than a filter expression. The most confusable finding: -generate-config-out hangs off two different commands and does different work on each. On plan it consumes import blocks you wrote and generates the missing resource blocks; on query it consumes list blocks and generates both, identities included. Individual import assumes you already know the IDs; bulk import is for when you do not. Two operational traps recorded: generated.tf is written to the local workstation even when connected to HCP Terraform or Terraform Enterprise, so remote execution does not remove the local step, and Terraform refuses to overwrite it — rerunning with the file present "results in an error", making the iterate-on-a-query loop rm generated.tf then re-run. The HCP capability is the one with real operational weight: "HCP Terraform uses resource identities to determine when resources are managed by another workspace", which guards against a bulk import adopting something another team's workspace already owns — tf-state-purpose's one-to-one mapping broken in the least visible way available, two states over one object with neither aware. A version claim settled rather than left open. The page's only version statement is "v1.12 or newer", scoped to identity-based search, and it never gives a minimum for the feature it documents — which sat awkwardly against this path's 1.14 for list resources and terraform query. Checked against the local checkout instead of guessing: internal/command/query.go is absent at v1.12.0, present at v1.13.0, tfquery already matches in the config parser at that tag, the 1.13 changelog names neither, and 1.14's NEW FEATURES section announces both verbatim. So the code shipped in 1.13 and was announced in 1.14 — the same in-the-tree-before-the-changelog pattern as state_store (release-feature-map) — and B8's existing date is correct, so no 🔄. Finally, the reframe: every State-collection tutorial performs discovery by hand (docker inspect, aws ec2 create-security-group plus echo $SG_ID, terraform output -raw instance_id), and that step is precisely what a list block replaces. I7 stays ⬜.

2026-08-20 — tf-import captured — the I7 import-resources reference had been a bare URL, and the page behind it has been rebuilt since anything in this path last looked at it. It is now a hub, not the block reference: three short sections routing to child pages, none of which are captured. Two things folded into I7. Resource identity gets a reason, where the path had only a version row. The existing callout said identity (1.12) exists "for providers that identify a resource by a structured identity object" and stopped. The page supplies the argument: Terraform identifies a resource "according to either the ID assigned by the cloud provider or a collection of specific attributes defined by the provider", and its example is decisive — an AWS s3_bucket identity is account_id + bucket + region, because a bucket name is not unique on its own, while an aws_instance ID already is globally unique and id suffices. Structured identity is for objects whose identity is genuinely compound, not a nicer syntax. And bulk import is a documented workflow with no hands-on anywhere in this path. The page presents two: individual import, which "works best when you can easily access unique infrastructure resource IDs", and — when you cannot — "define queries as HCL, add the results to your Terraform configuration, and use the terraform apply command to import the discovered resources." That is the language side of list resources / terraform query (1.14), which this path had tracked only as discovery; the join is that discovery and adoption are meant to be one workflow, replacing the manual aws ec2 describe-* step every tutorial performs by hand. It also explains a pattern noticed three times this session: the docs moved twice — CLI command → import block (1.5) → query-driven bulk — and the State-collection tutorials were patched with a pointer at the first move and not at all at the second. One question deliberately left open rather than guessed. The page never says what id/identity accept as expressions — literal only, or variables and each.key too. That is the uncaptured import block reference child, and the I7 callout now carries a ⚠️ saying so, because every tutorial uses a literal and inferring the rule from them would be exactly the kind of confident wrong answer this path tries not to produce. Also uncaptured and now named: Import resources in bulk and Import a single resource. Filed under a new Import resources nav group mirroring the docs sidebar. I7 stays ⬜.

2026-08-20 — The State collection's eleventh page turned out to be a page this path already had, published under a different URL — and that is worth recording as method, not just as a null result. state/move-config looked like the last uncaptured entry in the sidebar. It is tut-move-config, captured on 2026-08-08 from modules/move-config. Confirmed rather than assumed: fetched both URLs and diffed them, and the bodies are byte-identical — the only differences are collection chrome, the Previous/Next links and the "also appears in" block, each pointing at whichever collections the page is not currently being read under. A third path exists too, configuration-language/move-config, found as a link in tut-state-cli's Next-steps list and verified the same way; it sits between Terraform versions and Custom conditions there. So one tutorial, three URLs, three sidebar positions — 9-of-10 in Modules, 11-of-11 in State, mid-list in Configuration Language. The lesson for this project's capture workflow: "is this page already captured?" cannot be answered from a URL, because HashiCorp reuses one document across collections without any canonical marker on the page. Diff the body against the existing cache before treating a new path as a new source. Recorded on the note itself as an Also published as line plus a position table, and on the tutorials course index. No new note, no nav entry — a second nav slot would break the one-file-one-entry invariant the link check relies on — and the two redundant cache files were deleted so a later session does not mistake them for separate sources. The State collection is genuinely complete at 11 of 11, of which ten are distinct pages. No status changes.

2026-08-20 — tut-console captured — the last page of the State collection, and the one whose subject is not state at all. Reading state is the console's input, not its topic; the page is about authoring, which is what separates it from tut-variables's use of the same REPL for lookup. Two facts land in B7, whose step 1 had been a bare "open the REPL and experiment". The console takes the state lock — "you cannot plan or apply changes while the console is running" — so a forgotten session in another terminal is a plausible and easily-missed cause of a lock error before anyone reaches for tf-cmd-force-unlock. Combined with the gotcha the path already carried (configuration loads at startup only), the console is a snapshot in both directions: blind to your new configuration, and exclusive against everything that would write state. It also reads stdin, so echo 'expr' | terraform console evaluates one expression non-interactively and releases the lock immediately — the scriptable form, absent from the path until now. The JSON pattern is the transferable part and now has its own callout: jsondecode(file("policy.json")) in the console turns a vendor's JSON policy into HCL, which you paste into a jsonencode({ … }) and where "<BUCKET_ARN>/*" becomes "${aws_s3_bucket.data.arn}/*" — a real dependency edge a hand-edited string could never be. The payoff is visible in the diff, because Terraform special-cases jsonencode in the plan renderer and expands the structure line by line rather than printing one opaque blob. With the anti-pattern stated alongside it: having used jsonencode to verify the shape, the tutorial defines its output as a plain map and uses terraform output -json, since encoding inside the output would produce JSON nested inside a JSON string. Machine-readable form belongs on the command, not in the configuration. A second B7 callout records that the console prints cty types with values (tolist([]) versus toset([…]), tomap(null) /* of string */) where terraform show does not — which makes it the cheapest available type checker, and would have answered tut-troubleshooting-workflow's splat-into-for_each exercise in one line. Two glossary rows added: terraform console itself, and the <= plan symbol (read (data resources), a data source deferred to apply because its arguments are not yet known) — the fourth distinct action marker this session after +/-/~/-/+ and the . forget marker. One real error in the page recorded rather than repeated: its summary sentence says the configuration "uses the jsondecode() function to convert the policy back into JSON" when it uses jsonencode(), the exact opposite, in the code block directly above. Also: it calls the resource aws_bucket_policy (it is aws_s3_bucket_policy), and its HCP tab pins ~> 5.14.0 while the init transcript beneath installs v4.10.0. The State collection is now 11 of 11. Statuses unchanged — B7 stays ✅, I7 and E5 stay ⬜.

2026-08-20 — tut-refresh captured, and it settles the contradiction flagged two captures ago: the collection has a page that gets refresh right, and tut-state-cli is the outlier. The coverage check came out covered-but-unexercised — I7 already carried -refresh-only and tf-cmd-refresh already quoted the misconfigured-credentials hazard, but nothing in the path demonstrated it, and a warning nobody has seen fire is a warning people talk themselves out of. This tutorial fires it deliberately and cheaply: create an instance in the default region, write one line of terraform.tfvars moving the provider to us-west-2, and plan -refresh-only reports a running instance as # aws_instance.server has been deleted. Nothing is broken — the provider is answering honestly about a region with no such object — and terraform refresh would accept that answer and drop the resource unprompted. The tutorial then does something no other page in the collection does: it tells you not to apply. That refusal is the lesson, and cleanup begins with rm terraform.tfvars, treating removal of the misconfiguration as a step rather than an afterthought. Two facts here appear on no reference page this path cites. terraform refresh is not supported in workspaces using HCP Terraform as a remote backend while -refresh-only is, so on a cloud block the decision is already made. And the deprecation is explicitly not a removal — "Though Terraform will continue to support the refresh subcommand in future versions, it is deprecated" — which is the best available explanation for why the command keeps resurfacing in material written years apart, this collection included. A framing correction folded in too: the 2026-08-20 drift capture recorded refresh-only's output rewriting as a hazard for tf-remote-state-data consumers; this page presents the same behaviour as a feature, letting you "anticipate the downstream effects" before accepting. Both readings are correct and the plan step is what converts one into the other, so the I7 callout now states it that way rather than picking a side. The earlier ⚠️ on tut-state-cli now names its counter-examples instead of leaving the disagreement open. One transcript defect recorded: the HCP tab says Terraform will create the learn-terraform-locals workspace, while the cloud block above it names learn-terraform-refresh — text lifted from the locals tutorial. Also noted, unremarked by the page itself: its provider block is the collection's tidiest default_tags example, and its stated floor of v1.1+ is higher than -refresh-only needs, since the flag shipped in 0.15.4. I7 stays ⬜. The State collection is now 10 of 11 captured — only Console remains, and Move resources is tut-move-config under Modules.

2026-08-20 — tut-resource-targeting captured, and -target turns out to have been a verdict without mechanics. The coverage check was the name-dropped case in its purest form: core-workflow carried the clause "-target is an antipattern for exceptional recovery only", E4 referenced the flag only to contrast OpenTofu's -exclude, and nothing anywhere said what the option actually does. Three mechanics now sit in I7, directly above the -exclude callout so the pair reads together. The direction rule is the headline and the page states it in one sentence: "Resource targeting updates resources that the target depends on, but not resources that depend on it." Upstream only. Measured against one configuration change: untargeted 8 to add / 8 to destroy, -target on the random_pet 1/1, -target on the module 4/4 — the module plus the pet it depends on, which is the rule making a target a subgraph selection rather than a filter. Dependencies are computed per resource, not per instance — -target="aws_s3_object.objects[2]" planned the replacement of all four random_pet.object_names instances, because objects[2] → object_names[2] is not an edge Terraform has. That is the 2026-07-20 source verification in Topics → The dependency graph (nodeExpandPlannableResource created per managed resource, expansion decided before instances get nodes) appearing as observable behaviour, and it means instance-level targeting buys no upstream precision at all — the opposite of the blast-radius reduction someone reaching for it wants. And the two warnings are not the same warning: plan prints Warning: Resource targeting is in effect, apply prints Warning: Applied changes may be incomplete and names the follow-up (terraform plan). Both close with the legitimate-use list, whose final clause is worth knowing — "or when Terraform specifically suggests to use it as part of an error message" — the one context where the flag is an instruction rather than an improvisation. Also recorded: targeting leaves state internally inconsistent rather than corrupt (the tutorial's bucket_name and bucket_arn outputs ended up describing different buckets, every value correctly recorded), and the mandatory untargeted follow-up apply cost 7 to add / 7 to destroy — the partial apply deferred and fragmented the work rather than reducing it. One glossary row added. Three transcript defects recorded rather than reproduced: the prose says "all five of the random_pet.object_name resources" where there are four, the destroy transcripts use the deprecated aws_s3_bucket_object name while the configuration uses aws_s3_object, and the randomised bucket names drift inconsistently between steps. I7 stays ⬜. With this the State collection is nine-elevenths captured; Refresh state and Console remain, and Move resources is tut-move-config under Modules.

2026-08-20 — tut-state-cli captured, and it is the one page that puts all of I7 in a single narrative — but it also contradicts its own collection. The coverage check was mixed rather than clean: removed, state mv and -replace all had references behind them (tf-state-remove, tf-state-refactor, the B3 -replace callout), so this is not a gap-filling capture. What it supplies is transcripts the reference pages describe but never show, plus a sequence. Three additions to I7. The . plan symbol — a removed block with destroy = false plans as a lone period where +/-/~/-/+ would go, above "will no longer be managed by Terraform, but will not be destroyed", and the run reports 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy while rewriting state. No legend the plan prints explains that character. It is the exact counterpart to tf-block-removed's measured 1 to destroy for a bare block. state mv moves state and leaves the configuration behind — the cross-file form here is shorter than tf-state-refactor's (run from the source directory, only -state-out needed), but a successful move leaves the destination one plan away from # … will be destroyed # (because … is not in configuration), fixed only by pasting the resource block in by hand. That is tut-move-config's address-is-identity rule again, and the reason moved does not help: it works only within one state file. And a ⚠️ on the collection contradicting itself — this tutorial's final exercise reconciles an out-of-band delete with a bare terraform refresh, no deprecation notice and no -refresh-only alternative, two pages away from tut-resource-drift calling that command unsafe and tf-cmd-refresh deprecating it outright. The hazard is live in context, since the exercise's whole point is that refresh silently drops a resource from state. Its own closing note is worth keeping regardless: refresh runs automatically inside plan, apply and destroy, all of which "have the potential to modify your state file" — an ordinary plan can write state. Two glossary rows added (the . symbol, taint/untaint and why -replace supersedes it). Topics → State gains the mv-versus-moved distinction. Method note recorded on the course index: the State collection sidebar was resolved at rung 3 with fetch_nav.py, which confirmed the numbering used for all four captures this session and revealed three uncaptured pages — Target resources, Refresh state (which presumably treats -refresh-only properly) and Console — plus the fact that Move resources is tut-move-config filed in two collections. I7 stays ⬜; four tutorials captured, no chapter written.

2026-08-20 — tut-troubleshooting-workflow captured, and it lands in **E5 rather than I7 despite sitting in the State collection.** Only its second half is about state, and the coverage check on that half came out absent: E5 cited the TF_LOG docs page and terraform-env-vars for the variables, but the path had no procedure for deciding whether a failure is yours, core's, or a provider's, and nothing at all on filing. Two callouts now close that. The first is HashiCorp's four-layer model — language, state, core, provider, ordered by distance from the user — whose state row ("refreshing, importing, or replacing") is I7's entire subject, so the model quietly explains why so much of this path routes through that topic. The second is the four-step filing procedure, whose useful part is step 3: the log line prefix is the whole ownership test, provider-terraform-<name> means the provider's repository and everything else means hashicorp/terraform, which is what TF_LOG_CORE/TF_LOG_PROVIDER exist to make mechanical. Also recorded: TF_LOG_PATH appends rather than truncating, and an empty value (export TF_LOG_CORE=) unsets one stream while leaving the other. E5 step 3 stops asking the reader to build a cycle — this tutorial ships one, two aws_security_group resources each naming the other in an in-line ingress block — and the cycle tip gains the fix worth generalizing: split the association into its own resource, turning two nodes in a loop into three in a line, which works wherever a provider offers both an in-line and a standalone form (security-group rules, IAM policy attachments, route-table associations). The same pattern is now in Topics → The dependency graph beside the existing route-through-a-variable trick. B4 gains a smaller but load-bearing correction: terraform fmt is a parser, not only a formatter — it cannot rewrite what it cannot read, so on a broken configuration it reports what it reformatted and then prints ordinary HCL diagnostics with line numbers, which makes it a cheaper first gate than the style callout implied. The page's own boundary against validate is quoted, along with the reason validate needs init and fmt does not. Three defects in the tutorial recorded rather than reproduced: its prose says line 46 where its transcripts say 52, its allow_8080 rule opens port 80 inside a group named "Allow 8080" while user_data serves on 8080, and the corrected instance block has an unbalanced brace. Its transcripts are v1.8.3 / aws v5.56.1, dated 2024-07-02, so its central aws_security_group_rule fix is the pre-aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule idiom — the graph argument survives, the resource name does not — and the Error: Cycle single-line rendering it shows is what 1.16 replaces with one node per line. Two glossary rows added (four-layer model, TF_LOG_CORE/TF_LOG_PROVIDER). E5 and B4 statuses unchanged: B4 stays ✅, E5 stays ⬜.

2026-08-20 — tut-resource-drift captured, completing I7 step 1 — and it corrects the path's thinnest callout. The -refresh-only entry said what the flag does and stopped there. Four things the tutorial's transcripts show that the description does not: the plan speaks in the past tense (# aws_instance.example has been changed) where a normal plan states intent, which is how you tell the two outputs apart at a glance; the apply prompts before writing, which is precisely the review step tf-cmd-refresh's deprecated command cannot give you; the counters read 0 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed while the state file changes, because they count infrastructure actions rather than state writes; and outputs drift too, so a computed output over a drifted attribute is rewritten by the same apply and anything reading this state via terraform_remote_state inherits drift it never asked for. A second callout now states the three answers to drift as a set — revert with a plain apply, adopt via configuration plus import, or keep it with ignore_changes (tut-resource-lifecycle, same repo and same drift_example tag) — with the ordering rule that makes the adopt path work: import writes state and never touches the object, so the reconciling apply is a separate step, but skipping the import first would have created a second security group and orphaned the hand-made one. Two ageing flags recorded rather than repeated as current: the tutorial still drives terraform import from the CLI, with its own tip pointing at the 1.5+ block, and its transcripts run AWS provider v3.26.0 (2021), whose aws_security_group_rule idiom the provider no longer recommends — its aws_security_group page now prefers aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule with one CIDR per rule and warns that mixing the two styles causes "rule conflicts, perpetual differences". Unlike the import tutorial this one costs money: the drift is manufactured with three aws ec2 calls against a live EC2 instance, so there is no emulator version. One glossary row added (-refresh-only planning mode). Topics → State gains the three-answers framing. I7 stays ⬜ — both tutorials are now captured, but no chapter is written.

2026-08-20 — tut-state-import captured — the last of **I7's cited-but-unwritten tutorials, and it changes what the topic warns about.** I7 already recommended the tutorial by URL and already knew the flag (-generate-config-out), so the coverage check came out name-dropped, not covered: the path told you the flag existed and nothing about what it produces. What it produces is a draft containing every argument the schema has, defaults and nulls included — and in the tutorial's own run that draft's env = null (against a schema wanting a set of strings) made the first plan of an adoption destructive, 1 to import, 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy, with Terraform printing # Warning: this will destroy the imported resource. Pruning to env = [] plus the genuinely-non-default arguments produced the target shape, 1 to import, 0 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy. Folded into I7 as two callouts. The first covers the generated-draft trap and the harder half of it — the plan does not tell you which changes are safe, in the page's words "Provider documentation may not indicate if a change is safe" — since ~ update in-place reads identically for a state-only default and a restart. The second covers adoption without an import block (a resource identified by a unique tag can just be declared and applied) and the ordering rule that makes it fail: referencing docker_image.nginx.image_id before that resource is in state forces replacement, because unknown never compares equal — tut-dependencies' rule, met again in an adoption. Also recorded: import reports the provider's view of current state only, never health or intent, and adoption commits Terraform to the full lifecycle including destroy. Two glossary rows added (configuration-driven import, -generate-config-out), and Topics → State gains the way in alongside its existing exits — tf-state-purpose's one-to-one mapping rule is broken by hand on entry via import and on exit via removed, and the two are not symmetric. I7 stays ⬜; the drift half of its step 1 is still uncaptured.

2026-08-19 — I6 refocused on the three backends it should have been about: local, s3, gcs. The previous pass had widened it to the forges and to HCP, and the effect was that the topic's hands-on was a tour of managed platforms while the open-source backends were things to read about. The spine is now four labs, all run end to end before being written down (labs/chapter15/), and the managed tutorials have moved to one optional entry near the bottom. Two reference notes finally exist: tf-backend-s3, whose page had been sitting in cache since the 2026-08-17 review, and tf-backend-gcs, which nothing had covered. Reading them side by side is what the topic now teaches, because the differences are few and each one matters: gcs has no key and addresses state as <prefix>/<workspace>.tfstate, so the workspace name is always in the path, where s3 prefixes only non-default workspaces with the literal env:; locking is opt-in on s3 (use_lockfile, defaulting to false, so a valid backend block can be silently unlocked) and on by default on gcs; and encryption diverges at migration time, since a customer-supplied GCS key cannot be migrated automatically while a KMS one can, but only takes effect on the first write afterwards. Underneath, both locks are one conditional object write — 412 PreconditionFailed on S3, 412 ifGenerationMatch … conditionNotMet on GCS — which is the generalisation the module is now built to deliver, and both were verified rather than asserted. The forge material survived by changing what it demonstrates. Instead of GitLab-managed state, the lab now runs a GitLab CI pipeline against the s3 backend, ending with app/terraform.tfstate and ci/terraform.tfstate in one bucket: forge holds the code, object store holds the state. GitLab-managed state, the http protocol, HCP and Terrakube are all still here, demoted into one "backends that are not object stores" entry. Emulator note: the gcs lab needs a GCP emulator (floci-gcp, MIT) behind a compose profile — the AWS one has no Google surface, which was checked in its source rather than assumed. Two traps recorded from failed runs: gitlab/gitlab-runner:latest is a pre-release whose helper image does not exist, so every job fails in prepare_executor; and a runner needs an explicit --clone-url, because the URL GitLab advertises to a browser is unreachable from a job container. I6 stays ⬜ — the labs and references are ready, the chapter is not written.

2026-08-18 — I6 was drifting into an HCP Terraform topic, and the fix was structural rather than another callout. Three of its four hands-on entries were HCP tutorials, its only open-source exercise was a video to watch, and the question a team actually asks — where does state live when our code is on GitLab, GitHub or Bitbucket? — was not asked anywhere in the path. The backend catalogue settles the premise: local, remote, azurerm, consul, cos, gcs, http, kubernetes, oci, oss, pg, s3 (read from the v1.15.x sidebar, rung 1). No GitHub entry, no Bitbucket entry, no GitLab entry either — GitLab works because it implements the generic http protocol, which is now captured as tf-backend-http and is the highest-leverage short page in the catalogue: GET/POST/DELETE, LOCK/UNLOCK with 423 Locked or 409 Conflict on a taken lock, and lock_address defaulting to disabled so a minimal http backend is silently unlockless. gitlab-tf-state is the substantial new note. State at /api/v4/projects/<ID>/terraform/state/<NAME>, lock at that path plus /lock with POST/DELETE overriding the protocol's verbs, and an empty backend "http" {} in the configuration. Its access-control story is the honest one: project roles replace IAM — Maintainer to write, Developer to read — but “any user with the Developer role or higher can download and view Terraform state files”, and the only in-product mitigation is a custom role excluding admin_terraform_state, which is Ultimate-only. OpenTofu users can encrypt state through GitLab's own CI/CD component; Terraform users on GitLab cannot. It also carries a failure mode no cloud backend has: state is encrypted with a key derived from db_key_base, so “the instance must be available to decrypt a state file” — never keep the state for GitLab's own infrastructure inside it. And it argues the -backend-config warning from a functional consequence rather than a disclosure one, since the cached values are carried to the apply and “can lead to problems like being unable to lock the state files in CI jobs.” GitHub and Bitbucket got the other half — identity, not storage. gha-oidc (fetched for A9 in August and never written up) and bitbucket-pipelines-oidc, new. The pair contrast usefully: GitHub's sub is a readable path with environment, ref and job_workflow_ref beside it, and repositories created after 2026-07-15 use an immutable ID-based subject that breaks a copied trust policy; Bitbucket identifies everything by UUID, defaults oidc to true, and treats step max-time as an access control — with a 5-minute buffer silently added. Topic changes: What it is now leads with the open-source backends and names the forge question; the hands-on order is emulator-first (s3 + use_lockfile, no cloud account), then GitLab, then the three HCP tutorials demoted to the managed-platform comparison they are; two reference entries added; a forge-comparison table callout added; and the milestone now asks for a defensible answer per forge rather than just a migration. Three new source courses — GitLab Docs, GitHub Docs, Atlassian Bitbucket Docs — with the nav rung recorded on each index, including two traps: fetch_nav.py resolves GitLab at rung 3 to the version selector, and Bitbucket at rung 1 to the article's own heading list, so both were mirrored from the sidebar rendered in the page instead. I6 stays ⬜ — this changed what the chapter must cover, not whether it is written.

2026-08-18 — Terrakube belonged in I6 as well as A9, and the docs page that proves it was uncaptured. The path already knew Terrakube implements the TFE v2 API — terrakube-facts lists the endpoints, state-versions and workspace lock/unlock among them — but that fact lived only in A9, framed as platform comparison, so I6 never learned that an Apache-2.0 self-hosted option exists for the cloud {} block. terrakube-migrating captured, and the operative detail is one argument: hostname, mandatory in both cloud and backend "remote" because both otherwise default to app.terraform.io — “It's crucial to include the hostname parameter”, said twice on the page. The two migration paths differ in a way worth knowing before choosing one. From local state it is terraform state pull > tf.state then login, init, state push — so the lineage and serial guards in tf-state-backends are what stand between you and an overwrite, not the init copy prompt that tut-cloud-migrate answers. From HCP it is a plain init -migrate-state, since both ends speak the same API. And Terrakube stores nothing itself: state lands in “azure, aws, gcp or minio”, which is what makes a fully local deployment possible and also means its access-control story is your bucket's, not its own. The Workspaces Importer carries more than the CLI path does — name, description, Terraform version, execution mode, variables, tags and current state — with a sensitive-variable preview that only the source note records. I6 gains a reference entry and a fourth row in its forge table; the platform comparison stays in A9 rather than being duplicated. ⚠️ The page is dated ≈November 2025 and every example hostname is the authors' disposable Gitpod URL, so it predates the 2.30/2.32 RBAC work in terrakube-facts. New source course: Terrakube Docs, nav mirrored at rung 3 from the rendered GitBook sidebar. I6 stays ⬜.

2026-08-18 — tut-cloud-migrate captured; it was the one reference in **I6 cited by URL with no note behind it.** The tutorial had been fetched during the 2026-08-17 I6 review and promoted to the top of that topic’s hands-on list, but never written up, so the path pointed at a page rather than at anything readable offline. Three details the topic entry did not carry: an existing HCP workspace “must not have any existing states” while the workspace itself is created on demand and only the organization is a precondition; answering no at the init migration prompt “ignore[s] the existing state and just activate[s] the configured HCP Terraform workspace with its existing state, if any”, which makes it the right answer when the remote side is already authoritative rather than a way out of the prompt; and terraform login writes the token “in plain text” to ~/.terraform.d/credentials.tfrc.json. One conflict with the docs, recorded in the note rather than smoothed over: the tutorial ends by telling you to rm terraform.tfstate, while tf-backend-configure says to back the file up before migrating; the note keeps both and sides with the docs. Its transcripts are also internally inconsistent — random v3.3.2 on the first init and v3.0.1 on the migration init, and the pet id changes between steps — so they are illustrations, not a reproducible run. Cross-linked from the State and Workspaces topic pages; the latter now sends the cloud-block reader here for the hands-on version. Nav mirrored from the State tutorial collection, where it sits second, between Import Terraform configuration and Manage resources in Terraform state. I6 stays ⬜ — a note is not a chapter.

2026-08-18 — tut-cloud-state-api captured, the second of the two **I6 tutorials that had been fetched but never written up.** It is the only thing in the path that edits a state file on purpose, and the only coverage of the HCP state-versions API. Its premise is the argument for remote state that has nothing to do with collaboration: state “can get corrupted due to partial apply operations or incorrectly running terraform import or terraform taint”, and a store that keeps versions is what makes that recoverable. Three mechanics worth having written down. The workspace lock is a precondition of the API upload rather than hygiene, and it is identity-scoped to the user whose token you are using, which is a stricter thing than the per-command state lock in tf-state-locking. The document is not served inline — /workspaces/$ID/current-state-version returns a hosted-state-download-url pointing at an archivist.terraform.io object. And the POST body sends serial, lineage and an md5 as attributes beside the base64-encoded state, which is how the server applies the same lineage/serial guards tf-state-backends documents for terraform state push. The manual serial bump is the bridge to work already written: 06-state-management §6.5.4 gives it as the safe restore habit, and ch09-state-fundamentals measured what the counter actually tracks, so the tutorial's tidy 0 → 1 should not be read as what a real run looks like. One error recorded rather than repeated: the tutorial calls payload.json “an encrypted version of your state”; it is base64, and base64 -d reads every secret back. Version-mixed transcripts too — required_version = "~> 1.10" and state written by 1.10.3, but the apply output prints v0.15.1 and the API response is dated 2021. Filed eighth in the State collection, between Manage resource lifecycle and Refresh state; cross-linked from the State topic page, whose serial/lineage bullet now points here for the case where the pair stops being trivia. I6 stays ⬜.

2026-08-17 — I6 reviewed ahead of writing its chapter, and the gap was not depth but shape. The topic had eight callouts and only four entries in How to learn it — one tutorial, two reference bundles, one book chapter — so almost everything it knew sat in asides rather than in things to read or run. Six references added, and the list reordered into the path’s own sequence of video, hands-on, depth reading, reference docs. The most surprising omission is the S3 backend page itself, which was cited nowhere in the entire path despite being the backend every callout in this topic assumes and the one the verified lab already exercises. It carries four things the generic backend pages do not: dynamodb_table and dynamodb_endpoint are deprecated and “will be removed in a future minor version” while both may be configured alongside use_lockfile during migration; a non-default workspace stores state at <workspace_key_prefix>/<workspace_name>/<key> with the default prefix being the literal env:; the IAM permission set is specific enough to be worth copying, needing s3:DeleteObject on the .tflock object but explicitly not on the state object “as Terraform does not delete it”; and encryption has three separate shapes (encrypt, kms_key_id, sse_customer_key), the last of which the page warns “will cause it to be persisted to disk in terraform.tfstate” if you set it in a .tf file. TID Ch 6 §6.4 was the other structural gap — the chapter is cited from B9 for §6.1–§6.3 and from I7 for §6.5, and §6.4 “Storing state” is squarely this topic (possible backends, the backend block, alternative authentication, the cloud block, migrating and upgrading backends) yet belonged to no topic at all. TUR Ch 3 had been carrying the book half alone. Two uncaptured tutorials from the State collection. “Migrate state to HCP Terraform” now leads the hands-on, because it is the only remote-state exercise in the topic that needs no AWS account — its example provisions a random_pet — and it states a constraint the longer S3 tutorial does not: “Always use the same version of the Terraform CLI you used to create the resources. Using a newer version of Terraform may update the state file and cause state file corruption.” “Version remote state with the HCP Terraform API” adds the disaster-recovery half nothing else here covered: download the remote state, modify it, upload it as a new state version through the API, on the premise that state “can get corrupted due to partial apply operations or incorrectly running terraform import or terraform taint.” OpenTofu’s State and Plan Encryption gets its own entry rather than the passing mention it had inside the TUR caveat. It is the direct answer to this topic’s own four-properties hardening callout and Terraform has no equivalent: an encryption {} block pairing a key_provider with a method, applied to state, plan and remote_state_data_sources, or supplied wholesale through TF_ENCRYPTION. Its threat model is worth reading before adopting — encryption is at rest only and “does not protect against data loss … and it also does not protect against replay attack”, nor against “the person running the tofu command” — as is its deliberately non-seamless migration, where OpenTofu “will refuse to read plain text data” by design, and its narrow +1 minor version support promise for key providers and methods. And the topic gains its only video, TF2026 Lecture 07, which the course coverage map already mapped to I6 without the path ever citing it; it ships with a known defect, since its backend block locks with dynamodb_table. Checked and deliberately not added: the Krausen 004 lab repo, whose own inventory records zero occurrences of backend, workspaces, import or lifecycle — it stops at the Beginner half, so there is no lab resource to cite here rather than a missing citation. ot-early-eval-backend, which existed and was reachable only from E3, is now wired into the TUR entry that already mentioned the behaviour. Fetched to cache/web/tf-backend-s3.txt, tut-cloud-migrate.txt, tut-cloud-state-api.txt and ot-state-encryption.txt. I6 stays ⬜ — the chapter is next.

2026-08-17 — Validated Patterns audited end to end, and the first finding is that a third of the collection does not load. HashiCorp publishes a Validated Patterns library — field guides written by its own field engineers, hosted at developer.hashicorp.com/validated-patterns/, not linked from the tutorial library and cited nowhere in this path until now. The Terraform section advertises 12 tutorials. Five of the twelve return HTTP 404, verified from two independent clients (the headless browser and a plain fetch) and confirmed by navigating to one of them: Migrate Terraform Enterprise organizations to projects, Integrate Terraform with Cortex Cloud by Palo Alto Networks, Vulnerability and patch management of infrastructure images with HCP, Automate deployments with HCP Terraform and ServiceNow Catalog, and Use Terraform to build an Azure landing zone. Rechecked the same day, and the sitemaps settle what the 404s mean. server-sitemap.xml — the dynamic one, 1.2 MB — advertises all 12 of these URLs, while only 7 are actually served, and the static sitemap-0.xml lists a different, smaller subset again. A third access path was tried on the recheck: clicking through from the index as an in-app client-side route, rather than a fresh page load, which renders “We couldn't find the page you're looking for” — so direct fetch, hard navigation and in-app routing all agree. They are not deliberately retired: the index still says “12 tutorials” and still carries 12 links, the content index still advertises all 12, and search engines still hold their text. A page that is missing from the build but present in the sitemap is a publish regression, not a removal — which is the difference between waiting for them and replacing them. Recorded so a later pass re-checks them instead of re-discovering them; the Azure landing zone is the one whose absence actually costs this path something, since its AWS twin turned out to be the only landing-zone material anywhere in it. The seven reachable guides were read verbatim and all seven placed — none was below the threshold, which is unusual and is explained by what these documents are: they are not tutorials but the process layer around Terraform (who does what, in which order, and what a plan has to look like before you apply), which this path was thin on everywhere. A10 gains the manual workflow it automates (now vp-provider-upgrades): Manage Terraform provider upgrades names Renovate and Dependabot in its own recommendation, so HashiCorp's guidance and this topic agree, and what it adds is what to do once the bot's pull request exists — one branch per upgrade, first plan shows only the version change, one issue at a time, and apply only when a plan has "no errors, warnings, or actions", a bar stricter than an empty diff because a warning is a deprecation you are about to inherit. A8 gains the consumer half of I5's module split (now vp-upgrade-modules): Upgrade and refactor Terraform modules works terraform-aws-modules/s3-bucket 2.15.0 → 3.0.0, where the module split encryption into its own resource, and the consumer pays with an import block naming an address inside the module (module.s3_bucket.aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration.this[0]). Its acceptance criterion is the keeper — "Imports are the only acceptable change to see in a speculative plan when upgrading to a newer module version" — and it is exactly the bill that the moved blocks in I5's shim pattern exist to spare consumers, so the two topics now describe the same event from both sides. A7 gains its only landing-zone material (now vp-aws-landing-zone) (platform landing zone versus workload landing zone, and the design principle that puts each zone in its own AWS account and its own Terraform workspace, making the account boundary and the state boundary the same boundary), and A5 gains the Sentinel-versus-SCP split (now vp-aws-landing-zone) that the same guide states cleanly: Sentinel evaluates plans and applies, resource-level, pre-deployment, and is bypassed by anything that does not go through Terraform; an SCP evaluates every AWS API call at account level, at execution time, and cannot be bypassed at all — so a control that must hold against a console user was never a Sentinel control. A6 gains the two Vault guides (now vp-integrate-vault and vp-vault-dynamic-credentials), which between them separate four surfaces this path had been treating as one (authenticating Terraform to Vault, dynamic provider credentials, reading/writing secrets, and the Terraform secrets engine running the relationship in reverse), recommend Terraform Cloud agents so "Vault DNS is not exposed to the public internet", and supply the operational trap worth writing down: align the TTL of Vault's STS credentials with HCP Terraform's JWT lifetime, or a long apply dies partway on expired credentials. A1 gains the reverse of its own Ansible callout: the AAP pattern's aap_inventory / aap_job_template / aap_job resources let Terraform trigger Ansible rather than Ansible read Terraform, which reframes this topic's question from whether to shell out to where the handover boundary sits. I7 gains the migration route off CloudFormation (now vp-cloudformation-migration), whose recommended path is this topic's own import, with aws_cloudformation_stack as the transitional escape hatch and parallel stacks as the rollback — the only migrating-from-another-tool material in the path, where B1 compares the two tools without moving anything between them. Resources table gains VP with the 404 caveat attached. All seven captures are in cache/web/vp-*.txt. No topic status changes and no chapter is affected, so nothing flips to 🔄.

2026-08-17 — I5 audited for ordering and for missing hands-on work. Three of its cross-references pointed at the wrong entry, and the ordinals were the reason. Three entries each attributed their rule to whatever the list's first entry happened to be, which was TUR Ch 4 + Ch 8. The rules were the complexity test, the 80%-of-use-cases rule and the two-deep nesting rule. All three come from tut-pattern-module-creation, which sat ten entries down the list. The rot has a mechanical cause worth naming rather than just fixing: this list has now been renumbered twice by insertions (composition in, refactoring in), and both times the entries moved while the inline #N citations did not. Every cross-reference in and into I5 now names the page — "the recommended-pattern guide above", "I5's Standard Module Structure reference" — so the next insertion cannot silently misattribute a rule again. Inbound citations in I8, A4 and A8 were rewritten the same way. The list was also reordered to match the path's own stated pedagogy (hands-on → depth reading → reference docs), which it had inverted: six reference pages sat ahead of both tutorials. New shape — build a module, refactor its interface into objects, test it, then read the scoping guide and TUR, then the six Develop modules pages in the docs' sidebar order, then the no-code exception, then your own module. Two tutorials added, neither of them new to the site, both cross-cited rather than duplicated. "Write Terraform tests" is A2's, and belongs here as the third hands-on step because TUR Ch 8's rule that every example gets a test is unexecutable without it, and because a test is the second caller a module ever has. "Create and use no-code modules" is E6's, and earns an author-side entry because it is the only page that documents where I5's own rules stop: a no-code module declares its own provider blocks, and the page states the reason the prohibition existed — "Since users will not reference no-code modules in written configuration, there is no risk of this conflict" — so the ban was never about providers but about count/for_each/depends_on on a module block. It also tightens the standard structure ("define all resources in the root repository of the directory"), and it is the only page in the collection kept current, using ephemeral resources (1.10) and write-only arguments (1.11) where eight of the other nine still pin 2022 providers. Checked for genuinely uncaptured tutorials and found none in this collection: the live Reuse Configuration with Modules collection still lists exactly 10 tutorials and all ten are captured and placed (I4 ×2, I5 ×4, A4 ×2, A7 ×1, A8 ×1), so I5's hands-on surface is now exhausted. One uncovered surface found off to the side, recorded rather than folded in: HashiCorp publishes 12 "Validated Patterns" for Terraform under developer.hashicorp.com/validated-patterns/terraform, and this path cites none of them. The module-relevant one, "Upgrade and refactor Terraform modules" (23 min), is consumer-side — monitor for a new version, bump it, keep the speculative plan free of actions, import where the module split resources — so it belongs to A8/I4, not here; the rest map to A6, A7, A9 and E4. Fetched to cache/web/vp-terraform.txt and cache/web/vp-upgrade-refactor-modules.txt for a later pass. I5 stays ⬜ — no chapter exists yet, so nothing flips to 🔄.

2026-08-17 — I5 gains "Refactor modules" as a new reference, closing the modules/develop directory. The page was already captured (tf-modules-refactoring) and cited from A8, but only there — and A8 reads it as an operator refactoring a live codebase. I5 cited four of the section's five child pages (develop, structure, publish, composition, providers) and skipped the fifth, even though its own reference index names it: tf-modules-develop describes refactoring blocks as recording "how resource names and module structure have changed from previous module versions", which is an authoring concern by construction. The author-side slice now written into I5: scoping is what makes refactoring an author's privilege, since "a module may only make moved statements about its own objects and objects of its child modules" and addresses resolve relative to the module the block sits in, so internals can be re-shaped across a version bump and consumers get the migration in their next plan; chaining (a→b, b→c) makes the blocks the upgrade path rather than a changelog, each covering consumers arriving from a different starting version, and removal is safe only for a private module once every consumer has applied; and the module-split shim is the section an author reads twice, because the original module is kept as a shim carrying the moved blocks so existing users upgrade in place. HashiCorp flags the shim as violating the closed-box rule and bounds it — "all three of these modules are maintained by the same people and distributed together in a single module package" — so it licenses your own package and never someone else's. The pairing that motivates the placement: moved re-shapes structure and deprecated (TF 1.15, already an I5 callout) retires interface surface, and together they are the whole toolkit for evolving a published module without breaking consumers overnight — which is I5's subject, not A8's. A8's Refactor modules reference and the I5 deprecation callout now cross-reference each other so the split is explicit rather than a silent duplication. Renumbering: old I5 references 7–10 shift down one place to 8–11, and the README contradiction in I5's Build and use a local module entry now names the recommended-pattern guide rather than a number, since two-digit reference markers trip the bare-issue-ref check. No topic status changes — I5 stays ⬜, A8 stays ⬜, and no written chapter is affected, so nothing flips to 🔄.

2026-08-16 — TID Ch 12 "Terraform providers" captured (12-terraform-providers) — the last chapter, so TID is now read end to end: 12/12. It is the only chapter that leaves HCL entirely, building a Mastodon provider in Go with the Terraform Plugin Framework: design the user-facing HCL first (§12.1), dev_overrides for the local loop (§12.2), schemas/diagnostics/tflog (§12.3), the provider entry point (§12.4), a data source (§12.5), a resource with full CRUD (§12.6), a provider-defined function (§12.7), and signing/publishing (§12.8). Feeds E1, which had four references and no book note behind them. Two printed listings do not run, and both are correct in the author's published repository — so they are print-only defects. Listing 12.3 puts Default: stringdefault.StaticString("mastodon.social") on a provider schema attribute under the comment "schemas can have default values"; provider/schema.StringAttribute at framework v1.19.0 has exactly CustomType, Required, Optional, Sensitive, Description, MarkdownDescription, DeprecationMessage, Validators — no Default, no PlanModifiers, because a provider block has no plan or state to hold one in. The real Listing 12.7 four pages later is clean, and terraform-provider-mastodon's provider.go sets no defaults anywhere. The corollary is the useful part: a provider option's "default" is the os.Getenv fallback in Configure. Listing 12.12 then defines the data source's five output attributes with Optional: false, Required: false and no Computed, which the framework rejects at runtime — "Attribute missing Required, Optional, or Computed definition. This is always a problem with the provider and should be reported to the provider developer." The published account_data_source.go sets Computed: true on all five. Two smaller slips and a wrong make target: the prose calls the post's text parameter status while every listing calls it content, the file to copy is printed as port_resource.go, and §12.5.6 says make acctest where the scaffolding template's GNUmakefile has testacc (and no acctest) — §12.3.3 gets the same target right. The chapter's biggest gap is not an error but time: the provider interface has grown four methods since it was written. Verified on pkg.go.dev against v1.19.0 (2026-03-10): Functions is not part of provider.Provider at all but of ProviderWithFunctions, and the same opt-in pattern has since added ProviderWithEphemeralResources (TF 1.10), ProviderWithListResources and ProviderWithActions (both TF 1.14.0, 19 Nov 2025, per the local checkout's changelog), and an experimental ProviderWithStateStores; the resource side gained write-only attributes (1.11) and managed resource identity (1.12). Three OpenTofu divergences, all settled against repos/opentofu at v1.12.5 rather than the web. (1) The chapter says to edit ~/.terraformrc for dev_overrides; OpenTofu reads .tofurc and falls back to .terraformrc only when .tofurc does not exist (config_unix.go + util.go), so creating a .tofurc for anything else silently disables overrides left in the other file. (2) List resources and actions exist only as generated protobuf and mocks in the OpenTofu tree — no core support, no tofu query, no action block — so a provider exposing them degrades to its ordinary resources there. (3) Provider functions are OpenTofu 1.7.0 (opentofu#1439, which its 1.7.0 changelog credits) against Terraform's 1.8, confirming the correction Ch10 already recorded, and a second PR in the same release (opentofu#1491) added internal/addrs/provider_function.go with a ProviderAlias field, so OpenTofu also registers alias-qualified calls provider::<name>::<alias>::<fn> — Terraform has no equivalent, since internal/lang/functions.go at v1.15.8 builds exactly one name per function and anything else hits its "Unknown provider function" diagnostic. Two claims corrected in the path itself. E1's dev_overrides callout said "terraform init is skipped entirely"; HashiCorp's CLI-config docs say init "will still attempt to select a suitable published version of your provider to install and record in the dependency lock file" while other commands disregard the lock entry — which is why the chapter tells you to run init and ignore the failure, and why direct {} is mandatory rather than decorative. And the registry story is now split per engine: Terraform takes signing keys through User Settings → Signing Keys on registry.terraform.io and accepts RSA or DSA but not ECC, while OpenTofu accepts providers and keys only through the GitHub issue forms on opentofu/registry, whose README rejects pull requests outright because the validation automation parses the form fields. Two things worth stealing from the chapter regardless of whether you ever write a provider. First, normalise every value the server rewrites, in all three of create/read/update — Mastodon wraps post content in HTML, and missing the bluemonday pass in even one of the three functions produces permanent state drift; this is the provider-side origin of the "always detected changes" pathology Ch5 describes from the user's end. Second, collect diagnostics instead of returning early, and never log.Fatal in a plugin: the process dies without returning errors and can corrupt state. Also captured: the scaffolding template's go:generate directives now live in tools/tools.go (one of them runs copywrite against the .copywrite.hcl the chapter tells you to delete) and its headers read Copyright IBM Corp. 2021, 2025; resource.Test runs the real binary and is gated on TF_ACC=1, while resource.UnitTest is what functions use; and terraform-plugin-testing v1.16.0 offers a typed statecheck/knownvalue assertion API beside the chapter's string-based TestCheckResourceAttr. Topic backlog gains provider-development (single-source — TUR has no provider-authoring content at all, so the second source has to be the Plugin Framework docs). Glossary gains eight rows, resources gains a provider-development section. TID reading log: 12/12 done.

2026-08-16 — Verification pass on Ch 11 found its opening premise expired, which is a bigger correction than any of its listing bugs. §11.1 states there is no Terraform SDK and that teams "need to wrap the CLI to do so". Two things say otherwise. hashicorp/terraform-exec is an official Go module "for constructing and running Terraform CLI commands" with structured returns from terraform-json, and its README positions itself exactly where the chapter says nothing exists: importing it "is preferable to importing github.com/hashicorp/terraform/command, because the latter is not intended for use outside Terraform Core". It is still a CLI wrapper, so the architectural point survives — but a Go team should not hand-roll §11.1. And terraform rpcapi is a real non-CLI surface, registered in commands.go under a comment that answers the chapter directly: its "whole point … is to bypass the CLI layer so wrapping automation can get as-direct-as-possible access to Terraform Core functionality", bypassing the command package entirely. Version-gated with git tag --contains: out of experimental as of v1.13.0. Two caveats recorded rather than glossed — it sits in HiddenCommands (plumbing, not advertised) and came out of the Stacks work, so it is an integrator's channel and not a stability promise. The divergence is the practical part: OpenTofu has no rpcapi at all — zero occurrences in the 1.12.5 tree, no package, no registration — so a wrapper is still the only door there, and CLI-wrapping remains the right choice for anything that must serve both engines. Both added to E5's existing rpcapi row and to the glossary. Three smaller items from the same pass: check blocks work fine in JSON (assert takes the list form) even though the chapter's block list omits them and its Listing 11.33 drops the checks its own prose says it includes; show genuinely cannot read stdin (show -json - → "Failed to read the given file as a state or plan file"), so only the extension half of that claim was wrong; and the version event carries a ui version field of its own, 1.3 on 1.15.8 against the book's 1.2, which is the field a parser should watch for format changes.

2026-08-16 — TID Ch 11 "Alternative interfaces" captured (11-alternative-interfaces) — Terraform without HCL, and the chapter with the shortest shelf life in the book. Its subject is the three escape routes: wrap the CLI from another language (§11.1, three quarters of the chapter, built as a real Python library), write configuration as JSON so a program can generate it (§11.2), and write it in a general-purpose language and synthesise (§11.3). Feeds A3 (the machine-readable UI is what a pipeline parses), B4 (.tf.json), E5 (integrating the engine into your own tooling) and E1 (its closing pointer is Ch12). The headline is that §11.3's subject is dead: CDKTF was sunset and archived on 10 December 2025, per both HashiCorp's docs ("deprecated as of December 10, 2025 … no longer supports or maintains") and the repository README ("no further updates, fixes, or improvements (including compatibility updates)"). The chapter's own §11.3.1 argued against adopting it, so the recommendation aged better than the subject — and its argument generalises: "most of learning Terraform is not about the language but about the concepts around IaC", which is why switching to TypeScript buys less than teams expect. The chapter also does not contain two things its introduction promises — it says it covers "the CDKTF and Pulumi projects" and "we end the chapter with Terragrunt", and neither Pulumi nor Terragrunt appears anywhere in it; Terragrunt is uncovered by the book entirely, which is worth knowing before citing TID for E4. Six defects found by running the listings, three of which are in the published tofupy library rather than just in print. The worst is that _run_stream does not stream: it calls subprocess.run, which blocks until the child exits, so the event handlers whose stated purpose is live progress all fire after the command is over — measured with a one-line-per-second stand-in, subprocess.run returned at t+3.07s and all three events yielded at t+3.07s. Real streaming needs Popen. Second, ChangeContainer.__post_init__ assigns address, previous_address and module_address all from data["address"] (verified in the shipped schema.py), so previous_address — the field that tells you a resource was moved — is silently wrong for every change, in the class most likely to back a policy gate. Third, Listing 11.18 declares sensitive_values and never assigns it, so typed-in code raises AttributeError on the one field that says which attributes are secret; the library has the line. Then three print-level slips: Listing 11.10's sample validate output does not match either engine (both say Missing required provider, and the book's own tests four listings later assert exactly that), Listing 11.38 pluralises the top-level key and fails with No argument or block type is named "resources", and Listing 11.35 transposes a paren. Two of the chapter's factual claims measured, one right and one wrong. Right: show -json really is lossy against state pull — no serial, no lineage, and also no check_results, which the chapter does not mention and which matters because its own test module contains a check block. Wrong: show does not require a .tfstate extension; a state file copied to a name with no extension is read fine by both engines. Two smaller facts worth keeping: an apply that also plans emits two change_summary events (operation: "plan" then "apply"), so a last-write-wins parser discards the planned counts, and resource.terraform_data.main.output is valid — the explicit managed-resource prefix, counterpart to data., applied and resolved on 1.15.8. Topic backlog gains wrapping-and-machine-readable-ui and json-configuration; A3 and B4 gain callouts. TID reading log: 11/12 done, Ch12 (providers) remains.

2026-08-16 — Renovate promoted out of a callout into its own Advanced topic, A10, because the question it answers is "what runs on GitLab and Bitbucket" and A3's aside could not carry that. Everything is from the Renovate docs, fetched rather than remembered, since no book here covers the tool: TID Ch 7 §7.7.5 is Dependabot with one passing sentence on Renovate, and TUR predates both. The extraction surface came out wider than the old callout claimed. The Terraform manager matches **/*.tf and **/*.tofu and emits module, provider, required_provider, required_version, helm_release and tfe_workspace alongside about twenty Kubernetes kinds and the docker_* ones, each disableable by depType — and the sources are asymmetric, with modules resolvable from GitTags/GithubTags/registry but providers from a registry only. Three findings are the reason the topic exists. The OpenTofu default is stated in the docs as an admitted limitation, "Renovate can not know if you want to use the Terraform or OpenTofu registry", so an unqualified provider on an OpenTofu project resolves against registry.terraform.io — which lands directly on opentofu-migration-mechanics's finding that the two registries do not ship byte-for-byte identical builds, making it a supply-chain mistake rather than a cosmetic one. The lock file is computed, not delegated: Renovate "performs lock file maintenance itself, without calling the underlying package manager", so no engine binary is needed in the runner image, but lockFileMaintenance defaults to false, meaning a default install bumps constraints and leaves the recorded checksums behind. And the failure mode of computing hashes yourself is silent: discussion #30984 is aws 5.64.0 producing no regenerated lock and no error, self-healing at 5.65.0. The platform gaps are per-forge and worth checking before promising a workflow: GitLab has not implemented automergeStrategy at all and needs gitAuthor to match the bot where push rules verify committers; Bitbucket Cloud has no assignees, no rebase merge strategy and no collapsible markdown, which is what Renovate's PR bodies use; Bitbucket Data Center adds no labels and no config-error issues. The Dependency Dashboard needs "issues with dynamic Markdown checkboxes", so it is not a Bitbucket feature. The GitLab setup needs no marketplace app — the Renovate Runner templates run it from a scheduled pipeline (3 * * * * recommended) with RENOVATE_TOKEN, RENOVATE_GITHUB_COM_TOKEN and RENOVATE_EXTRA_FLAGS, which is the concrete answer to the question that started this. One thing carried over unchanged: neither bot moves a SHA-pinned Git module source, so I4's manual cadence survives automation; the Terragrunt manager says so outright, limiting itself to registry sources and GitHub sources with SemVer refs. Also recorded: .terraform-version and .terragrunt-version are separate managers, so a tenv-pinned engine stays frozen unless they are switched on. Advanced re-estimated at ~76 hrs. No chapter flips to 🔄 — A3 is still ⬜, so nothing written has gone stale.

2026-08-16 — TID Ch 10 "Advanced Terraform topics" captured (10-advanced-topics), which is the chapter A1 has been citing without a note behind it. It is the book's grab-bag — naming schemes, a dynamically subnetted network module, provisioners, the external and local providers, checks and conditions, .tofu files, and when Terraform is the wrong tool — so it feeds A1 (which it largely owns), A2's condition half, E3, I3/I4 and B7. Two of its version claims did not survive checking, both against the local checkouts rather than the web. Its §10.5.1 NOTE dates provider-defined functions to "Terraform and OpenTofu 1.8.0"; OpenTofu shipped them in 1.7.0 (opentofu#1439), so the engines were not level and OpenTofu was ahead. And the winrm connection type its §10.3.1 documents without qualification is deprecated as of OpenTofu 1.12 (opentofu#3899) — it warns on every use, the stated reason being that the Go WinRM libraries are unmaintained, and the changelog says it is expected to error in 1.13, which git tag --contains confirms is still unreleased. Terraform has made no matching move, so this is a divergence that breaks Windows provisioning on an OpenTofu upgrade only. Three gaps between the chapter and the docs are folded into A1 rather than left in the note. The chapter's provisioner argument list omits environment, interpreter, working_dir and quiet on both local-exec and remote-exec, and environment is the difference between passing a secret and printing it. The external data source's failure contract — exit zero, or write to stderr and exit non-zero with stdout ignored — is in the provider docs and not in the chapter, as is the fact that Terraform Enterprise guarantees no language runtimes beyond shell utilities, which rules the whole technique out there. And direxists errors on a file path rather than returning false, and does not expand ~. The framing worth keeping from §10.6 is blocking versus reporting: precondition/postcondition stop the run, check only warns, and that is what makes a scoped data source doing a live HTTP health check safe on every plan — provided it carries depends_on, or it runs on the first plan before the infrastructure exists and reports a failure that means nothing. A2 gains that as its own item, and the four-mechanism ordering table (variable validation → precondition → postcondition → check) is in the chapter note.
