What it adds to B1: the five-category taxonomy (ad hoc scripts → configuration management → server templating → orchestration → provisioning), which reframes "Ansible vs Terraform" as a cross-category comparison rather than a head-to-head; the 10 → 15 servers worked example, which demonstrates declarativeness where every other source asserts it (edit Ansible's count and you get 25 servers; edit Terraform's and you get Plan: 5 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy); and the two consequences that follow — procedural code doesn't capture state, and procedural code resists reuse. Also the seven benefits of IaC including happiness, the bus-factor argument, and the honest sidebar that cross-cloud portability is a red herring (Terraform gives you one language and toolchain, not one configuration). Ch 1 of the book already answers B1's milestone, so no 🔄 — this is enrichment, and the taxonomy plus the 10→15 example are the obvious candidates if that chapter is ever expanded. ⚠️ The chapter is the most perishable in TUR, being a June-2022 landscape survey, so the note carries a long Version reckoning, all of it verified 2026-08-11 into iac-tool-comparison: Terraform's BSL relicensing (2023-08-10, all HashiCorp products incl. Packer) makes Table 1-4's "Source: Open" row wrong and needs an OpenTofu column; Terraform and Ansible now share an owner (IBM closed HashiCorp 2025-02-27 and has owned Red Hat since 2019), so "independent commercial backing" no longer separates them; Puppet repeated the pattern — Perforce restricted packages Nov 2024, Vox Pupuli forked OpenVox 2025-01-21; rkt was archived by CNCF (2019) and Apache Mesos retired to the Attic (2025), so two named runtimes in the chapter are dead; Terraform Cloud is HCP Terraform since 2024-04-22; and Pulumi's paid-only state locking is gone ("a basic file-based locking system is enabled by default for all DIY backends"), though the non-transactional-checkpointing limitation stands. B1 stays ✅.

2026-08-08 — TUR added as the site's second book, Ch 4 written (04-reusable-modules; reading log, page map and nine placeholder chapters under docs/books/tur/). Brikman, Terraform: Up & Running 3rd ed., O'Reilly, first release 2022-09-19. Referenced in I4 and I5 since the path was written; now actually captured. The Modules topic page gains its second book-length source and a comparison table, since TID Ch3 and TUR Ch4 split cleanly: read TUR for why each feature exists, TID for what the feature can do. TUR arrives at inputs, locals and outputs because its running example broke without them; TID enumerates the type system, validation, sensitive and registry publishing, none of which TUR covers — it never mentions a module registry at all. Three formulations worth keeping from TUR: "the input variables are the API of the module"; a variable is permission to change a value (the port/protocol constants became locals precisely so callers could not override them accidentally — the author-side twin of tut-module-use's NAT-gateway advice); and prefer separate resources to inline blocks in a module, argued from encapsulation rather than style, because a separate resource "can be added anywhere" while an inline block can only be added by the module that owns the resource. It is also the only source here with the promotion workflow end to end. One correction filed against the book: its "Git tags are as stable as a commit" is right against accidental drift and wrong against an adversary — a tag is a movable pointer, which is the supply-chain exposure I4 already records. ⚠️ And a version finding big enough for the resources table: TUR's running example is built on aws_launch_configuration, and AWS closed that path — no instance type released after 2023-01-01 works in one, and accounts created on or after 2024-10-01 cannot create one by any method (launch-configurations-eol, new research-cache entry). Not a style nit; the example is unrunnable for a reader with a recent account, though none of the teaching depends on it. Its aws_security_group_rule advice also now points at a superseded resource. I4 and I5 both stay ⬜.

2026-08-08 — The module block reference captured, closing the Modules docs section 8/8 (tf-block-module), inserted into I4's reference list. It has absorbed the old Module Sources page, so it is the exhaustive source catalogue. Things that live only here: // marks a sub-directory within a package with query parameters placed after it, and since Terraform extracts the whole package to disk, sibling modules inside it can reference each other by local path — which is what makes A8's module-split shim resolve; same source, different labels is legal, and is the multi-region workaround forced by I8's static provider association; absolute local paths are copied into the module cache rather than referenced in place; localterraform.com resolves against whichever HCP/TFE instance runs the config; HCP Terraform can authenticate to Git sources only with SSH keys, repeated four times and prominent nowhere; and ignore_nested_deprecations (1.15) is the consumer's opt-out from an author's deprecated warnings. ⚠️ The page contradicts itself on source ten lines apart — "You must specify a literal string… does not support template sequences or arbitrary expressions" against "The source attribute can reference constant input variables and local values". The second is current (1.15 dynamic sources); the first is stale text that survived a restructure, and the surrounding typo density fits a recently-rewritten page. Its depth "default is 1" also cannot be right — that would make every Git source shallow and break the SHA refs the same page documents, while the vendored go-getter takes its full-clone branch when depth < 1.

Correction to the 2026-08-08 depth entry below: that entry called the depth-rejects-SHA restriction undocumented. It is documented — on this page, under GitHub, Git and BitBucket alike: "you must specify a named branch or tag known to the remote repository. You cannot use raw commit IDs." The two how-to pages I had read describe depth with no caveat, which is what I generalized from. The finding itself stands, and so does the I4 callout: no page connects the restriction to the SHA-pinning advice, so the cost still only surfaces when the pin fails. Corrected in tf-modules-configuration, the I4 Git-sources callout, and cache/search/git-module-shallow-clone-vs-sha-pin.md.

2026-08-08 — A8's primary reference captured (tf-modules-refactoring, HCDocs "Refactor modules"), folded into A8's Refactor modules reference — the deep moved reference whose removal rules tut-move-config already quoted, with everything else new. The governing rule is about addressing: a bare address moves a resource as a whole and covers every instance, but an instance key on either side flips the block into instance mode. That single toggle is what makes count ↔ for_each ↔ neither migrations expressible, one moved block per index — and neither tut-count nor tut-for-each mentions moved at all, so the migration those tutorials walk through is a destroy-and-recreate as written. One case is already free: adding count to a resource that lacked it auto-proposes a move to index 0, while for_each needs a key you pick and a rename is never free — which is exactly the "8 added, 4 destroyed" tut-count measured. Two hard limits worth memorizing: cross-type moves exist but are provider-dependent (ask the provider docs, not the language docs), and a managed resource can never become a data block — that path is removed with lifecycle { destroy = false } plus a separate data block. The find worth keeping is the module-split shim, which solves something nothing else in the docs addresses: splitting a published module without breaking consumers. The original module is kept as a shim that calls the new modules and carries the moved blocks, so existing users upgrade in place. HashiCorp flags it as violating the closed-box rule and attaches the precondition — "all three of these modules are maintained by the same people and distributed together in a single module package" — so this licence does not extend to writing cross-module moved blocks against someone else's module. Scoping bounds it: addresses resolve relative to the module they are written in, and "a module may only make moved statements about its own objects and objects of its child modules" — down, never up or sideways. Finally, chaining (a→b, b→c) is the mechanism that makes retention make sense: each block covers consumers arriving from a different starting version, so a module's moved blocks accumulate like database migrations rather than as a courtesy changelog. A8 stays ⬜.

2026-08-08 — "Publish modules" captured, mostly to record where it isn't (tf-modules-publish), folded into I5's Module Development reference. Thinnest page in the Modules section and a third of it is ecosystem prose. The find is a navigation trap: the Configuration Language sidebar's Publish modules entry contains none of the publishing requirements — no repository-naming rule, no semver-tag rule, no structure requirement. Those live under the separate Registry Publishing top-level section, already captured in cache/search/module-repo-naming-convention.md, which now carries that pointer. A reader following this section's sidebar will not find them. Two things it does supply. The cleanest one-line case for a registry source over a Git one — "The alternative sources do not support the first-class versioning mechanism" — which is I4's registry-versus-Git argument compressed to a sentence. And the public registry's curation model, stated plainly: partner and community modules "both have their place… accessible to practitioners who can decide which modules best fit their requirements", i.e. it hosts, it does not vet, which is why tut-private-registry-add's review checklist exists. ⚠️ Its own example omits the version argument on the very page selling version constraints. Also worth keeping: it recommends the standard module structure even for Git-distributed modules so they can "be published on the registry at a later time" — structure as a migration path, not just tidiness. I5 stays ⬜.

2026-08-08 — I5 gains its design reference (tf-modules-composition, HCDocs "Best practices for composing modules"), inserted into I5's reference list with the rest renumbered. The most substantial page in the Modules section, and stricter than the enterprise guide it overlaps: keep the tree flat, one level of child modules, wire them with expressions, because "instead of a module embedding its dependencies… the module receives its dependencies from the root module, which can therefore connect the same modules in different ways to produce different results." The find worth keeping is that its headline pattern runs on the mechanism Ch 12 recorded as a footgun. Its conditional-creation advice — never write a module that detects whether something exists; declare an object(...) input naming only the attributes you need and let the caller pass a resource or a data source — works because "Terraform will allow any object that has at least these attributes", which is the same discard the Type Constraints page specifies and Ch 12 measured turning a caller's typo into a silent no-op. So structural typing and typo detection are one knob turned two ways: a deliberately partial object type is this pattern, an accidentally partial one is the footgun, and you cannot have both. OpenTofu's Warning: Object attribute is ignored makes it noisier for the pattern and safer against the typo. Two more keepers. Assumptions versus guarantees — an assumption is what must hold for a resource to be usable, a guarantee is what the rest of the configuration may rely on, and a precondition on an output is how a module asserts the latter (A2); an object type enforces shape while only a validation enforces content. And data-only modules, whose real trick is the last line of the page: give a join-network module the same outputs as a create-network module and the two become swappable, so promoting an environment from sharing infrastructure to owning it is a one-line source change — the most useful idea here for A7, and neither tut-organize-configuration nor tut-pattern-module-creation mentions it. Also a flat statement worth quoting back at people: Terraform "intentionally does not attempt to abstract over similar services offered by different vendors" because unification means a lowest common denominator; multi-cloud abstractions are yours to build from shared object types and matching output names. ⚠️ Two of its examples would fail validate — aws_ami takes owners (a list), not owner, and aws_subnet_ids no longer exists (docs 404 in the provider repo on main; aws_subnets returns 200) — plus its recordsets type requires ttl while the for-generated records omit it, which wants optional(number). I5 stays ⬜.

2026-08-08 — I8 gains the module-boundary reference, and a rule cited five times finally gets its reason (tf-modules-providers, HCDocs "Providers Within Modules"), inserted into I8's reference list with the rest renumbered; it is the page tf-meta-providers explicitly defers all module-author guidance to, and that forward reference is now resolved. The find that changes the story: every tutorial in the Modules collection explains "no provider blocks in a module" by the count/for_each/depends_on conflict. That is the later, mechanical enforcement, added in v0.13. The actual reason is a lifecycle one — a provider configuration is required to destroy a resource as well as create it, and Terraform stores in state which configuration last applied each resource, so "a provider configuration must always stay present in the overall Terraform configuration for longer than all of the resources it manages." A module holding both would remove them simultaneously, leaving state pointing at a configuration that no longer exists, and planning errors until it is reintroduced. That generalizes past modules: never delete a provider block while anything in state still references it. The inheritance asymmetry is the other keeper: default configurations inherit, aliased ones never do, and source/version requirements never do either — "especially important for non-HashiCorp providers", since a child omitting required_providers loses the source address and Terraform assumes hashicorp/<name>. And it states plainly what tut-for-each could only infer: the resource-to-provider association is static, so a count/for_each module call cannot vary providers per instance — multi-region fan-out is one module block per provider set, by design rather than omission. Also closes an open docs discrepancy: this page carries the corrected per-provider scoping ("overrides the default inheritance behavior for that provider") while tf-meta-providers still carries the un-narrowed "cancels the default behavior" wording that issue #35781 was filed against — the two reference pages disagree as they stand, and this one is right. Noted in both notes. Resolved in passing: tut-no-code-provisioning is not an exception to the rule, because a no-code module is the root module of the workspace HCP generates. I8 stays ⬜.

2026-08-08 — The standard module structure captured (tf-modules-structure), folded into I5's Module Development reference beside tf-modules-develop. The layout is a machine-readable convention, not a style preference — "Terraform tooling is built to understand the standard module structure and use that structure to generate documentation, index modules for the module registry" — which is why the registry's publishing bar requires it. Four rules that cannot be guessed from the file tree. A submodule's README.md is its public/private marker: "Any nested module with a README.md is considered usable by an external user. If a README doesn't exist, it is considered for internal use only", and this is "purely advisory" — so a private submodule stays private by staying undocumented, which is an odd incentive worth knowing about. The two source-address rules point opposite ways: a root calling its own nested module uses a relative path so Terraform treats it as the same package rather than downloading it again, while a block in examples/ must use the external address, because examples are expected to be copied into other repositories. Resources may be split across files; module blocks may not — nested calls stay in main.tf. And the root module "is expected to be opinionated" with nested modules as the escape hatch, which is the structural form of the 80%-of-use-cases rule. One real conflict recorded: this page says "The README doesn't need to document inputs or outputs … because tooling will automatically generate this", where tut-pattern-module-creation instructs you to document required inputs, optional inputs and outputs in the README. Reconciled — the registry generates those tables from the description arguments, so writing descriptions is documenting the interface and a duplicated table only goes stale; what the guide adds on top is advertising default values and never defaulting a variable whose right value differs on every use. Smaller: use commit-specific absolute URLs in a module README or the registry renders them against the wrong version (the mutable-reference problem of I4's Git ref one layer up), and the page's own minimal-module/ tree omits the LICENSE its prose says to always include. I5 stays ⬜.

2026-08-08 — I5's reference index captured (tf-modules-develop, HCDocs "Creating Modules" — the Develop modules overview), folded into I5's Module Development reference and nested under the docs course's Modules › Develop modules group. Short page, kept for one section: when not to write a module. "Over-using modules can make your overall Terraform configuration harder to understand and maintain"; a good module "raise[s] the level of abstraction by describing a new concept in your architecture"; and the test worth memorizing — "If you have trouble finding a name for your module that isn't the same as the main resource type inside it, that may be a sign that your module is not creating any new abstraction." Paired with tut-pattern-module-creation's complexity test, the target gets sharp: a module should be nameable in a phrase that is neither a paragraph nor a resource type. The two heuristics guard opposite failure modes, and together they qualify the tutorial's "aim for small and simple" — small is a scoping instruction, not a licence to wrap one resource. Noted honestly against it: terraform-aws-modules/ec2-instance/aws, which tut-module-use consumes, fails the naming test but not the substance test (at v6.4.0 it also creates an IAM instance profile, security group, EIP and EBS volumes), so the heuristic is a smell detector rather than a rule. Two smaller keeps: this is now the third official definition of "module" — container of resources used together, raising abstraction — and it is the only one that gives grounds to call a module a bad module, where tut-module's is the mechanism and tf-modules's is the unit. And its description of refactoring blocks, "reinterpret existing objects as if they had been created at the corresponding new addresses", is the most precise one-liner on moved anywhere in the docs — and explains why tut-move-config's plan still reported 3 to change, since reinterpreting where an object came from says nothing about whether its desired configuration still matches. I5 stays ⬜.

2026-08-08 — I4's primary reference captured (tf-modules-configuration, HCDocs "Use modules in your configuration"), inserted into I4's reference list and filed under the docs course's new Modules group. It is the consumer-side reference behind tut-module-use, and it covers five things that tutorial never mentions: Git ref selection, shallow clones, const-gated source expressions, -replace addressing inside modules, and removing a module without destroying it. The find worth keeping is an undocumented incompatibility, and it sharpens I4's own Git-sources callout: ?depth=1 — the documented way to avoid cloning a large repository's whole history — rejects a SHA ref outright. go-getter passes --depth together with --branch <ref> and git clone --branch accepts only a branch or tag, so a commit-shaped ref is caught by a regex and fails with "note that setting 'depth' requires 'ref' to be a branch or tag name". Version-gated against go-getter v1.8.6, the release Terraform 1.15.8 vendors per go.mod in the local checkout at the release commit. So immutable pin or shallow clone, not both — a third cost of SHA-pinning alongside the two update-bot gaps already recorded, and neither docs page connects them. Marked as read from vendored source rather than reproduced. Two smaller things: the const requirement is a timing argument, not a safety one (modules install at init, before plan-time evaluation exists), and it constrains the whole dependency chain rather than the syntax — a local composed from const variables is legal in the source position; and init honours what is already installed while -upgrade re-resolves the constraint, which with no module lock file is precisely where an untested version lands. ⚠️ The page's removal section is garbled four ways, including a closing link to the moved block reference at the end of a section about removed. Also worth noting against the tutorials: its example pins the VPC module at 6.0.1, a current major, where every page in the Modules tutorial collection still pins 3.x — the reference docs are maintained, the tutorials are not. Evidence: cache/search/git-module-shallow-clone-vs-sha-pin.md. I4 stays ⬜.

2026-08-08 — The language reference's Modules section index captured (tf-modules), inserted into I4's reference list ahead of Module Sources and creating a new Modules nav group under Configuration Language in the docs course (sidebar rung 1, positioned after Outputs as the source puts it). A thin index page, kept for two things. It defines a module differently from the tutorials, and both definitions are load-bearing: "a collection of resources that Terraform manages together" here, against tut-module's "a set of Terraform configuration files in a single directory". The structural one makes "every configuration is already a module" true; the semantic one is what makes the scoping question in I5 answerable — if a module is just a directory, "what belongs in it?" has no answer. And it supplies the Develop → Distribute → Provision frame the whole docs section is built on, which maps cleanly onto the tutorial collection just captured: Develop is tut-module-create / tut-module-object-attributes / tut-pattern-module-creation, Distribute is tut-module-private-registry-share / tut-private-registry-add, Provision is tut-module-use — and tut-move-config belongs to none of them, because refactoring is what happens after all three. Recorded for later capture: the section has eight pages and this is one, with Refactor modules and Publish modules already quoted secondhand (in tut-move-config and cache/search/module-repo-naming-convention.md) but not yet captured directly. Also noted: the page says "Every Terraform workspace includes configuration files in its root directory" where it means working directory — a loose use of a word that already means two other things (tf-state-workspaces). I4 stays ⬜.

2026-08-08 — E6 gains its named hands-on, and the Modules collection is closed at 10/10 (tut-no-code-provisioning, HCTut "Create and use no-code modules"). E6's no-code modules tutorial entry was already pointing at this tutorial by an alias URL with no notes behind it; it now has both, plus a worked-example callout in A6. The design rule that defines no-code: a workspace's entire change surface is (variable values) × (module version) — "You cannot directly apply configuration changes to existing no-code workspaces" — so anything the author did not expose is fixed until they ship a release, which turns tut-pattern-module-creation's minimize-inputs advice into a hard requirement. The find worth keeping is that it inverts the no-provider-blocks rule and, in doing so, explains why the rule ever existed: provider blocks are forbidden in modules because they conflict with count/for_each/depends_on (the constraint tut-for-each measured), and "Since users will not reference no-code modules in written configuration, there is no risk of this conflict." The prohibition was never about providers. Its cost is that HCP spawns a workspace per provision, so credentials must arrive automatically — a project-scoped variable set in the tutorial, dynamic credentials in the page's own next steps. Governance lives in Configure Settings: pinning which version no-code deploys (pushing a tag publishes but does not roll out), and converting a free-text variable into a dropdown of allowed values, which is input validation at the UI layer rather than in HCL. Also folded into A6: its RDS module is the shortest complete ephemeral + write-only example available — one ephemeral password feeding password_wo and value_wo, with both _version companions pointed at a single local so the database and its SSM copy rotate together. ⚠️ Its own 1.0.1 upgrade adds a variable with no default, forcing every consuming workspace to answer a prompt — the breaking way to make an additive change, and a live counterexample to tut-module-object-attributes, made worse by the fact that no-code users are by definition the people who don't write Terraform. Two things not to copy from the module: publicly_accessible = true on an RDS instance in a module meant to codify standards, and cidr_blocks = ["192.80.0.0/16"] described as an internal VPN when that is public address space (RFC 1918 is 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16). One counter-observation: this is the only maintained page in the collection — ephemeral resources (1.10), write-only arguments (1.11), postgres16 — where the other nine carry 2022-era pins. E6 and A6 both stay ⬜.

2026-08-08 — A8 gains its hands-on, and the Modules collection is now fully captured (tut-move-config, HCTut "Use configuration to move resources"), inserted at the head of A8's reference list, ahead of the reading, with a companion callout in I7. Ninth and last page of the collection, and the one that makes the other eight survivable on live infrastructure: extract a root resource into a local module and swap a hand-written module for a registry one, then reconcile with moved. The find worth keeping is that the fixed plan is not empty — 0 to add, **3 to change**, 0 to destroy.movedpreserves **identity, not configuration**, so swapping implementations is a move *and* a config change landing in one apply (the registry module's defaults differ), while extracting your own code is a clean move that printshas moved towith no action symbol at all. **A zero-destroy plan is not a zero-impact plan** — read the~lines. Also recorded: the un-movedplan's tell-tale reason line *"because X is not in configuration"*, which is what an address in state with no matching block looks like whether you deleted it or renamed it; module-levelmovedcascading to every address beneath it but **requiringterraform init** because the install key changes; andmovedblocks living in the **root** while naming in-module addresses on both sides, with[0]index keys taken from the destination module's internals. **Corrects the tutorial against its own reference docs on two points:** removing amovedblock is safe *"when you are maintaining private modules within an organization and you are certain that all users have successfully runterraform apply"*, not never — the absolute phrasing is the page's, and the real rule is about whose state still holds the old address; andmoved` needs v1.1, not the v1.3 the page sets as a prerequisite. This is also the block tut-count needed and never named. A8 and I7 both stay ⬜.

2026-08-08 — I5 gains its design theory, and the A4/A5 seam gets closed (tut-pattern-module-creation, HCTut "Module creation — recommended pattern"), inserted into I5's reference list with a new callout in A5. No code — it is an architecture guide from the Recommended Enterprise Patterns series, and it answers the question the rest of the collection skips: not which arguments should be variables, but which resources belong in the same module at all. The three scoping axes are the most portable idea in the collection: Encapsulation (group what always deploys together), Privileges (never span a segregation-of-duties boundary), Volatility (keep long-lived infrastructure out of a module that ships daily). The last two are blast-radius arguments, which is why they decide state boundaries as well as module boundaries — the same argument A7 makes one granularity up, and the principled version of what tut-organize-configuration demonstrates by destroying production from a dev file. Also worth keeping: its too-big heuristic ("If a module's function or purpose is hard to explain, the module is probably too complex"); the deliberate minimize inputs, maximize outputs asymmetry, since every input is a promise to maintain while an output is a value you already computed; the default test (var.vpc_id should never have one — if the right value differs on every use, a default is a trap); and the nesting trade, where an external child module can change behavior "with no changes to the parent's calling code or version" — an unpinned transitive dependency, I4's no-module-lock hazard one level deeper — while an embedded submodule is version-locked but unreusable. Its "avoid conditional expressions in an MVP" is sequencing advice, not a contradiction of tut-module-object-attributes: ship narrow, then add flexibility with optional() so the first consumer doesn't break. The find that closes an open thread: tut-private-registry-add left "approved module list" ambiguous, since curation enforces nothing; this page states the control outright — "With Sentinel … only modules from the private Terraform registry can be used" — so A4 publishes the set and A5 makes it binding, now written into A5 as a worked-policy suggestion. ⚠️ Its naming table gives terraform-azure-database, but the provider is azurerm (verified against the Registry API; no hashicorp/azure exists), and the same three-row table mixes an underscore with hyphens. Third page in this collection to fumble that convention. Diagram captured. I5 and A5 both stay ⬜.

2026-08-08 — A7 gains its hands-on (tut-organize-configuration, HCTut "Refactor monolithic Terraform configuration"), inserted into A7's reference list. Seventh page of the Modules collection and it contains no modules — it makes the case for them by showing what a flat configuration costs. The find worth keeping is its middle step, which demonstrates blast radius instead of describing it: a shared random_pet feeds both bucket names, so changing its length in dev.tf — a file containing nothing but development resources — destroys and recreates production. So splitting main.tf into dev.tf and prod.tf buys readability and nothing else, because the coupling lives in the reference graph, not the filesystem. That is the sharpest available answer to "we separated our environments into files". Three more: -target is named and dismissed as "risky and not a sustainable way to manage distinct environments" (so it stays an I7 recovery tool, not a layout strategy); converting one state into per-directory states needs state mv work, which the exercise dodges by destroying everything first; and the local backend relocates non-default workspace state to terraform.tfstate.d/<name>/terraform.tfstate. ⚠️ The page teaches CLI workspaces as environment separation, which A7's Workspaces CLI-vs-HCP reference exists to contradict — the language reference marks "Workspaces are not appropriate for system decomposition or deployments requiring separate credentials and access controls" as Important (tf-state-workspaces), and dev/prod is the canonical case of the second clause. Its own mitigation is "be aware of the workspace you are working in", which is human vigilance standing in for an access boundary. Read its decision rule as being about configuration duplication, not isolation, and A7's existing position stands unchanged. Page defects: resource counts wrong twice over (says 5, its own prose describes 9, the repo defines 15), and it instructs you to comment out a terraform block the current repo does not contain — that repo has no required_providers anywhere, so nothing is version-pinned in a tutorial about growing a project safely. A7 stays ⬜.

2026-08-08 — A4 gains the registry-curation hands-on (tut-private-registry-add, HCTut "Add public providers and modules to your private registry"), inserted into A4's reference list. A five-minute UI page with no configuration in it, but it forced a boundary worth drawing between A4 and A5. The tutorial says curation lets you "define a list of approved components", which reads like a control; the docs say the registry "stores a pointer", that the feature "designate[s] which public providers and modules are recommended", and that after removal "Users in the organization can still use the removed provider or module without changing their configurations." Two things follow that the page never states: curation does not change the source address (which is exactly why removal breaks nothing), and it enforces nothing at all — so "approved" is a label, and the actual control is Sentinel/OPA policy in A5, or the exact-pin discipline already noted in I4. Four omissions from the page also folded in: the permission is Manage Private Registry, not org ownership, so curation is delegable to a platform team; it is drivable through the Registry Providers/Modules APIs, which makes the approved list a reviewable artifact instead of hand-maintained drift; Terraform Enterprise must reach the Algolia search host as well as registry.terraform.io, or the search box silently returns nothing on an egress-filtered install; and no-code provisioning can be enabled on a curated public module (Standard/Premium), which is the E6 self-service story without authoring or maintaining a module — the tutorial's own Tip points only at building your own. Evidence appended to cache/search/hcp-private-registry-publishing.md. A4 stays ⬜.

2026-08-08 — A4 gains the private-registry hands-on (tut-module-private-registry-share, HCTut "Share modules in the private registry"), inserted into A4's reference list, with a companion callout in I5 since publishing is the step after authoring. First page in the Modules collection with no Community Edition path — it is HCP-only and almost entirely UI. Facts worth holding: the private-module address is <HOSTNAME>/<ORGANIZATION>/<MODULE_NAME>/<PROVIDER_NAME>; versions come from git release tags (semver x.y.z, optional v, non-matching tags ignored, ≥1 tag required to publish), so versioning is a release-process decision in the repo rather than an HCL argument; and registry scope differs by product — HCP shares within an organization, Terraform Enterprise within or across. The find worth keeping is the publishing-workflow split, which the tutorial renders as a variant toggle and never explains: tag-based auto-imports on tag push, while branch-based needs a Publish New Version click and a commit SHA, cannot re-use a version number, and is the only workflow supporting module testing — which makes it the one to pick once terraform test (A2) is part of shipping a module. Branch-based versions still pin to a commit, so this is not the mutable-ref hazard from I4's Git-sources callout. ⚠️ Two errors on the page, both self-contradicting: it states the address format with a spurious literal terraform/ segment, and it tells you to set the registry Module Name to the repository name (terraform-aws-s3-webapp), either of which would produce an address its own module block disagrees with. It does, however, state the terraform-<PROVIDER>-<NAME> convention correctly as a repository rule — so the collection contradicts itself, and tut-module is the page that has it wrong. Both variants were then read in full, which turned up a content asymmetry rather than another typo: the branch path removes the tag/release section outright, so a reader who picks that variant never meets the semver-tag rules at all, and the variant's own summary still claims they "created and versioned a GitHub repository" when the version was typed into HCP and the repo carries no tag. Read the tag variant first whichever workflow you intend to use. Evidence: cache/search/hcp-private-registry-publishing.md. A4 and I5 both stay ⬜.

2026-08-08 — Ch 13 written, I4 → ✅. Blends tf-modules, tf-modules-configuration, tf-block-module, tf-expr-version-constraints, tut-module, tut-module-use, tut-private-registry-add and TUR Ch 4 04-reusable-modules. The chapter's spine is that source decides everything else — whether version is legal, what pins the code, where it lands on disk, and whether an update bot can move it. The headline measurement: the same main.tf with version = "~> 4.1" ran 4.1.0 in one directory and 4.11.0 in a fresh one on the same machine, same day, no warning — because .terraform.lock.hcl records providers only and modules.json is never committed. Unpinned, the same module resolved 5.15.4, a whole major away. Second measured find: the init / init -upgrade asymmetry holds for Git refs as well as registry versions, which makes the mutable-tag exposure demonstrable — git tag -f -a v0.0.1 HEAD was invisible to plan, then flipped the installed module on the next init -upgrade with the config byte-identical. Third: the depth+SHA restriction, which tf-block-module had only inferred from vendored go-getter source, is now reproduced live — ?ref=<sha>&depth=1 fails with fatal: Remote branch <sha> not found in upstream origin (note that setting 'depth' requires 'ref' to be a branch or tag name), while the same address with a tag installs fine. Fourth, and it corrects a note: tut-module-use says local modules are symlinked into .terraform/modules/; on 1.15.8 that directory holds only modules.json, whose Dir points straight back at the relative source path. No copy, no symlink. The consequence the tutorial draws is still exactly right — a local-module edit is live with no re-init, and both callers move together (0 to add, 2 to change), which is the coupling versioned sources exist to break. 1.15 dynamic module sources measured end to end: a source composed from two const = true variables through a local installs at init, accepts -var and *.auto.tfvars, and without const fails with Only literal values and const variables can be evaluated during init. OpenTofu 1.12.4 diverges twice: it installs the same variable-composed source with or without const (early evaluation since 1.8), and has no modules command at all (OpenTofu has no command named "modules"). Also captured: a child module contributes provider constraints to your resolution (>= 5.83.0, ~> 6.0 from one module block), and terraform get installs modules without touching providers or the backend. Lab committed at labs/chapter13/ (three parts, lab 3 self-contained via a local git init repo built by setup.ps1/setup.sh). ⚠️ Emulator fidelity note: Floci does not persist bucket tags, so a tagged bucket replans the same tag change forever — an emulator gap, not Terraform. Next: I5 — Authoring modules.

2026-08-08 — I5 gains its interface-design hands-on (tut-module-object-attributes, HCTut "Customize modules with object attributes"), inserted into I5's reference list; its CORS half also folded into I3's "build a security-group module" entry, which had been unsourced. Nothing here contradicts Ch 12, so I3 stays ✅ — the tutorial illustrates the chapter rather than revising it. The page's own argument for objects is API evolution: optional attributes "make it easier for you to ship new module versions without changing the variables that module users need to define", which makes them the additive counterpart to the 1.15 deprecated mechanism already noted in I5. Two transferable finds. A shared prefix or suffix across flat variable names is an object hiding in the interface — terraform_managed_files becomes files.terraform_managed, the suffix having existed only because a flat namespace had nowhere to put the qualifier. And the module's type constraint should mirror the wrapped resource's own required/optional split (its cors_rules deliberately matches aws_s3_bucket_cors_configuration), or the module rejects valid configurations and defers errors to apply. Ch 12's silent-discard footgun has no better illustration than this page, and the page never mentions it: misspell www_path inside the files object and the object constraint drops the key, optional(string) fills null, the ternary falls back to the module's own www directory, and you ship a placeholder page with validate reporting Success!. ⚠️ Page defects beyond stale pins: its transcripts predate its own repo (Plan: 6 to add where a current clone gives 8, since the repo has since gained the ownership-controls and public-access-block resources), the "Clean up your infrastructure" section prints an apply that adds a resource under a terraform destroy heading, and the delete-these-four-variables snippet lists five. Its repo also omits the depends_on that learn-terraform-modules-create uses to order the bucket policy after the public-access block, leaving no graph edge between them — flagged as a graph reading, not a measured failure. One counter-observation worth keeping: hashicorp/dir/template 1.0.2 is still the latest published version (2020-07-29), so not every old pin is a stale pin. I5 stays ⬜.

2026-08-08 — I5 gains its first hands-on (tut-module-create, HCTut "Build and use a local module"), inserted into I5's reference list. The authoring counterpart to I4's two consumption tutorials, and its real content is interface design, not syntax: a value your module's purpose fixes is not a variable (its example is the ACL, which must be public-read for website hosting — the author-side twin of tut-module-use's NAT-gateway advice), and "outputs are the only supported way for users to get information about resources configured by the module". Also confirms no provider block in a module — tut-for-each already showed that's a hard constraint once count/for_each is on the module block, not the recommendation this page calls it. ⚠️ This one is not merely stale, it is broken. Two AWS defaults changed underneath it: new buckets are Bucket-owner-enforced so ACLs are disabled (400 AccessControlListNotSupported), and Block Public Access is on, so PutBucketPolicy rejects a Principal = "*" policy. The page's four-resource module trips both. Its example repo is already fixed and the rendered page is not — the repo carries aws_s3_bucket_ownership_controls, aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block with all four settings false, and depends_on chains, for six resources. Third page-vs-repo divergence in this collection and the only one where following the page fails outright. The find worth keeping beyond S3: those depends_on blocks are the legitimate kind, and they're now the counterexample in I1's "prefer an attribute reference" callout — the ACL consumes no attribute from either resource yet must be applied after both, so ordering-without-data-flow is exactly what depends_on is for. Smaller: the module outputs website_domain ("used to create Route 53 alias records") where website_endpoint is the browsable URL, so the tutorial's own destroy log prints a bare regional suffix with no bucket name in it — a live example of the output-choice judgment the page is teaching. Evidence: cache/search/s3-acl-bpa-defaults.md. I5 stays ⬜.

2026-08-08 — I4 gains its hands-on (tut-module-use, HCTut "Use registry modules in configuration", Community Edition variant), rewriting I4's registry-modules entry. Two registry modules produce 22 resources — the encapsulation benefit and the review problem in the same number. The constraint worth memorizing: "Terraform will not display module outputs by default" — a child module's outputs are readable inside the configuration but invisible at the CLI until the root module re-exports them, so module.MODULE_NAME.OUTPUT_NAME is a config-level reference, not a CLI-level one. The best line on the page is about variables, not modules: you should not declare a variable for a value your organization has already decided (its example is enable_nat_gateway) — a variable is a permission to vary, and declaring one hands the decision to the caller. The tutorial then does exactly that. Also confirms count on a module block (the tut-for-each two-axis mechanism, seen here in its plain form) and that local modules are symlinked into .terraform/modules/, so edits land without re-init or terraform get. ⚠️ Staleness checked rather than assumed, and the result cuts the other way from tut-count: the pins are years old (provider ~> 4.49.0, vpc 3.18.1 vs. current 6.6.1, ec2-instance 4.3.0 vs. current 6.4.0) but every argument and output the tutorial uses is still declared at vpc v6.6.1 and ec2-instance v6.4.0 — verified against the tagged source 2026-08-08. So this one is a version bump, not a rewrite; the three bumps are coupled, since ec2-instance 6.4.0 alone forces AWS provider >= 6.37. Its hardcoded ami-0c5204531f799e0c6 is the part not to copy (ami_ssm_parameter exists at v6.4.0). Rendered page vs. example repo disagree on the instance name, and here the page is correct. Cache updated: cache/search/aws-modules-current-versions.md gains the ec2-instance row and the surviving-interface check. I4 stays ⬜.

2026-08-08 — I4 gains its conceptual opener (tut-module, HCTut "Modules overview" — first page of the Modules tutorial collection, new Modules nav group under HashiCorp Terraform Tutorials). Inserted at the head of I4's reference list, renumbering the rest. It is a no-code page, so what it buys is vocabulary and motivation: every configuration is already a module (the directory you run commands in is the root module; one reached through a module block is a child module), Terraform reads exactly one directory unless a module block sends it elsewhere, and the strongest case for modules is security, not tidiness — object storage has too many options to get right repeatedly, so encode the correct settings once. Found an error in the source page: its best-practices list says "Name your provider terraform-<PROVIDER>-<NAME>", but that three-part name is the module repository convention (terraform-google-vault, terraform-aws-ec2-instance); providers use terraform-provider-<NAME>. Verified against Publishing Modules and folded into I5's Module Development reference with the rest of the registry's publishing bar (public GitHub repo, standard module structure, ≥1 semver tag). Cached at cache/search/module-repo-naming-convention.md. Glossary gains root module, child module, no-code ready module. Topic status unchanged — I4 stays ⬜ until a chapter exists.

2026-08-05 — Ch 12 written, I3 → ✅. Blends the dynamic-blocks and Type Constraints references, TID Ch 3 §3.6 and Ch 4 §4.10, and the splat/conditional notes. The chapter's spine is that a type constraint is a conversion step, not a gate — it can convert a value, silently discard part of it, or reject it, and only rejection is loud. The find worth keeping: an object(...) constraint deletes undeclared attributes by design, so a caller's typo becomes a no-op with Success! from terraform validate. Measured at a module boundary on 1.15.8. Refined during review: the discard is always silent, but whether it hurts depends on optional() — misspell a required attribute and Terraform rejects the call by name, misspell an optional() one and its default fills the hole so the mistake ships. The footgun needs both halves of the chapter: the object constraint removes the attribute, optional() removes the evidence. OpenTofu 1.12.4 catches it and Terraform never does (Warning: Object attribute is ignored), but the boundary is narrower than it first appeared — OpenTofu warns for module calls and variable defaults and stays silent for .tfvars, which is where much real input arrives. Second measured find: optional() and a variable default disagree about null. A variable default covers absence only and keeps an explicit null; an optional() default covers both, always, behaving like nullable = false with no opt-out — which is exactly why the docs can promise optional() is never null in the receiving module. Third: dynamic "lifecycle" and dynamic "nonexistent" give the same error, so the meta-argument rule is invisible to anyone who doesn't already know it. Also verified against the AWS provider at tag v6.54.0: the canonical dynamic "ingress" security-group example is one the provider now advises against, recommending aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule with for_each instead — resource iteration (I1) displacing block iteration for that resource type, though dynamic remains the only answer wherever a provider hasn't promoted its nested blocks. A fourth find came out of the lab, once the provider would load: generated blocks do not keep declaration order, and the two ways they lose it are different. Through a provider set (aws_security_group.ingress) rules declared 443, 80, 5432 come back 80, 443, 5432 — the provider's order, not yours, and not predictable from the input. Through a map (for_each over lifecycle rules) they come back in sorted key order, deterministically, every run — logs, tmp, everything declared renders everything, logs, tmp. So a map-driven dynamic block is the one whose output order you can state in advance, which is Ch 10's for_each-over-count argument one level down. Also measured: optional() defaults are visible in the plan (rules omitting cidr_blocks got the default, all three omitting protocol got "tcp"), and the zero-or-one toggle is an in-place update (0 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy) rather than a replacement. Lab committed at labs/chapter12/ (four parts); all four ran, and Parts A and B were then re-run under OpenTofu 1.12.4 with no divergence — same blocks, same defaults, same set reordering, same sorted-key map order, so block generation is tool-independent and the reordering is the provider's doing rather than either CLI's. That re-run also corrected a line in Ch 2: .terraform.lock.hcl is keyed by the fully-qualified provider address, so Terraform's lock names registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws while OpenTofu wants registry.opentofu.org/hashicorp/aws from the identical source — running tofu against Terraform's lock fails with Inconsistent dependency lock file before it plans anything. Ch 2 had said the lock file "behave[s] the same in both tools"; the format and purpose do, a written lock file does not transfer, and the two registries even resolved ~> 6.0 to different patches on the same day (6.58.0 vs 6.57.1). Facts cache: docs/research-cache/dynamic-blocks-facts.md. Next: I4 — Using modules.

2026-08-03 — Ch 11 written, I2 → ✅. Blends the lifecycle reference, the State-collection tutorial, TID Ch2 §2.7.2 and Ch5 §5.7, the resource/removed/data block references, terraform_data, and the OpenTofu divergences. The chapter's spine is the state fact: lifecycle rules live only in the configuration, except create_before_destroy, so prevent_destroy dies with the block that carries it. Measured end to end in labs/chapter11/lab1 — the destroy is rejected with Error: Instance cannot be destroyed, then deleting the block plans 1 to destroy with no error and applies. A documented claim was corrected by measurement: the docs say a dependency that inherits create_before_destroy cannot override it to false. It can be written, and Terraform silently discards it — no error, no warning, only ForcedCBDTransformer: forcing create_before_destroy on for … in a trace. Identical under OpenTofu 1.12.4. The note, the topic page and this page's I2 callout were all corrected. Also measured on 1.15.8: propagation writing create_before_destroy = true into the state of a bucket that never declared it; +/- versus -/+ and the (deposed object 6fc41790) line; a fixed-name DynamoDB table failing create-first with ResourceInUseException while leaving state clean; ignore_changes holding a drifted tag with 0 changed while config and state disagree; ignore_changes = all valid but both [all] and ["all"] errors; replace_triggered_by firing on an in-place update of its terraform_data, and rejecting a variable with "Only resources, count.index, and each.key may be used"; and dynamic prevent_destroy failing on Terraform with "Variables not allowed" while validating on OpenTofu. Lab committed at labs/chapter11/ (five parts). Next: I3 — Dynamic blocks & complex types.

2026-08-03 — I2 gains its hands-on (tut-resource-lifecycle), inserted into I2's reference list — one exercise per rule on an EC2 instance plus security group, from the State tutorial collection (a collection this project had not touched before; new nav group). What it adds over the reference page is all terminal output. prevent_destroy fails at plan with no override flag, and Terraform's own suggested escape is -target — one of the few places HashiCorp recommends it. create_before_destroy flips the plan symbol from -/+ destroy and then create replacement to +/- create replacement and then destroy; read literally, the symbol is the operation order, and nothing else in the plan announces CBD is active (confirmed at tag v1.15.8, internal/command/jsonformat/plan.go:688). The apply log then shows the prior object being destroyed under a deposed key — current Terraform renders it (deposed object 940b3833) (internal/command/views/hook_ui.go, v1.15.8), where the tutorial shows an older bare-parenthesis form. The unstated cost of CBD: a deposed object left behind by a failed apply stays in state and is destroyed by the next plan. Neither the reference nor the tutorial says so. (Corrected 2026-08-03 while reviewing Ch 11: it does not show in terraform state list, which prints only current objects — use terraform show -json and read deposed_key.) For ignore_changes the tutorial manufactures real drift with aws ec2 create-tags, then shows apply reporting 0 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed while state refreshes to the drifted value — the rule suppresses the plan to update, not the read, so config and state legitimately disagree until a replacement. It also accidentally demonstrates the propagation from the previous entry: the instance depends on the security group, so CBD was enabled on the security group too, invisibly — invisible only because that group is updated in-place. Had the port change forced it to be replaced, create-first would have collided on the unique name. Written up as an I2 experiment. ⚠️ Tutorial targets Terraform 0.14 and AWS provider 3.26.0, and typos drift_example as Drift_example in one code block. I2 stays ⬜.

2026-08-03 — I2's primary reference captured (tf-meta-lifecycle), inserted at the head of I2's reference list and closing the last uncaptured meta-argument page. The find that reframes the topic: "Except for create_before_destroy, Terraform does not explicitly record a resource's lifecycle rule to state." That is the mechanism behind the already-noted prevent_destroy caveat — the guard lives in the config, so deleting the block deletes the guard — and it makes I7's removed block with destroy = false the only real protection. The find that is new: create_before_destroy propagates along dependency edges and cannot be switched back off — enable it on A and Terraform enables it on everything A depends on, writes it to state, and rejects an override to false because that would imply a graph cycle. Confirmed in source at tag v1.15.8: ForcedCBDTransformer (internal/terraform/transform_destroy_cbd.go) runs in the plan graph builder, and state v4 carries create_before_destroy per instance (internal/states/statefile/version4.go:719), with the field comment giving the reason — destroy ordering must still work after the config is gone. Since CBD is opt-in precisely because some object types cannot coexist with their replacement, propagation can push an upstream resource into a mode it cannot support, from an edit you made elsewhere. Also captured: ignore_changes is honored on create and ignored only on update (which is what makes the AMI case work), takes relative addresses with index notation (tags["Name"]), and cannot target a meta-argument; the three replace_triggered_by trigger conditions, where resource/instance references watch a planned action but an attribute reference watches a value; and the precondition/postcondition ordering guarantees — preconditions run before argument evaluation and after count/for_each, a failed postcondition blocks every downstream resource. Unusually for this docs set, the applicability data holds up: lifecycle has no Supported constructs matrix at all, and the per-rule lines scattered through the page agree with tf-block-data. I2 stays ⬜ — the note is a reference, not the chapter.

2026-08-02 — I8's providers reference captured (tf-meta-providers), inserted under I8 as the HCDocs "providers" reference and closing one of the three meta-arguments the 2026-08-01 entry listed as uncaptured. The find is a reframing, not a fact: the map is a remap, not an injection. Keys are configuration names used inside the child, values are configuration names in the parent, so providers = { aws = aws.usw2 } rewrites what the child's own aws means rather than handing it something new. The child keeps writing plain aws_* resources with no provider argument, and the caller decides which region they land in — which is why the argument exists: you retarget a module without editing it. Neither tf-meta-arguments nor tf-provider-block says this; both describe the argument as "passing configurations in". Two applicability facts: providers is optional only while the child declares no configuration_aliases (declaring one makes it mandatory, since non-default configurations are never inherited), and it applies to Stacks' component and removed blocks — the index page's table lists module alone, a fourth instance of the lower-bound rule. The defect: this page still says supplying providers "cancels the default behavior" so the child "only has access to the provider configurations you specify" — the exact un-narrowed wording terraform#35781 was filed against. The correction landed on Providers Within Modules and never propagated here, so the docs now disagree with themselves; per-provider is the accurate reading, and the I8 warning box already said so. Folded into providers and meta-arguments-lifecycle. I8 stays ⬜; Providers Within Modules is still uncaptured and is where the module-author guidance lives.

2026-08-01 — I1 gains the for_each hands-on lab (tut-for-each), inserted into I1's reference list. The thing worth the whole tutorial: count and for_each are illegal in the same block, and this is the only HashiCorp page that shows the way around it — move the count resource into a module, put for_each on the module block, so the two multiply without sharing a block. Neither reference page mentions it. It comes with a constraint stated in a bare Note: a module using count/for_each cannot declare a provider block and must inherit from its caller, so the trick buys multiplication but not multi-provider fan-out — which is exactly the gap OpenTofu's core-language provider for_each fills and Terraform confines to Stacks. Both now on meta-arguments-lifecycle, along with the chaining-vs-re-iterating distinction (this tutorial re-iterates var.project across five blocks and correlates with [each.key], rather than chaining). Two statements on the page are wrong, both re-verified locally on TF 1.15.8: "the for_each argument also supports lists" — for_each = ["a","b"] fails with "must be a map, or set of strings, and you have provided a value of type tuple"; and "each.key is the index of the item in the collection" for sets — it is the member string, the instance address is ["alpha"], and each.key == each.value. That second sentence is the one a reader is most likely to internalize, since it is the only place either page explains sets in terms of each.key. Also recorded: its own Note warns against for_each for independently-lifecycled environments and its example then puts dev and test in one configuration, so one destroy takes both (75 destroyed); and it re-addresses everything again (74 added / 39 destroyed) without mentioning moved — the second consecutive tutorial to teach refactoring without state refactoring. One corroboration: this page uses the correct security_group_id for the same module at the same pin where tut-count's page uses this_security_group_id, confirming that one is a stale rendering rather than a real API difference. I1 stays ⬜.

2026-08-01 — I1's for_each reference captured (tf-meta-for-each), completing the pair with tf-meta-count. Folded into the same I1 reference as tf-meta-count and a new for_each section on meta-arguments-lifecycle. Most of the page is capability count has no equivalent for: chaining (for_each = aws_vpc.example, where each.value is a whole upstream object — the docs argue for it on coupling, since it "tells Terraform to expect the instance keys for both to always change together", not on brevity), the sensitive-value ban (an error, not a warning: keys are "always disclosed in UI output", so a secret can never be an instance key — escape is toset([for k, v in local.map : k])), and the refusal to implicitly convert lists or tuples to sets, which is why toset() is mandatory and is the one place the docs' type story is strict. Existing correction reinforced: the page's "accepts a map or a set of strings" is still incomplete — the implementation also accepts objects, so for_each = { a = "1", b = "2" } needs no tomap(), and the page's own chaining section calls a for_each resource "a map of objects" when it is an object. Already recorded from conditional-branch-evaluation; now attributed to the page that states it. New find: this page's Supported constructs list omits action and import — both described in its own examples — doubling the count page's single omission and reinforcing the lower-bound rule on the topic page. Divergence sharpened: the page lists provider under Stack configuration blocks, so Terraform does support provider iteration, just not in ordinary modules. ot-provider-for-each updated — the OpenTofu difference is the configuration surface, not the feature. Glossary gained each.key/each.value and for_each chaining. I1 stays ⬜; lifecycle, provider, and providers remain uncaptured.

2026-08-01 — I1 gains the count hands-on lab (tut-count, HCTut "Manage similar resources with count" — the same tutorial tf-meta-arguments links to as /tutorials/0-13/count). Inserted into I1's reference list. Contributes two patterns the reference page never shows: the count is a product, not a literal (var.instances_per_subnet * length(module.vpc.private_subnets), so adding a subnet scales the fleet), and modulo round-robins instances across buckets (count.index % length(...)) — a clean illustration of where for_each's criterion does not apply, since these distinct values can be derived from an integer index. Both now on meta-arguments-lifecycle. The find: the exercise is a refactor, and its own apply output reads "8 added, 0 changed, 4 destroyed" — renaming aws_instance.app_a → aws_instance.app rebuilt everything, because a resource address is its identity in state. moved blocks (TF 1.1+) are the fix and the tutorial requires 1.2+, so they were available; it never mentions them. Teaching a refactor without the refactor-safety tool leaves the reader thinking a rename normally costs a rebuild. Two currency defects recorded: the page's elb_http snippet references this_security_group_id, an output name dropped in security-group module v4.0 while the page pins v4.9.0 — its example repo is correct, only the rendered snippet is stale, so the tutorial works if you clone and breaks if you copy-paste; and every pin is majors behind (AWS provider ~> 4.22 vs 6.x, vpc 3.14.2 vs 6.6.1, security-group 4.9.0 vs 6.0.0, elb 3.0.1 vs 4.0.2). Verified against the module's outputs.tf at v4.9.0, the example repo's main.tf, and the Registry API; cached at cache/search/aws-modules-current-versions.md. Also flagged: its aws_instance.app.*.id is the legacy splat (tf-expr-splat). I1 stays ⬜.

2026-08-01 — I1's count reference captured (tf-meta-count). Closes a dangling gap: the page had been fetched on 2026-07-10 and quoted inside tf-meta-arguments for its two corrections, but never written up, so the addressing rules lived nowhere. Folded into I1's meta-argument reference and into a new count section on meta-arguments-lifecycle. The find: the page's Supported constructs list omits action — while the same page's opening paragraph and one of its own use cases both describe count in an action block. That makes three mutually inconsistent applicability lists across two pages (index vs count on data, index vs depends_on on five block types, count vs itself on action), so the working rule is now "treat every applicability list in these docs as a lower bound", and the page body beats the page's own summary list. Also recorded as things the page never says, both of which matter more than most of what it does say: count keys instances by position (delete a middle element and everything after it re-indexes — TID Ch4 §4.8 is where this is actually taught), and a count block reference is a tuple, not a list (conditional-branch-evaluation, TF 1.15.8). The page does explicitly endorse count = cond ? 1 : 0 as the conditional-creation idiom, which is the gap OpenTofu 1.11's enabled fills. action blocks remain uncaptured anywhere in these notes. I1 stays ⬜.

2026-08-01 — I1 gains the depends_on hands-on lab (tut-dependencies, HCTut "Create resource dependencies"). Inserted into I1's reference list, ahead of the DAG-inspection practice item. The concepts were already covered by tf-meta-depends-on and dependency-graph; what the tutorial adds is evidence you can read. Its apply log shows two EC2 instances starting together while an Elastic IP waits on only one of them, which makes the log itself a free dependency check: interleaved Creating... lines mean Terraform believes those nodes are independent. Captured as a fourth inspection route on dependency-graph, alongside terraform graph, the state file, and reading the config. It also demonstrates depends_on on a module block with a two-element list — the case the reference page names but never shows — and names a second cost the reference page omits: longer apply wall-clock from serialized work, distinct from the plan degradation (spurious known after apply, over-replacement) that is the usual quote. Both costs are now tabulated on the topic page. Currency trap flagged: the tutorial pins AWS provider ~> 4.17.1 and writes vpc = true on aws_eip; that argument was removed in provider v6.0.0 ("Remove vpc—it is no longer supported. Use domain instead"), so the block breaks if copied into an unpinned config. Verified against the provider's own v6 upgrade guide and current resource docs; cached at cache/search/aws-eip-vpc-argument-removed.md. I1 stays ⬜ — a lab note is not a written chapter.

2026-07-23 — TID Ch6 (State management) reading note captured (06-state-management) — the primary source for the not-yet-written B9 (state fundamentals) and much of I6/I7. Covers: why state exists (real-world linkage / reduced complexity / performance / state-only resources), the three storage properties (resiliency/security/availability), the tfstate JSON field-by-field (version vs terraform_version, serial, lineage, resources/outputs/check_results) with the sensitive-in-plaintext and root-outputs-only rules, backends (built-in, local = dev-only, partial config + -backend-config, cloud block, -migrate-state, CLI-vs-HCP workspace overloading), safe state manipulation (moved 1.1 / removed 1.7 first → state rm/replace-provider → hand-edit last), the four drift categories and their fixes, terraform_remote_state (root outputs, defaults, security-vs-data-source tradeoff), and the state-only providers (random/time/null/terraform_data). Currency correction folded in: the book's Table 6.1 "S3 requires DynamoDB for locking" is stale — S3 native locking (use_lockfile) landed in TF 1.10 / OpenTofu 1.10, DynamoDB deprecated (see version-facts, feature-history); flagged in the chapter's version callout. Glossary gained lineage, serial, State backend, Partial backend config, S3-native locking, State drift, moved/removed blocks, State-only provider, keepers/triggers. Topics backlog: state now has three sources (promotable once TUR's state chapters land); refactoring gains §6.5. Next book chapter: B9 → docs/book/ch09 blending this note with the HCDocs state notes.

2026-07-29 — HCDocs "State" overview captured (tf-state) — the reference cited by B9 step 2 now has a note behind it. Three things the book treatment doesn't state as sharply: state's primary purpose is storing bindings between remote objects and resource instances (not the file's contents); the one-to-one mapping rule is an invariant Terraform only guarantees while it does the creating and destroying, so terraform import and terraform state rm hand the invariant back to the operator; and terraform output -json / terraform show -json are the supported parse targets for external software, since the state format itself is explicitly allowed to change between versions. Glossary gained One-to-one mapping rule. Nav gained a State group mirroring the docs sidebar, which also relocated the previously-flat removed block reference note into it. Topics backlog state now names four sources. Status unchanged — B9 stays ⬜ until the chapter is written.

2026-07-29 — HCDocs "Purpose of Terraform State" captured (tf-state-purpose) — the why-state-exists argument behind B9 step 1. One reason here is absent from TID Ch6 §6.1, which otherwise covers the same ground: state retains each resource's most recent dependency set, and it does so for destroy ordering. Delete a resource from the configuration and the edges that would order its destruction are deleted with it, so the order must come from state. The rejected alternative (a built-in per-resource-type ordering hierarchy) would need Terraform to know ordering semantics for every resource in every provider and across providers. Also new: the AWS-tag mapping was a shipped early prototype, not a hypothetical; the attribute cache is "the most optional feature" of state; and -refresh=false + -target make "the cached state the record of truth", which silently disables detection of the accidental-manual drift category from Ch6 §6.6. Glossary gained Retained dependencies. When B9's chapter is written, the dependency-retention reason should join Ch6's four. Status unchanged — B9 stays ⬜.

2026-07-29 — HCDocs "State Storage and Locking" captured (tf-state-backends) — the State-section counterpart to the Backends reference in I6 step 2. A backend has exactly two responsibilities: store state, and provide a locking API, with locking optional and not universally supported. The operationally useful guarantee: a non-local backend "will not persist the state anywhere on disk" — except when writing to the backend fails, in which case Terraform drops state locally to avoid data loss and the operator must push it manually once fixed. That exception is worth knowing for A6, since it leaves a plaintext state file on a machine the guarantee otherwise excludes. Also records the state push guards (differing lineage, higher serial, both -force-able) and cross-references TID Ch6 §6.3.3, where the lineage check was traced in the 1.15.8 source and found narrower than this page's plain "Terraform will not allow this" — empty existing state is always overwritable, a missing lineage on either side is allowed, and the check never runs during a routine plan/apply. Doc-staleness flagged: the page still lists terraform taint among working commands, deprecated since v0.15.2 in favour of apply -replace, with no deprecation notice in the 1.15.8 CLI help. The state push/pull half also serves I7. Status unchanged — I6 and I7 stay ⬜.

2026-07-29 — HCDocs "Refactor Terraform state" captured (tf-state-refactor) — the cross-configuration refactor guide, folded into A8 step 1 alongside the module-refactoring reference it complements. moved blocks relocate addresses inside one state; this page is about moving resources between state files, which moved cannot do. The recommended path is now removed + import blocks (1.7+), with terraform state mv -state/-state-out (1.0+) explicitly labelled "a legacy command" carrying "some risk of corrupting your remote state". Also captured: the four refactor triggers, the three grouping properties (volatility, stateful-vs-stateless, team ownership), the three dynamic-reference options ranked data source → tfe_outputs → terraform_remote_state (the same ranking tf-remote-state-data justifies on security grounds), and the six-step verification where empty plans on both sides are the proof. Two flaws in the page's own example are flagged in the note: it writes the state backup to terraform.tfstate.backup, the filename the local backend uses for its own automatic backup, and the apply transcript imports a different instance ID than the rest of the page. The destroy = false requirement on the removed block is cross-linked to tf-block-removed, where it was verified on 1.15.6 — omit it in a refactor and the resource you are migrating gets destroyed. Status unchanged — A8 stays ⬜.

2026-07-30 — HCDocs "Remove a resource from state" captured (tf-state-remove) — the forget-without-destroying how-to, folded into I7 step 2 and its removed danger callout. Two constraints this page adds that no other note had. from rejects instance keys — "aws_instance.example[1]" is not accepted, so a count/for_each resource is forgotten in full or not at all. And removal is not undone by editing configuration: resuming management requires an import. Also the reason HashiCorp prefers the block over terraform state rm, stated explicitly for the first time in the docs we've captured: the removed block goes through plan, so the operation can be previewed; state rm mutates state immediately. Worth noting this is the one State page that gets the destroy semantics right on first reading — it never claims removed is inherently non-destructive, unlike the block reference itself (tf-block-removed). Status unchanged — I7 stays ⬜.

2026-07-30 — HCDocs "State Locking" captured (tf-state-locking) — the page tf-state-backends defers to, cited by I6 step 2 since the path was written and now backed by a note. Sharpens three things the path stated loosely. Locking covers every operation that could write state, not just apply. It is silent on success — "you do not see any message that it happens" — so no output is not evidence that no lock was taken. And acquisition failure is fatal: "if state locking fails, Terraform does not continue." The force-unlock callout was scoped tighter to match the docs: it is for your own lock after automatic unlocking failed, not for clearing a colleague's stuck run, and the lock ID is a nonce for one acquisition, so a stale ID will not release the current lock. The page never mentions -lock-timeout, so the note pairs it with the terraform plan command reference (verified 2026-07-30) — under contention the choice is three-way: fail now, retry for a duration, or skip the lock. Status unchanged — I6 stays ⬜.

2026-07-30 — HCDocs "Workspaces" captured (tf-state-workspaces) — the CLI-workspaces page cited by A7 step 2, and already a primary source behind the workspaces topic page; now traceable to a note of its own. The fact worth extracting is one neither the topic page nor TID Ch6 had: the docs enumerate the backends that support named workspaces — AzureRM, Consul, COS, GCS, Kubernetes, Local, OSS, Postgres, Remote, S3. http and oci are absent, so "remote backend" and "supports multiple states" are separate properties, and a backend choice does not settle the workspace question. Folded into A7 step 2 and into the topic page's state-layout section. Also noted: the page's Current Workspace Interpolation heading is pre-0.12 vocabulary — terraform.workspace is a named value, usable bare in any expression, and the page's own count example uses it that way. Status unchanged — A7 stays ⬜.

2026-07-30 — HCDocs "Backend block configuration overview" captured (tf-backend-configure) — the first reference I6 step 2 names, and the configuration counterpart to tf-state-backends. Three things folded into the path. The three block limitations, of which "a backend block cannot refer to named values" is the one that shapes real setups — it is why partial configuration exists, and OpenTofu 1.8 lifts it (ot-early-eval-backend), making this a live Terraform/OpenTofu divergence rather than a version lag. The leak path stated at the source: backend config is written in plaintext to .terraform/terraform.tfstate and captured into every plan file, which yields a consequence the path had not recorded — a saved plan applies with its own frozen backend config, so short-lived credentials inside it can expire before the apply. And the documented *.backendname.tfbackend filename convention for -backend-config files, which 06-state-management §6.4 shows as backend.tfvars; both work, but .tfvars misfiles backend input as variable input. Nav gained a Backends group mirroring the docs sidebar. Status unchanged — I6 stays ⬜.

2026-07-30 — HCDocs "local backend" captured (tf-backend-local) — first of the per-backend pages, folded into I6 step 2. Confirms the default backend locks (through system APIs), which matters because tf-state-locking says locking is optional and backend-specific. Two arguments only: path, and workspace_dir — the knob behind the terraform.tfstate.d layout workspaces traces to the source. The section worth knowing is the legacy one: -state / -state-out / -backup apply to the local backend (and to no backend block at all), and setting them overrides workspace-based state filename selection entirely — with all three set, terraform workspace select no longer changes which file is read or written. Also two defaulting traps: -state without -state-out overwrites the input file, and -state without -backup turns the state filename into a backup prefix (-backup=- disables backups). HashiCorp recommends against all of it "even if you are running Terraform in automation". Status unchanged — I6 stays ⬜.

2026-07-30 — HCDocs "Remote State" captured (tf-state-remote) — the conceptual page behind I6 step 1, folded in there, with its one genuinely new idea folded into A4. Local state makes two separate things a human responsibility, freshness and exclusion; the remote store fixes the first and locking the second, which is why the page keeps them in separate sections. Its delegation framing is the useful one: remote state is a read-only sharing channel between configurations "without relying on any additional configuration store" — the same team-ownership split tf-state-refactor lists as a refactoring trigger, seen from the consuming side, and the reason tf-remote-state-data's whole-snapshot warning matters. New to the path: HCP's run queue is not a state lock. A state lock covers one command and is released when it ends, so two people can each plan against the same state and the second apply invalidates the first's reviewed plan; HCP "detect[s] attempts to create a new plan when an existing plan is already awaiting approval, by queuing Terraform operations in a central location", holding the whole plan-then-approve cycle. S3 with use_lockfile gives the lock, not the queue.
